title: Mobile Financial Services (MFS) for Online and In-Store Purchases: Users' Experiences and Scam Vulnerabilities
authors: Md. Khaled Amin; Vichayanan Rattanawiboonsom; Md. Kamrul Bari
venue: IGI Global eBooks
abstract: This study aims to explore the usage patterns, users' experiences, and scam vulnerabilities associated with Mobile Financial Services (MFS) in developing countries like Bangladesh. While the notion of m-wallet is getting much more popular, it also poses some risk of digital fraud. The study used primary data collected from one hundred and ten users employing a standard questionnaire. The link to the questionnaire, which was designed with MS Form, was distributed among the users by email and instant messaging service. The study highlights several challenges and scams that may deter users from using the service. To fully use the potential of MFS technology, it is essential to address the challenges by incorporating robust security measures, designing user-friendly interfaces, and providing widespread education. This study also stresses the urgent need for stronger authentication protocols, enhanced data encryption, and comprehensive user education initiatives to secure m-wallet platforms that support sustainable digital financial inclusion in strengthening the economy.

title: AI Fraud Detection, Privacy Safeguards, and Continued Use of Mobile Financial Services in Bangladesh
authors: Poushia Hossen Megha; Asura Jaman Osru; Md Wahidul Bari; Kazi Abdul Mannan
venue: Journal of Formal and Informal Sectors
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being incorporated into financial-sector risk management, including automated anomaly detection and fraud monitoring. Yet the legitimacy of AI-enabled fraud controls depends not only on technical security gains but also on whether users perceive monitoring as proportionate, privacy-protective, reviewable, and institutionally accountable. This study develops a security-privacy-continuance perspective for mobile financial services (MFS) in Bangladesh and examines how AI literacy, perceived regulatory protection, and procedural fairness relate to users’ acceptance of AI-enabled fraud controls and continued-use intentions. The study follows the Group 8 research design and uses the Q8 five-point Likert questionnaire. The supplied database contains 385 records; however, its Codebook identifies the respondent sequence and contextual comments as synthetic, so the empirical results are explicitly treated as demonstrative rather than field evidence. Composite reliability diagnostics reveal a major measurement problem: Cronbach’s alpha is low for AI literacy (α=.322), fairness (α=.193), regulatory protection (α=.250), and the full fraud/privacy/continuance block (α=.224). This finding is substantively important rather than merely technical: the instrument’s items appear to combine related but non-identical governance dimensions, making a single latent construct inappropriate without refinement. Item-level robust regressions nevertheless show that regulatory protection is positively associated with both continued-use indicators (FPC4: b=.335, p=.002; FPC5: b=.255, p=.009), while AI literacy is positively associated with perceived fraud-detection benefit (FPC1: b=.242, p=.019) and false-alert reviewability (FPC3: b=.267, p=.015). In the aggregate model, AI literacy, fairness, and regulatory protection jointly explain 15.8% of variance in the FPC composite. The study’s principal contribution is therefore a measurement-aware account of AI financial trust: users may support fraud detection while simultaneously requiring privacy safeguards, review mechanisms, and credible regulatory protection. For Bangladesh, the implication is that AI fraud governance should be designed as a socio-technical consumer-protection architecture rather than as surveillance technology alone. The manuscript identifies precise questionnaire revisions and a validation pathway required before substantive publication. Keywords: artificial intelligence; fraud detection; privacy safeguards; mobile financial services; regulatory protection; continuance intention; Bangladesh

title: A BERT-Based Multilingual Framework for Detecting Online Recruitment Scams in the Bangladesh Job Market
venue: Journal of FST
abstract: Online recruitment scams pose a growing threat in digital job markets, particularly in emerging economies such as Bangladesh, where socioeconomic conditions create a highly vulnerable population. With a youth unemployment rate of 7.2%, a gender skewed victimization pattern (59% of the victims are female), and widespread adoption of mobile financial services such as bKash and Nagad, Bangladesh presents a uniquely challenging environment for fraud detection. Existing machine learning models for scam detection have been predominantly trained on Western datasets and therefore fail to capture fraud signals specific to emerging markets. This paper proposes a localized detection framework based on an Enhanced Multilingual BERT architecture with custom regularization, trained on a dataset of 20,000 annotated job postings collected from major Bangladeshi recruitment platforms (BDJobs and LinkedIn) as well as informal channels such as Telegram and WhatsApp groups over a 21-month period. The dataset incorporates Bangladesh-specific fraud signals, including references to mobile financial services, informal communication patterns and Bengali-English code-mixing. The proposed model achieves a test accuracy of 95.6% with precision of 94.0% and 89.0% for legitimate and fraudulent postings respectively and F1-scores of 95.0% and 87.0% for the same classes. The framework outperforms existing global models on Bangladesh-specific evaluation data by 3.3 to 8.1 percentage points.

title: TakaGuard: Mitigating Fraud Risks in Bangladesh’s Mobile Financial Services through BERT-based Sentence Classification
authors: Natasha Tanzila Monalisa; Pranta Biswas; Anika Afrin; Shirin Sultana; Shinthi Tasnim Himi
venue: Advances in intelligent systems research/Advances in Intelligent Systems Research
abstract: The rapid growth of Mobile Financial Services (MFS) has increased concerns about fraud, highlighting the need for language-specific detection systems.While machine learning has advanced digital security, most solutions focus on English, leaving major languages like Bangla underserved.This study introduces TakaGuard, a BERT-based fraud detection framework for SMS written in Bangla, English, and Romanized Bangla.Trained on a curated dataset of 50,000 real-world messages, the system evaluates multiple BERT models, with Bangla-BERT-base achieving the best performance.TakaGuard also includes user-friendly popup alerts to support individuals with limited technical skills.Overall, the framework addresses linguistic and usability gaps, offering a practical solution for reducing fraud in mobile financial services.

title: FARMERS’ PERCEPTION AND CONSTRAINTS FACED USING MOBILE FINANCIAL SERVICE: A CASE STUDY FROM BANGLADESH
venue: SAU Institutional Repository (Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University)
abstract: Executive Summary The Mobile Financial Service (MFS) began providing banking services to rural communities in remote areas across the country. MFS has become popular for providing nationwide financial support, alongside the central bank and other financial institutions. The majority of underprivileged people in rural areas who work as farmers are not served by banks, so MFSs set out to bring these significant numbers of farmers into the mainstream of banking services. This study aimed to determine the significance of factors contributing to farmers’ inclusion in mobile financial services and the constraints they faced in using them. A survey method was used to collect data from the respondents in a face-to-face setting and a multiple regression analysis was used to analyze the data. The findings showed that the frequency of using MFS and customer protection perception were positively significant, with standardized β coefficients of .362 and .213, respectively; and bank account ownership was negatively significant, with a standardized β coefficient of .254 on the dependent variable, financial inclusion. Results showed that 77.2 percent of respondents believe transaction costs are high and worry about sending to the wrong number, while 52.7 percent and 41.8 percent worry about network problems and fraudsters, respectively. Other results showed that 35.3 percent of respondents believe the transaction process is complicated, 9.8 percent experienced delays in the transaction, and 9.2 percent faced fraudulent activities once or several times. MFS service providers and regulators, most importantly Bangladesh Bank, should curb fraudulent activities, reduce transaction costs, enable cross-platform transfers, and improve verification, while ensuring fast, efficient customer support.

title: Perception of Deepfakes among Bangladeshi Women
authors: Sharifa Sultana; Pratyasha Saha; Nadira Nowsher; Sumaia Arefin Ritu; Zinnat Sultana; Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed; S M Taiabul Haque
venue: CHI Conference Extended Abstracts on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA)
abstract: As deepfake technology becomes more accessible, concerns about its misuse and societal impact are escalating, particularly in regions like the Global South where digital literacy and regulatory measures are often limited. While previous research has explored deepfakes in contexts such as detection and media manipulation, there is a noticeable gap in understanding how individuals in these regions perceive and interact with deepfake media. This study addresses this gap by investigating how Bangladeshi women perceive deepfakes and the socio-cultural factors influencing their awareness, concerns, and responses to this technology. Drawing on 15 semi-structured interviews, we uncover how cultural values, gendered norms, trust in institutions, and the prevalence of digital harassment shape their perceptions and coping mechanisms. Through this research, we aim to advance existing scholarship in HCI by offering insights into the design of culturally sensitive interventions, educational initiatives, and policy frameworks to address the challenges posed by deepfakes in the Global South.

title: A Comparative Legal Analysis of Deepfake Evidence in Bangladesh
venue: Iconic Research and Engineering Journals
abstract: Deepfake technology, which involves the creation of synthetic audio, video, and image content through artificial intelligence to portray real individuals engaging in actions or speech that never occurred, poses a significant evidentiary challenge that the traditional digital-evidence doctrine is not equipped to handle. Bangladeshi courts are increasingly dependent on electronic records; however, the Evidence Act of 1872, even after its amendment in 2022, lacks provisions addressing AI-generated content, authentication standards specific to synthetic media, and qualification frameworks for experts required to identify such content. This study explores whether Bangladesh's evidentiary framework is sufficient to meet this challenge and, if not, what reforms are necessary to bridge this gap. Utilizing doctrinal and comparative methods, this paper analyzes the statutory and case law treatment of digital evidence in Bangladesh in comparison with the approaches adopted in the United Kingdom and Malaysia. These jurisdictions were chosen for their shared evidentiary heritage and differing regulatory styles: judicial reliability review in the UK and codified statutory presumption in Malaysia. The analysis reveals that none of the jurisdictions reviewed have established a deepfake-specific evidentiary regime, but each provides transferable doctrinal elements: Malaysia's structured certification mechanism, the UK's substantive reliability inquiry, and an emerging legislative trend, as seen in the Cyber Security Act of 2026 in Bangladesh, which considers the direct regulation of AI-generated content. This study proposes a sequential authentication framework and a series of legislative, institutional, and procedural reforms designed to be integrated within Bangladesh's current judicial infrastructure rather than relying on it alone.

title: Cybercrime and Criminal Justice in Bangladesh: An Examination of Emerging Threats and Legal Responses
authors: Nafiul Haque Kingshuk; S M Azad Rahman
venue: ABC Journal of Advanced Research
abstract: Cybercrime has emerged as a significant challenge for contemporary criminal justice systems, particularly in developing countries undergoing rapid digital transformation. This study critically examines the relationship between emerging cybercrime threats and criminal justice responses in Bangladesh through a socio-legal review approach. Drawing upon legislative documents, official reports, and relevant scholarly literature, the study explores the evolving cyber threat landscape, assesses Bangladesh's legal and regulatory responses, and evaluates the institutional capacities of criminal justice actors responsible for preventing, investigating, prosecuting, and adjudicating cyber offenses. The findings indicate that Bangladesh has made substantial progress through successive legislative reforms, evolving from the Information and Communication Technology Act 2006 and the Digital Security Act 2018 to the Cyber Security Act 2023 and, most recently, the Cyber Security Act 2026. Nevertheless, significant challenges remain in areas such as digital forensic capabilities, electronic evidence management, institutional coordination, specialized human resource development, cross-border cooperation, and operational preparedness. The study further highlights the growing implications of emerging cyber threats, including ransomware, AI-assisted fraud, deepfakes, synthetic identity crimes, and other technology-enabled offenses. It argues that effective cyber justice requires more than legislative reform, emphasizing the need for stronger institutional capacity, rights-sensitive cyber governance, continuous professional training, effective implementation of the Cyber Security Act 2026, and enhanced international collaboration. The study contributes to the growing body of socio-legal scholarship on cybercrime and offers evidence-informed policy recommendations for strengthening Bangladesh's cyber resilience and criminal justice system.

title: Legal Challenges and Regulatory Responses to Digital Finance and E-Commerce Fraud in Bangladesh.
authors: Silma Subah Chowdhury Chowdhury; Fouzia Sultana Chowdhury
venue: Social Science and Humanities Journal
abstract: This study analyses Bangladesh’s legal framework for regulating fraud in digital finance and e-commerce amid the rapid expansion of mobile financial services and online marketplaces. It finds that existing laws and regulatory measures are fragmented, reactive, and insufficient to address emerging forms of digital fraud, including payment scams, identity theft, and unauthorized transactions. Using a doctrinal approach, the research identifies key regulatory gaps and proposes legal and institutional reforms to enhance fraud prevention, enforcement, and consumer protection while supporting sustainable digital economic growth.

title: Cyber Threats in South Asian Mobile Financial Services: A Systematic Review of Fraud Risks, Detection Methods, and Policy Responses (2020–2026)
abstract: This project is a systematic literature review examining cyber threats, fraud risks, and countermeasures in mobile financial services (MFS) across six South Asian economies — Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Bhutan — between 2020 and 2026. MFS platforms (including mobile money, digital wallets, and interbank payment systems such as UPI) have driven rapid financial inclusion across the region, but this expansion has been accompanied by a proportional rise in fraud incidents, ranging from social engineering and OTP interception to SIM swap fraud, account takeover, identity fraud, and agent-facilitated collusion. The review follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching eight databases (Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, PubMed, Google Scholar, ProQuest, and EconLit) to identify peer-reviewed empirical studies meeting PICOS-based eligibility criteria. Included studies are quality-appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT 2018) and synthesized narratively around four research questions: What cyber threats and fraud typologies are documented in South Asian MFS literature? What technological and organizational countermeasures are proposed or implemented? What regulatory frameworks govern MFS cybersecurity across the region, and how mature are they? What research gaps remain in the South Asian MFS security literature? Expected outcomes: A cross-country comparative mapping of fraud typologies, countermeasure effectiveness (including machine learning-based detection systems), and regulatory maturity across the six countries; identification of geographic and methodological research gaps (particularly the underrepresentation of Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Bhutan); and an actionable research and policy agenda for MFS providers, regulators, and future scholars, including recommendations on authentication design, agent oversight, and regional regulatory harmonization.

title: Deepfake Awareness and Judgements about Digital Evidence in Bangladesh
authors: Md Asraful Islam; Aungon Saha; Mst. Dilara Islam Anny; Kazi Abdul Mannan
venue: Perception Motivation and Attitude Studies
abstract: Deepfake awareness, caution about authenticity and perceived need for professional training concern different aspects of digital evidence. This cross-sectional study uses 385 adult responses from Bangladesh to examine how these judgements coexist and whether reported awareness is associated with endorsement of stronger skills for legal professionals. We report item distributions, joint endorsement, paired contrasts and exploratory adjusted regressions. Caution about treating digital media as authentic without verification was endorsed by 298 respondents (77.4%), compared with 246 (63.9%) who endorsed stronger professional skills. The paired difference was 13.5 percentage points (95% CI 7.3 to 19.7; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Technical authentication when manipulation was suspected was endorsed by 242 (62.9%). Of the 216 who reported understanding that AI can generate realistic fabricated media, 143 also endorsed stronger professional skills. Adjusted associations of awareness, caution and perceived loss of trust in unauthenticated evidence with the skills rating were small and imprecise; no focal term met the multiplicity-adjusted threshold. The results distinguish a general expectation of verification from endorsement of specific professional responses. They support assessing provenance, authentication and evidentiary reasoning as separate tasks when designing training. Survey responses do not measure actual detection accuracy, trust in a specific record, or legal admissibility. The mixed sample, which includes 253 law students, does not establish national prevalence or the views of practising lawyers as a distinct population. Keywords: deepfakes; digital evidence; authenticity; provenance; legal education; Bangladesh.

title: The Silent Threat of Cyber Bullying in Bangladesh: Exploring the Legislative Solution
authors: Mostafizur Rahaman; Rajib Chandra Das; Md.Rimon
venue: Psychosocia Journal of Applied Psychology and Social Psychology
abstract: Cyberbullying has become a new form of digital violence that can be dangerous to the safety of individuals, their mental health and social inclusion. Ongoing gender discrimination and power dynamics place women at a particular risk of cyberbullying and other forms of online harassment. The goal of this study is to explore the existing situation and the dominant trends of cyberbullying in Bangladesh, specifically how cyberbullying affects women's cyber-safety and well-being. The study is qualitative secondary data analysis based on relevant academic articles, reports, policy documents and previous studies on cyberbullying, cybercrime, gender-based violence, and digital safety in Bangladesh. The findings reveal that the adoption of social media platforms like Facebook, WhatsApp, Messenger and other digital communication platforms has facilitated an increased ability to engage in harassment, threats, abuse, discrimination and the sharing of harmful content online. Gender-based online violence disproportionately impacts women and can limit their access to online spaces and adversely impact their psychological and social health. Likewise, the study also reveals that low digital literacy, low awareness about online safety, lack of cybercrime law enforcement, and negative attitudes towards gender are the factors that have left cyberbullying practices persistent. The study finds that the implementation of existing legal provisions, digital literacy and awareness building, reporting and support processes, and dealing with gender-based discriminatory attitudes and social norms are the key areas that need to be emphasized to help reduce cyberbullying in Bangladesh. They will play a crucial role in making Bangladesh's digital space safer, more inclusive and gender-responsive.

title: BanglaHarassNet: A Multi-Platform Annotated Dataset for Online Harassment and Cyberbullying Detection in Bangladeshi Social Media
authors: Md Mijanur Rahman; Md. Amdadul Islam; Sonjoy Babu Sumon; Md. Amdadul Islam; Md Rafi Hossain
venue: Mendeley Data
abstract: This dataset contains over 5500 text-based instances collected from various social media platforms for research in natural language processing (NLP), text classification, and automated content moderation. The dataset includes content written in Bangla, English, and Banglish (Bangla written using the Roman alphabet), reflecting diverse online communication patterns and user interactions. The collected texts represent multiple forms of abusive and non-abusive language commonly observed in digital environments. The dataset is organized into five separate spreadsheet files: "Hate Speech.xlsx", "Cyberbullying.xlsx", "Sexual Harassment.xlsx", "Trolling.xlsx", and "Neutral.xlsx". Each entry has been manually reviewed, categorized, and structured with consistent annotations to maintain data quality and reliability. The dataset is designed to support the development, training, validation, and evaluation of machine learning and deep learning models for detecting harmful online content. Due to the nature of social media communication, the data may include informal language, spelling variations, code-switching, and contextual expressions. Categories for this data: Neutral: Non-abusive, safe, and ordinary conversational content representing regular online interactions without harmful intent (Severity: 0) found inside "Neutral.xlsx". Trolling: Content containing provocative, sarcastic, mocking, or disruptive comments intended to annoy, provoke, or derail discussions (Moderate Abuse Level; Severity: 2) found inside "Trolling.xlsx". Cyberbullying: Content involving personal attacks, harassment, humiliation, threats, or repeated harmful behavior targeting specific individuals (Moderate Abuse Level; Severity: 2) found inside "Cyberbullying.xlsx". dividuals or groups (Extreme Abuse Level; Severity: 4) found inside "Sexual Harassment.xlsx". Hate Speech: Content containing attacks, discrimination, insults, or hostile expressions directed toward groups, communities, religions, ethnicities, or political identities (Severe Abuse Level; Severity: 3) found inside "Hate Speech.xlsx".. Sexual Harassment: Content containing sexually explicit, suggestive, objectifying, or predatory language directed toward individuals or groups (Extreme Abuse Level; Severity: 4) found inside "Sexual Harassment.xlsx".

title: AI Enabled Cybercrime Awareness and Preventive Behaviour among Law Students in Bangladesh
authors: Aungon Saha; Mst. Dilara Islam Anny; Md Asraful Islam; Kazi Abdul Mannan
venue: Journal of State Government and Mass Media
abstract: AI-assisted impersonation and social engineering make it necessary to distinguish threat recognition from protective practices. This study examines associations between AI-enabled cybercrime awareness and self-reported prevention among law students in Bangladesh. Protection Motivation Theory informs the interpretation of awareness and protective responses. Of 385 survey records, 253 respondents identified as law students and constituted the primary sample. Following reliability diagnostics, awareness and preventive-practice items were analysed separately. Ordinary least squares models used HC3 robust inference, with ordered logistic models, Holm correction and full-sample analyses as sensitivity checks. Among students, 49.0% endorsed recognition of AI misuse for phishing or impersonation, 80.6% reported verifying unusual requests, and 82.2% endorsed security practices. Adjusted awareness coefficients were small and uncertain for both outcomes; all four confidence intervals included zero, and all Holm-adjusted p values were 1.000. Daily AI use was positively associated with verification (b = 0.308, 95% CI 0.115-0.502) and security practices (b = 0.255, 95% CI 0.067-0.444). Ordered logistic models showed a comparable pattern. The findings support distinguishing recognition, perceived detection capability and behaviour-specific responses in cybersecurity research and university education. They identify contextual associations rather than causal effects and highlight the need for validated measures and prospective behavioural assessments. Generalisation is limited by the available recruitment documentation and the self-reported cross-sectional design. Keywords: cybercrime awareness; preventive practices; law students; protection motivation; generative artificial intelligence; Bangladesh; measurement validity

Explainable and Adaptive Machine Learning for Fraud Risk Detection in Bangladesh's Digital Banking Ecosystem
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital banking and mobile financial services creates growing challenges for fraud detection, particularly under severe class imbalance and operational constraints. This study presents an explainable and adaptive machine-learning framework integrating chronological evaluation, leakage-conscious feature engineering, probability calibration, SHAP-based explainability, and adaptive risk prioritization. Experiments use the synthetic PaySim mobile-money benchmark and compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. XGBoost achieved the strongest fixed-threshold performance, with PR-AUC of 0.5658, ROC-AUC of 0.9068, and F1-score of 0.5369. Platt calibration reduced the test Brier score from 0.1141 to 0.0245, improving probability reliability. SHAP analysis identified temporal, destination-account, transaction-type, and amount features as important model drivers. An adaptive top-1% policy reduced false positives from 192 to 117, but recall declined from 0.4236 to 0.2122, demonstrating a clear alert-capacity trade-off. The results provide a reproducible methodological framework rather than evidence of deployment performance in Bangladesh, since PaySim is synthetic. Validation using governed real-world financial data is therefore an important direction for future research.

title: Evolving Cyber Governance and Human Rights in Bangladesh: From the Digital Security Act to the Cyber Security Ordinance, 2025
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Bangladesh has experienced an unprecedented expansion of digital technologies over the past two decades, fundamentally transforming governance, economic activity, civic participation, and social interaction. As internet penetration, mobile connectivity, and digital public services have changed how citizens communicate, access information, and engage with the state, the Government of Bangladesh has enacted a series of cyber-related laws to regulate the digital space, prevent cybercrime, and safeguard national security. These laws include the Information and Communication Technology Act 2006, the Digital Security Act 2018, the Cyber Security Act 2023, and the Cyber Security Ordinance 2025. While these legal instruments were crafted in response to genuine concerns about cyber threats, misinformation, and digital crime, they have also generated sustained controversy over their compatibility with constitutional guarantees and international human rights obligations. This article critically analyzes the evolution of cyber governance in Bangladesh by closely examining how successive legislative reforms have affected fundamental human rights, including freedom of expression, privacy, and due process. Employing a mixed-method research design—combining doctrinal legal analysis, empirical data from regulatory agencies and civil society reports, and an extensive review of existing scholarship—the study finds that structural risks to digital rights persist. Based on these findings, the article argues that sustainable and democratic cyber governance in Bangladesh requires clearer legal definitions, robust judicial oversight, strengthened institutional accountability, comprehensive data protection laws, and greater alignment with international human rights norms.

Between silence and the state: Victim-survivors’ justice journeys in cases of image-based abuse and sextortion in Bangladesh
venue: International Review of Victimology
abstract: Image-based abuse and sextortion are increasingly recognised as serious forms of technology-facilitated sexual violence, yet limited empirical research has examined how victim-survivors navigate justice-seeking in high-stigma contexts. This article examines victim-survivors’ justice journeys in cases of image-based abuse and sextortion in Bangladesh, focusing on silence and disclosure, institutional responses, and evolving understandings of justice. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 18 victim-survivors and 12 stakeholders, the study adopts a victim-centred analytical approach informed by secondary victimisation, procedural justice, and access to justice frameworks. The findings show that silence and delayed disclosure often functioned as deliberate and protective strategies shaped by stigma, reputational risk, and concerns about loss of control over personal information. For those who engaged with formal or semi-formal systems, fragmented reporting pathways, repeated disclosure demands, evidentiary burdens, and limited communication frequently contributed to secondary harm and disengagement. Attrition emerged as a cumulative and reasoned response to emotional exhaustion and procedural burden rather than indifference or failure. Many victim-survivors ultimately redefined justice in experiential terms, prioritising safety and restoration of control over formal legal outcomes. The study demonstrates that legal reform alone is insufficient to ensure meaningful access to justice for victim-survivors of technology-facilitated abuse.

title: Data and Code for Phishing Detection Bias Study on Bangladeshi Web Infrastructure
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This repository contains the dataset, feature-extraction pipeline, and analysis scripts accompanying an empirical study on phishing detection bias against Bangladeshi web infrastructure. The study evaluates a Random Forest classifier trained on the UCI Phishing Websites benchmark (96.7% accuracy) against a novel test set of 178 independently-verified legitimate Bangladeshi government, banking, telecommunications, and higher-education domains, alongside 300 live phishing URLs sourced from the OpenPhish feed. Accuracy on legitimate Bangladeshi domains fell to 65.2%, a statistically significant 31.6 percentage-point gap (p = 4.25 x 10^-34). Through feature-level diagnosis and independent third-party verification (SSL Labs, direct WHOIS reproduction), three mechanisms were identified: systematic WHOIS non-response for .gov.bd/.org.bd domains (confirmed across 29 domains, 100% non-response rate), SSL/TLS certificate chain and hostname misconfigurations (confirmed via SSL Labs in 68.8% of a verified sub-sample), and outdated heuristic features calibrated on a 2015 dataset. An ablation study empirically tested proposed corrections for each mechanism. Contents: Curated list of 178 verified Bangladeshi legitimate domains (government, banking, telecom, education) Feature-extraction pipeline (25 live-extracted features per URL: SSL/TLS validation, WHOIS lookup, DNS resolution, HTML parsing) Full extraction results dataset (478 URLs x 29 features, CSV) Baseline model training script (UCI Phishing Websites dataset) Bias diagnosis and root-cause analysis scripts WHOIS verification scripts Keywords: phishing detection, machine learning, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity, Bangladesh, Global South, SSL/TLS, WHOIS, domain infrastructure

title: Technology-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence in Bangladesh: A Scoping Review of Manifestations, Drivers and Responses Through a Masculinities Lens
authors: Md. Mamunur Rashid Sheikh; Airin Sultana AKhi
venue: Open Science Framework
abstract: Technology-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV) has become a significant concern in Bangladesh as access to mobile internet and social media has expanded. The Violence Against Women Survey 2024 provided the country's first national estimate: just over 8% of women with access to technology reported lifetime exposure to selected forms of TFGBV, and the figure was much higher among younger women. Smaller studies report considerably higher rates and describe harassment, image-based sexual abuse, impersonation, hate speech and blackmail, mostly on Facebook and messaging apps. Yet the evidence remains scattered across journals, conference proceedings and organisational reports. Existing reviews treat Bangladesh as one country among many and do not examine how the Bangladeshi literature explains this violence or responds to it. This scoping review aims to identify and synthesise evidence on TFGBV against women and girls in Bangladesh and to identify gaps for research, policy and practice. It asks four questions: what forms TFGBV takes and how common it is; what drivers are reported, with particular attention to masculinities and gender norms; what impacts it has on women and girls and how they seek help; and what legal, institutional and technological responses exist. The review follows the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and will be reported according to PRISMA-ScR. We will search ten academic databases and relevant grey literature for sources published in English or Bangla from 2006 onwards. Two reviewers will screen records independently, and the findings will be charted and analysed using qualitative content analysis, informed by the ecological framework and the concept of hegemonic masculinity. The expected outcome is a comprehensive map of what is known about TFGBV in Bangladesh, where the evidence is thin, and how far current laws and services match women's reported experiences. The findings are intended to inform researchers, policymakers and organisations working to prevent violence against women in Bangladesh.

title: Cybercrime Prosecution in Cross-Border Jurisdictions: Legal Challenges and Paths to Harmonization
authors: Md. Mutasim Billah Kandaker* Md. Mutasim Billah Kandaker*
venue: Asian Journal of Social Sciences and Legal Studies
abstract: The global rise of cybercrime presents unprecedented challenges to national legal systems, particularly where offences transcend territorial boundaries. Cybercriminals commonly take advantage of fragmented jurisdictional frameworks, disparate legal standards, and cumbersome mutual legal assistance procedures, all of which hamper effective prosecution. This paper analyses the legal and procedural challenges involved in prosecuting transnational cybercrime, with Bangladesh as its primary jurisdiction of focus. Through a doctrinal and comparative legal analysis, the study examines substantive and procedural cybercrime laws in Bangladesh as well as in selected jurisdictions such as the United States and the European Union, while also assessing international mechanisms including Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs) and the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime. The findings reveal significant discrepancies among jurisdictions in cybercrime definitions, jurisdictional rules, standards for digital evidence, and procedures for accessing data stored abroad, which together constitute institutional barriers to effective law enforcement. Comparative analysis further demonstrates that the United States and the European Union have developed sophisticated and convergent frameworks such as the CLOUD Act, the European Investigation Order (EIO), and emerging e-Evidence mechanisms to facilitate expedited cross-border data access and coordinated prosecution. By contrast, Bangladesh continues to face substantial techno-legislative constraints, limited treaty networks, and outdated procedural mechanisms, resulting in investigative delays and prosecutorial inefficiencies. The study proposes a harmonization-oriented model emphasizing unified cybercrime definitions, streamlined MLAT procedures, reforms in digital evidence law, institutional capacity-building, and accession to key international conventions. It concludes that, without substantive legal harmonization and enhanced international cooperation, Bangladesh and similarly situated developing states will remain vulnerable to transnational cyber threats, thereby undermining national security and global cyber governance.

title: Detecting Audio Deepfakes by Harnessing Classical Machine Learning Algorithms
authors: Md. Tasbirul Alom; Rahma Alam Samiha; Ajmery Sultana; R Rafiul Islam
venue: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence & Networking (QPAIN)
abstract: The concept of deepfakes has come to light with the exponential growth of the field of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). Moreover, social media, being the major entity of engagement, became the prime area for wrongdoers to abuse these deepfakes. Hence, the misuse of audio deepfakes is a global concern, comparable to the threats posed by other types of deepfakes, and Bangladesh is no exception. Most of these research works are found to be conducted using readily available English audio datasets. However, Bengali audio deepfake-related works and Bengali audio datasets consisting of real and deepfake speeches for research purposes are hardly available. In this study, we attempted to contribute to the field of deepfake audio detection involving the Bengali domain. We experimented with several traditional machine learning classification models, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Decision Tree, Random Forest, and AdaBoost. We created a primary dataset by collecting our own Bengali audio data, besides incorporated two secondary datasets, one entitled “Bangla Audio Dataset: Original and DeepFake Voices for AI-Based Voice Analysis and Detection” and the other “Bangla Common Voice Corpus”. We processed audio data and extracted seven distinct features for feature-based analysis of the models. We found the Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficient (MFCC) feature to be the most dominant among the selected features. Additionally, we performed a comparative analysis on the performance of the models; thus, SVM and MLP obtained the highest accuracy, 94.14 % and 92.66 % with MFCC, respectively.

title: CYBERCRIME LAW: FROM THEORY TO THE BATTLEFIELD LEGISLATION, PENALTIES, AND THE MOST DANGEROUS ATTACKS IN HISTORY
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This comprehensive work bridges cybercrime law with the reality of history's most dangerous cyberattacks, creating a unique reference that unites legislative rigor with battlefield dynamics. Spanning six major parts, the book progresses from conceptual foundations (definition, elements, classification of cybercrimes) through legal liability and penalties, criminal procedure and digital evidence, international cooperation and jurisdictional conflicts, detailed case studies of landmark attacks, to emerging threats in the age of artificial intelligence. The work examines transformative cyber incidents including Stuxnet (the first cyber weapon), NotPetya (the most destructive attack), SolarWinds (supply chain espionage), the Bangladesh Bank heist, WannaCry, and Colonial Pipeline, demonstrating how abstract legal principles apply to concrete threats. Four critical additions distinguish this revised edition: analysis of cyber insurance and the ransom payment dilemma under international sanctions; legal protections for ethical security researchers and responsible disclosure; export controls on dual-use surveillance tools under the Wassenaar Arrangement; and a novel framework for cognitive security and neural rights, protecting human cognition from deepfakes and AI-driven attacks. Licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 for academic use with commercial licensing reserved, this work provides foundational understanding for navigating cybercrime law's past, present, and future across twenty languages and multiple legal traditions.

title: Social Media as a Hub for Crime in Bangladesh
venue: Research Square
abstract: Abstract The rapid expansion of social media usage in Bangladesh has transformed digital platforms into critical spaces for communication, commerce, and social interaction. However, alongside these benefits, social media has increasingly emerged as a facilitative hub for various forms of criminal activity. This study examines how platforms such as Facebook, WhatsApp, Telegram, and TikTok are being utilized to organize, execute, and amplify crimes in Bangladesh. Drawing on a mixed-method approach that combines content analysis, survey data, and qualitative case examinations, the research identifies key patterns in cyber-enabled criminal practices, including financial fraud, drug trafficking, cyberbullying, blackmail, and the dissemination of extremist or hate content. The findings reveal that the affordances of social media—such as anonymity, algorithmic amplification, encrypted communication, and low regulatory oversight—significantly enhance opportunities for criminal behavior. Youth populations appear particularly vulnerable both as perpetrators and victims, driven by digital literacy gaps, socio-economic pressures, and peer-network influences. The study further demonstrates that existing legal frameworks and enforcement mechanisms in Bangladesh struggle to keep pace with the evolving dynamics of platform-mediated crime. The paper contributes to the growing scholarship on digital criminology by situating Bangladesh within broader global debates on cybercrime and platform governance. It offers policy-relevant insights into the need for stronger regulatory interventions, enhanced digital literacy, and collaborative governance involving state institutions, civil society, and technology companies.

title: Corruption Reduction in Bangladesh by Introducing Modern FinTech: Opportunities, Challenges, and Policy Framework
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Corruption remains one of the major barriers to sustainable economic development in Bangladesh.Traditional cash-based transactions, weak institutional monitoring, financial exclusion, bureaucraticinefficiency, and political interference have intensified bribery, money laundering, tax evasion, andfinancial fraud. Modern Financial Technology (FinTech) provides a transformative opportunity toreduce corruption through digital payments, blockchain systems, artificial intelligence (AI), biometricverification, regulatory technology (RegTech), and transparent financial ecosystems. This paperinvestigates how FinTech can reduce corruption in Bangladesh by improving transparency,accountability, transaction traceability, and financial inclusion. The study adopts a qualitativeanalytical approach supplemented by quantitative secondary data drawn from policy reports,academic literature, Bangladesh Bank publications, Transparency International datasets, and recentfinancial-crime investigations. Findings indicate that Mobile Financial Services (MFS), digital banking,e-governance platforms, blockchain-enabled public procurement, and AI-driven Anti-MoneyLaundering (AML) systems can significantly reduce informal cash transactions and administrativecorruption. However, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, regulatory weaknesses, political influence, anddigital inequality remain substantial challenges. The paper proposes a comprehensive policyframework integrating central-bank oversight, digital identity systems, blockchain governance,AI-powered fraud detection, and financial-literacy initiatives.Keywords: FinTech, Corruption Reduction, Digital Payments, Blockchain, Bangladesh, Mobile FinancialServices, Financial Transparency, AI Governance, E-Governance, Digital Banking

title: ‘The Blogger Issue Is Over’ Bangladesh (Sylhet)
authors: Jacob Copeman; Amélie Blom; Ben Laws; Johannes Quack; Mascha Schulz
venue: Cambridge University Press eBooks
abstract: Prologue: Ahmed Rajib Haider, 15 February 2013, Dhaka It was on this date that blogger and activist Ahmed Rajib Haider, known by his pen name Thaba Baba, was hacked to death just outside his home. A leading voice in the Shahbag protests and a sharp critic of Islamist politics, Haider had used his blog to advocate for secular justice and to condemn religious fundamentalism. His murder – not the first attack, but the first in what would become a series of brutal killings – marked a turning point in the public visibility and vulnerability of non-religious dissent. The next day, his coffin was carried in a vast public procession to Shahbag Square, draped in the national flag and accompanied by over 100,000 mourners. However, the act of public grieving became a political flashpoint. Islamist groups seized upon Haider's known atheism to brand the entire movement as nāstik – heretical and immoral. What began as a protest for justice swiftly became a referendum on the legitimacy of atheism in public life, setting in motion a period of heightened risk for secular activists. This chapter returns to the enduring reverberations of that moment – to the quieter and more lasting traces left behind after the spectacle receded. Introduction When I revisited Sylhet for a research stint in February and March 2022, I was warmly welcomed by my former research interlocutors and friends.1 Seeing me again after a long time, some of my atheist interlocutors emphasised, ‘Things are very different from when you came before.’

title: ENTERTAINMENT NEWS AND PUBLIC CONNECTION IN BANGLADESH
venue: EKONOMIKA I UPRAVLENIE PROBLEMY RESHENIYA
abstract: Entertainment journalism in Bangladesh is actively shedding its historical reputation as a trivial, hyper-commercialized distraction. Today, it operates as a vital conduit shaping serious, high stakes political discourse. As the digital media landscape evolves under the heavy constraints of state surveillance, coverage of Dhallywood cinema, television natoks (dramas), and local streaming shows increasingly collides with deeply entrenched societal issues, including gender violence, colorism, and religious conservatism. Drawing on in-depth qualitative interviews with 35 active Facebook users across urban and rural demographics, this study explores how digital audiences utilize pop culture news to navigate identity representation, decode celebrity scandals, and mobilize conservative ideological backlash against secular institutions. The central takeaway reveals a profound shift in civic behavior. As the state heavily censors traditional political speech through draconian legislation like the Cyber ​​Security Act, citizens are adopting alternative methods to express their socio-political realities. Culture and entertainment news have stepped up to fill this democratic void, transforming from a space of mere escapism into a fiercely contested, alternative public square where Bangladesh's deepest mental and political battles are now being actively fought.

title: BanglishChat: A Human vs. AI-Generated Banglish Chat Dataset for AI-Text and Impersonation-Scam Detection
authors: MD Sozon; Raju Md. Humayun Kabir; Md. Soleman; Hossain Md. Saif; Md. Asifuzzamman
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This dataset supports research on detecting AI-generated text in Banglish (Bangla written using Latin/English characters), a code-mixed writing style widely used for everyday digital communication in Bangladesh. Motivation: fraudsters increasingly use AI chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok) to impersonate friends, relatives, or institutional representatives in Banglish SMS/chat conversations to build trust, then extract money, credentials (OTP/PIN/passwords), or sensitive personal information from victims. Banglish is under-studied compared to standard Bangla or English, so existing AI-text-detection tools generalize poorly to it. This dataset supports building and evaluating classifiers that distinguish human-written from AI-generated Banglish text. Contents: 8,389 rows in a CSV with two columns — Human_chat (6,991 human-written Banglish messages) and AI_chat (7,976 AI-generated Banglish messages, produced by prompting ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini, and Grok to converse casually in Banglish). Full column definitions and summary statistics are provided in the accompanying DATA_DICTIONARY.md; usage notes and known limitations are in README.md. Intended use: training/evaluating human-vs-AI text classifiers for Banglish, code-mixed/low-resource NLP research, and research on impersonation-scam detection in South Asian digital communication. This dataset does not itself label messages as fraudulent; it labels only the authorship source (human or AI).

title: Explainable Hybrid Deep Learning Approach For Phishing Detection From Bangla English Mixed Datasets with Application to Bangladesh's Fintech Ecosystem.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This thesis presents an explainable hybrid deep learning framework for detecting phishing attacks in Bangla-English (Banglish) mixed datasets, with a specific focus on Bangladesh’s fintech ecosystem. The study integrates machine learning models such as Random Forest and XGBoost with deep learning architectures including BERT and BiLSTM to capture both structural and semantic patterns of phishing messages. A custom Banglish phishing dataset was developed to address the challenges of multilingual and low-resource environments, particularly in mobile financial services such as bKash, Nagad, and Rocket. The proposed hybrid model significantly improves detection accuracy, robustness, and generalization compared to individual models. Furthermore, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques, including SHAP and LIME, are incorporated to provide transparent and interpretable predictions. This enhances trust, usability, and real-world applicability in financial cybersecurity systems. The findings of this research contribute to the development of scalable, efficient, and deployment-ready phishing detection solutions tailored for multilingual and emerging digital financial ecosystems.

title: Deepfakes and Intellectual Property: Copyright licensing, personality rights, and civil/criminal liability for synthetic media generation
abstract: Background.Generative AI now makes realistic synthetic video, images and voices of real people cheap and widespread.Law must deter nonconsensual deepfakes while allowing a lawful market in licensed digital replicas, but copyright, personality rights and criminal law each address only part of the problem.Objective.To compare how legal systems allocate control over a person's likeness and voice, govern licensing, and distribute civil and criminal liability for synthetic media.Methods.A doctrinal, functional comparative analysis of eight legal systems (the EU layer, Italy, the United Kingdom, the United States, China, South Korea, India and Bangladesh) as of 20 October 2026.Each system was scored on a nine-dimension Synthetic Media Legal Coverage Index (SMLCI, 0-18) grouped into three pillars: rights and licensing, transparency and platforms, and liability.Four IP-style likeness-right models (Denmark, Cyprus, the U.S. NO FAKES bill and Tennessee's ELVIS Act) were compared separately.Results.SMLCI scores ranged from 6 (Bangladesh; 33.3%) to 15 (United States; 83.3%), with a mean of 9.9.The rights and licensing pillar reached only 32.8% of its maximum, against 75.0%for transparency and platforms and 70.8% for liability.Sexual-deepfake offences were the most widely covered dimension (87.5%), while copyright or IP vehicles for likeness (6.3%) and post-mortem control (25.0%) were the least.Rankings were robust to equal pillar weighting (Spearman ρ = 0.99).Conclusion.Deepfake law has built sanctions and takedown duties faster than the property and licensing rules that define lawful use.Copyright is best used as an enforcement container for a dignity-based personality right, not as its foundation.A four-layer model (right, licence, transparency, liability) is proposed for jurisdictions such as Bangladesh.

title: AI and Cybersecurity – An Indian and Bangladeshi Cyber-Border Perspective
venue: Iconic Research and Engineering Journals
abstract: As globalization gears up every decade, the blurred borders are enhancing geo-political and economic inclusivity on one hand but on the other are causing significant and potentially severe security implications. Among these, Cybercrimes since the past two and a half decades have increased exponentially resulting in fueling political, social and economic instability. The increase in cyber threats and attacks has prompted many countries to collaborate in addressing this shared challenge. Similarly, in the south Asia block - India and Bangladesh formalized an MOU on joint cybersecurity cooperation in 2017 to facilitate and enhance bilateral cooperation to tackle the issue related to cyber-threats. This research paper navigates the loopholes with respect to framework and implementations of the MOU under India's CERT-In and Bangladesh's BGD e-Gov CIRT and how it can be made more effective and reliable in dealing with cyber-border security.

title: Media Regulation in The Digital Age: A Comparative Analysis of Nigeria and Bangladesh
authors: Abubakar Umar Gachi; Maryam Eti Shehu; Joseph Ojomugbo Bala; Mohammed Musa Saleh; Musa Garba Baba
venue: Iconic Research and Engineering Journals
abstract: This study examines the difficulties of policing free speech in the internet era by contrasting Bangladesh and Nigeria. As lower-middle-income democracies with active online populations, both countries are increasingly concerned about digital dissent, hate speech, and disinformation. To investigate three main themes (1) ambiguous and punitive legal frameworks, (2) misinformation as a rationale for censorship, and (3) surveillance and platform governance—the study employs a qualitative comparative case study methodology and consults legal texts, civil society reports, and secondary literature. The results show that the wording of Bangladesh's Digital Security Act (2018) and Nigeria's Cybercrimes Act (2015) is unclear, allowing for selective enforcement against people, journalists, and activists. The study concludes that while regulation of digital harms is necessary, the current approaches in Nigeria and Bangladesh prioritize state control over fundamental freedoms, undermining democratic values. Despite these challenges, opportunities for reform are emerging. Civil society organizations, judicial interventions, and international human rights advocacy continue to push for greater accountability, transparent platform governance, and alignment of national laws with global standards. While disinformation is a real threat during elections and protests, governments in both contexts frequently weaponize it to suppress opposition rather than promote transparency. Additionally, surveillance regimes and opaque partnerships with global technology platforms further erode user rights and civic trust. Maintaining democratic governance in the digital age requires a rights-based framework that strikes a balance between security considerations and freedom of speech.

title: Carcerality, Under-age Marriage and the Making-Up of “Victims” in Bangladesh
venue: South Asia Multidisciplinary Academic Journal
abstract: Based on the cases of young women held in a “Safe House” in Dhaka, this paper argues that the label “marriage victim” is used discursively to discipline young women who have eloped against parental wishes. Whilst the Bangladeshi 2017 Child Marriage Restraint Act is used to accuse husbands of kidnap and rape, daughters who refuse to return home or divorce are incarcerated as “victims” of under-age marriage, their ages often falsified. Drawing on Hacking’s concept of “making up,” the paper argues that within the assemblage of NGOs, shelters and support centers providing services for women and children in Dhaka, different types of victim are “made-up” via bureaucratic systems and procedures. As the paper shows, the term “victim” allows out-of-place women and children to be sorted and placed in different institutions. Whilst victims of domestic violence are offered shelter, unruly young women who have eloped for love are classified as “marriage victims” and held in carceral institutions, where what Ticktin calls “armed love” generates containment and discipline.

title: Attention and residual mechanism-based CNN architecture (ARC-Net) with enhanced fairness generalization for deepfake facial image detection
authors: Md Shihab Reza; Farhana Elias; Monirul Islam Mahmud; Nova Ahmed
venue: PLoS ONE
abstract: Deepfake (DF) content poses a major challenge to digital media authentication, that can mimic facial movements, creating realistic replicas that risk spreading misinformation and enabling harassment, as can be seen in Bangladesh. Previous studies applied residual convolutional blocks or attention mechanisms for DF detection; however, these approaches often treat these components in isolation and lack explicit consideration of fairness, out-of-distribution generalization, statistical analysis or artifact-focused detection. Our study introduces an approach, called ARC-Net, which uses a combination of attention and residual convolutional layers along with the EfficientNet B0 base, the attention mechanism of which allows the model to pay more attention to details that could resemble the ones seen in non-perfectly executed DF, which enhances the model's potential to distinguish them, addressing limitations in pre-trained and also advanced DL models. A dataset of 500 real images from Bangladesh combined with a 140k real and fake faces dataset was used to train and test our model alongside four pre-trained DL models. ARC-Net performed much better than the other traditional and state of art methods with 99% accuracy, 1.0 precision, 0.97 recall and 0.98 F1 score, reaching the highest level of reliability in spotting DF images. To assess the external reliability and generalizability of ARC-Net, the model was evaluated on the Deepfake Dataset and the Deepfake Database datasets, achieving consistently high and balanced performance across different scales. Three out-of-distribution (OOD) experiments were conducted, where the first one evaluated South Asian images, showing that incorporating fewer than one percent real Bangladeshi images reduced the false positive rate by more than half and improved probability calibration, while the remaining two cross-dataset experiments demonstrated strong transferability. An ablation study further showed the impact of different components within a model by systematically removing or modifying them and statistical significance between competing classifiers was assessed using McNemar's Statistical test. In addition, we've applied Explainable AI (XAI) techniques, Grad-CAM and LIME to offer transparency of the results, as giving attention to the facial region is also important for DF detection. This study will help advance DF detection by integrating ARC-Net's attention-residual mechanisms and XAI, offering insights for developing models in security and media forensics.

title: Bangladesh Defense Policy: Foundations, Futures And Frameworks
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Comprehensive Summary: "Bangladesh Defense Policy: Foundations, Futures and Frameworks" Overview This 16-part academic textbook (2026) by S M Nazmuz Sakib is a comprehensive examination of Bangladesh's defense policy challenges, written in the aftermath of the July 2024 Revolution that ended Sheikh Hasina's 15-year rule. The book addresses the urgent need for a coherent defense framework as Bangladesh navigates a complex geopolitical environment involving India, China, Myanmar, and the United States. Part One: Foundations of Defense Policy Philosophical and Conceptual Origins traces defense thinking from antiquity (Kautilya's Arthashastra, Sun Tzu) through Clausewitz, Mahan, to contemporary hybrid warfare theory. The author establishes defense as "the organized capacity of a political community to protect the conditions of its own existence." National Security Theory examines the security dilemma, deterrence, and strategic autonomy - concepts directly applied to Bangladesh's position between India and China. The book argues that Bangladesh cannot achieve symmetric military parity but can pursue "asymmetric deterrence" through cost-imposition capabilities. Historical Formation covers the colonial legacy, the 1971 Liberation War, and the pattern of military coups (1975, 1982) that shaped Bangladesh's troubled civil-military relations. Forces Goal 2030 (2009) is identified as the first formal defense planning framework. Geopolitical Analysis describes Bangladesh's position as "India-locked" on three sides, with a Bay of Bengal coastline of 580km and an EEZ of 118,813 sq km. Key relationships analyzed: India: Asymmetric partnership with structural tensions (water sharing, border killings, trade imbalances) China: Primary arms supplier (70%+ of major hardware) and infrastructure financier Myanmar: Collapsing state, civil war, Arakan Army control of Rakhine State Bay of Bengal: Emerging strategic locus for Indo-Pacific competition Constitutional and Legal Framework examines Articles 61 (President as Supreme Commander), 31-32 (right to life/liberty), and the emergency powers framework. The book identifies the Army Act 1952, Navy Ordinance 1961, and Air Force Act 1953 as colonial-era instruments inadequate for democratic governance. Part Two: Comparative Analysis Case studies examined for lessons applicable to Bangladesh: Vietnam: "Four Nos" doctrine (no alliances, no foreign bases, no alignment, no use of force) - strategic autonomy master class South Korea: Alliance management with US while maintaining China relationship; defense white paper transparency Indonesia: "Bebas dan Aktif" (free and active) doctrine; archipelagic security challenges Turkey: Defense industrial transformation from 80% import dependence to export power; Baykar drone revolution Israel: Small-state defense model; three pillars of deterrence, early warning, decisive victory Singapore: "Poisonous shrimp" strategy - too costly to attack despite small size Finland: Total defense concept; reserve system (280,000 trained reserves from 5.5M population) 2024-2026 Developments documented include: Eurofighter Typhoon Letter of Intent (December 2025) Japan defense equipment transfer agreement (February 2026) Pakistan defense engagement (ISI visit February 2025) CETC drone manufacturing agreement (January 2026) Budget reduction to 40,698 crore taka (operational costs 37,812 crore, development 916 crore) Part Three: Legislative Architecture Security Sector Reform Theory examines principal-agent problems in security governance and why previous reform efforts failed. The 2024-2026 period is identified as a genuine "constitutional moment" for reform. Constitutional Foundations analyze the gap between text (civilian supremacy) and practice (military autonomy). The OHCHR February 2025 fact-finding report documented 1,400 deaths during the July-August 2024 uprising. National Defense Act Proposal is the centerpiece: Establishes statutory basis for armed forces Defines command authority (President → PM → Minister of Defence) Requires parliamentary authorization for combat deployments Creates independent military justice system Establishes Defense Procurement Authority Military Justice Reform addresses the enforced disappearances crisis (October 2025 arrest warrants against 16 army officers). Proposed reforms include civilian court jurisdiction for gross human rights violations. Intelligence Reform addresses the DGFI and NSI, which operate without statutory charters. Proposes warrant requirements for surveillance and a Parliamentary Intelligence Committee. Domestic Military Deployment legal framework would restrict armed forces internal deployment to exceptional circumstances with parliamentary approval. Cyber Safety Ordinance 2025 is analyzed as a partial improvement over the abusive Digital Security Act. Part Four: Military Doctrine and Force Structure Military Doctrine Theory distinguishes between strategy (political objectives) and doctrine (principles guiding operations). The book proposes a synthesized doctrine of "Defensive Realism with Asymmetric Deterrence." Three-Corps Army Reorganization: I Corps (Bogura): Western Command facing India - area denial focus II Corps (Sylhet): Central-Eastern Command - limited strategic depth problem III Corps (Chattogram): Southeastern Command - littoral warfare, CHT, Rohingya camps Naval Doctrine pursues the "three-dimensional navy" concept (surface, sub-surface, aviation). The submarine program (two Ming-class, negotiations for six KSS-I from South Korea) is strategically significant but operationally limited. Air Power identifies the fighter aircraft decision as the most consequential procurement choice. Options analyzed: J-10CE (China, $2.2B for 20), Eurofighter Typhoon (Italy, $2.5-3B for 12-16), JF-17 Block III (Pakistan-China, most affordable). Drone Revolution is examined through the Ukraine war lens. The CETC UAV manufacturing agreement could provide indigenous production capability. Electronic Warfare lessons from the April-May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict drive the proposal for an Electronic Warfare Brigade. Part Five: Political Economy of Defense Defense-Economy Relationship examines the guns-versus-butter trade-off. Bangladesh spends ~1.02% of GDP on defense (vs. India 2.1%, Pakistan 3.5%). The book argues this is low but cautions against uncritical increases. Defense Budget Analysis reveals a structural problem: 97% operational, 3% capital in formal budget. Major procurement is financed through off-budget government-to-government loans (primarily from China), creating hidden debt obligations. Military Business Enterprises are extensively documented: Sena Kalyan Sangstha (assets estimated $700M+) Army Welfare Trust (more dynamic commercial operator) Trust Bank, Sena Insurance, Sena Cement, etc. The book argues these create institutional autonomy that undermines civilian control Peacekeeping Economy is significant: Bangladesh is the world's largest troop contributor (168 killed, 257 wounded). Annual reimbursements ~$100M. US funding cuts threaten to reduce deployment by 25% (1,400 personnel). $75 Billion Modernization Proposal (2026-2040) is assessed as strategically desirable but fiscally challenging. The book calls for realistic prioritization. Part Six: Geopolitical Environment India Relationship analysis is extensive. The "golden era" (2009-2024) collapsed after the July Revolution. Key tensions: Hasina asylum, Teesta water dispute (blocked since 2011), Ganges Treaty expiring December 2026, BSF border killings, trade restrictions. The book advocates "calibrated strategic autonomy" rather than subordination or confrontation. China Relationship is characterized as Bangladesh's most economically significant and strategically complex. China supplies 70%+ of major arms. The CETC drone agreement and potential J-10CE acquisition deepen dependency. The book recommends managed diversification rather than decoupling. Myanmar Border has been transformed by the Arakan Army's consolidation of Rakhine State. The Arakan Army is a non-state actor with de facto territorial control. The Rohingya crisis (1.18M refugees) has become a security imperative as armed groups (ARSA) mobilize in the camps. United States Relationship involves pressure for ACSA and GSOMIA agreements. The book recommends signing GSOMIA (technology access) while carefully negotiating ACSA with parliamentary approval provisions and no-foreign-bases clauses. Middle Powers (Turkey, Japan, South Korea, Italy) are identified as crucial diversification partners. Turkey's defense industrial transformation offers the most relevant model. Part Seven: Legislative Architecture (Detailed) Constitutional Framework analysis: Articles 31-32 (right to life/liberty) have been systematically violated through extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, and arbitrary detention. Article 141A emergency powers have been abused (2007-2008 emergency). Army Act Reform proposals: Section 125A: civilian court jurisdiction for gross human rights violations Reform of court martial system with independent judicial members Right of appeal to High Court Division Police Reform addresses the Police Act of 1861 (colonial instrument). The 2007 Police Ordinance remains unenacted. RAB's documented pattern of extrajudicial killings ("crossfire") has led to US Magnitsky sanctions (December 2021). Intelligence Legislation proposals: Statutory charter for DGFI, NSI, and new Domestic Intelligence Service Judicial warrant requirements for intrusive surveillance Intelligence Oversight Commissioner Parliamentary Intelligence Committee Official Secrets Act 1923 is identified as incompatible with the Right to Information Act 2009. Reform would narrow protectable categories. Nation

title: Victims of AI: Addressing the Legal Response Gap to AI-Related Crimes in Bangladesh
authors: M Sabbir Ahmed Shihab; Mostafizur Rahaman; Md. Omar Faruk Shakib; Md. Easin
venue: International journal of research and scientific innovation
abstract: AI technologies improving rapidly in Bangladesh have eased the path to novel forms of digital harm, such as deepfake harassment (using manipulated videos or images to create false representations), AI-assisted impersonation (using AI to mimic someone's identity), extortion, phishing, and algorithmic discrimination (bias in automated decision-making processes). This scenario raises doubts about the robustness of our current legal system in safeguarding individuals from AI-induced harm. The study examines the absence of a legal response to violence against women in Bangladesh by asking if laws are sufficient, whether institutions are prepared and capable of assisting victims and how accessible justice is for them. Using a mixed-methods approach, we analyzed survey data from 435 respondents aged 18–35 and two case studies of AI-generated deepfake harassment and blackmail. Overall, the results show that a majority of respondents (55%) perceive AI misuse as “very common," with women and children being perceived as particularly vulnerable groups. In addition, most respondents (65%) believe that existing laws and regulations are inadequate at preventing new harms caused by AI. The report also says that most people support new or updated laws and that digital literacy is a good way to stop problems before they happen. The paper concludes that to address the legal response deficit and ensure robust protection in an AI-driven society, Bangladesh requires victim-centered legal reform, enhanced digital forensic capabilities, clear liability regulations, and a more cohesive framework for AI governance.

title: Behind the Headlines: Media Control in Bangladesh Post July Revolution
venue: eYLS (Yale Law School)
abstract: “I have always written for truth, for peo­ple, and for my country . . . [b]ut today, when I look at my own life, I feel that living by writing the truth is not easy.” The words from Bibhuran­jan Sarkar’s suicide note echo into the minds of all Bangladeshi journalists as fears of retaliation took precedent over the work of informing the public. Journalism in South Asia has always been a toxic balance between writing what is fair versus writing what people in power want you to write. In Bangladesh, the autocracy led by former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina created countless obstacles to journalistic speech. Through the Cyber Security Act (CSA), Hasina threatened the livelihoods and safety of journalists by creating an environment of impunity where extrajudicial killings were ignored and censorship was commonplace. There were countless reports of disappearances and murders of journalists, baseless revocations of credentials, and censorship through internet shutdowns. Though the Hasina government was toppled in 2024, Bangladeshi journalists still feel unsafe to report news unfavorable to the ideals of the Muslim majority or anti-government stances. Journalists in Bangladesh still face many obstacles in exercising the basic right to free speech and freedom of the press, a problem that remains unrectified by the interim government. Instead, the substitution of a surveillance-based legal framework and pressure to exclude certain anti-government and anti-Muslim views have hindered journalistic speech by placing blocks on the flow of information online. With the upcoming elections in February 2026, there must be a focus on reforming press freedom and ensuring that the Cyber Security Ordinance (CSO) 2025, the replacement for the CSA, is fully repealed.

title: Altruism as Infrastructure: Volunteer Moderation in a Bangladeshi Higher Education Facebook Group
authors: Umme Jannat Taposhi; Md. Tawhid Anwar; Alvi Islam Ratul; S M Taiabul Haque
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
abstract: Aspiring international students across Asian countries increasingly depend on commercial education agents to navigate scholarships, documentation, and visas. Alongside this commercial infrastructure, volunteer-run Facebook groups have emerged. Unpaid admins and moderators, often under their real identities, vet information, screen scams, and guide members through scholarships, visas, and departure logistics. We study one such Bangladeshi group, \textit{HigherStudyAbroad: Global Hub of Bangladeshis}, founded in 2010. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 17 volunteer admins and moderators, we found that altruism becomes an organizing logic. It shapes moderators' identities, sustains invisible labor, and grants the group legitimacy against paid agents, even amid new technologies such as AI that could reshape this work. Human judgment remains central to how moderators sustain trust. We discuss implications for HCI's understanding of volunteer labor and migration infrastructure, along with design implications for platforms that depend on unpaid, long-term contribution.

title: University Campus Bullying on Digital Platforms in Bangladesh: A Multimodal Discourse Analysis
authors: Abdullah Al Mahmud; Syeda Kamrunnahar Eti
venue: Asiatic IIUM Journal of English Language and Literature
abstract: This paper investigates how university-based digital platforms in Bangladesh have transformed bullying into complex and insidious forms. Using a multimodal discourse analysis framework, the study examines the linguistic and non-linguistic markers that bullies employ on these platforms. It collected qualitative data on digital bullying through 43 interviews with victims and from their social media conversations to identify specific patterns of language and digital discourses. The findings reveal that the rising types of bullying comprise identity-based practices, interactional aggression, and technologically mediated manipulation. Additionally, bullies strategically use language such as sarcasm, humour, insults, and backhanded compliments with multi-modal features (memes, GIFs, emojis, and captions) to disguise hostility. The study provides useful examples with critical reflections and insights for university digital platform administrators, cybercrime investigators, and policymakers at institutional and governmental levels.
