title: Empowering Voices: A Survey on Harassment of Girls on Social Media in Bangladesh
venue: Harvard Dataverse
abstract: This dataset contains de-identified responses from an online survey (Google Forms) on the harassment of girls and women on social media in Bangladesh. Responses were collected between October-November 2024 and September 2026. The survey covers respondents' demographics (age group, gender, district, city, occupation), social media platforms used, frequency and types of harassment experienced (e.g., offensive comments, sexual harassment, cyberstalking, doxxing, threats of violence, unwanted romantic attention), the platforms where harassment occurred, harassment from real-life acquaintances, reporting behaviour, psychological and behavioural effects, actions taken and their effectiveness, perceptions of platform and government responsibility, awareness of local support organisations, willingness to join online-safety education programmes, and optional open-ended comments. All respondents gave voluntary consent. To protect participants, email addresses were removed, timestamps were reduced to the date only, responses from participants under 18 were excluded, and each record was assigned an anonymous Respondent ID. The file contains 78 responses.

title: Rule by Law vs. The People’s Will: An Anthropological Inquiry into Constitutional Legitimacy in Bangladesh
authors: Sheikh Mehbuba Moitree; Sheikh Mehzabin Chitra; Chayan Chakma; Sujeya Khisa; Samanta Samiha Raisa; Md Sojib; Tahsina Marjan
venue: Journal of South Asian Issues (JSAI)
abstract: The “Monsoon Revolution” in Bangladesh (2024) represents a strong political and constitutional ‎history. Unlike the other developments perceived in other constitutional democracies, despite the ‎official justifications, this crisis combined the systematic corruption. İt also involved the parallels ‎violation of constitutional rules. While the constitutional framework of democracy was maintained the ‎constitutional mechanisms were regularly rigged to build the strengthening of executive as dominance ‎and fundamental rights were suppressed. The approach uses a doctrinal analysis of the law coupled ‎with empirical tools and data gotten from student-led political mobilization, this forms the basis for ‎examining the role that Article 70 of the Constitution and Cyber Security Act 2023 play as the ‎principal instruments of authoritarian governance. Drawing on deliberative democracy, moral ‎constitutionalism, and constitutional moments theories, it posits that in Bangladesh’s context revolt of ‎‎2024 has been an essential moment for constitution-making in terms of reassertion of popular ‎sovereignty. The paper further discusses the July National Charter as a spontaneous attempt towards ‎constitutional reconstruction and zooms into legislative independence, executive power, judicial ‎autonomy and participatory governance. As much as in order to re-legitimize constitutional ‎procedures it is necessary for a transition beyond procedural electoralism; just so how much with ‎normatively grounded constitutional order based on moral rights, public deliberation and enforceable ‎democratic safeguards.‎

title: Empowering Digital Women: Overcoming Challenges in Bangladesh’s E-Commerce Landscape
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
abstract: This study examines the types of support that women entrepreneurs require to overcome business challenges, particularly in Facebook commerce (e-commerce), focusing on respondents from Rangpur and Dinajpur districts in Bangladesh. Using both open- and closed-ended questions, data were collected from 300 women entrepreneurs. The findings highlight nine key supports identified by respondents: stopping online harassment (87%), government-arranged training (85%), family support (81%), recognition of hard work (78%), support from NGOs and private sectors (70%), improved network speed (67%), removal of patriarchal attitudes (60%), simplified trading license procedures (52%), and government-provided loans (47%).

title: Application of Blockchain Technology into Public Sector Accountability and Financial Reporting Transparency in Bangladesh
authors: Prasenjit Sarker; Chironjit Sarker; Md. Abu Hanif; Khadija Huq
venue: American Journal of Financial Technology and Innovation
abstract: Accessibility to authentic and reliable financial reports is sin qua non for investors, consumers or any other stake holders, ensuring data credibility, real time data traceability making shield against corruption and window dressing. Nowadays, the surge of real-time data traceability has become a very significant factor, while blockchain technology undoubtedly plays a pivotal role as the data protector. In this study, it has been shown that how blockchain technology can be coined with operating system to protect and provide reliable financial reports to the stake holders connected to the public sectors of Bangladesh. Moreover, a proper frame work about how authentic and reliable financial reports can be provided to public sector stake holders has been proposed. In this frame work, different levels of service providers and analysists remain connected to one another providing data collected from field levels and analyze this data to make the proper reports to the superior level without data manipulation and thus ensuring data reliability. All participants in the frame work remain connected to the operating system, distributed ledger, and cloud computing as well. Nods are designed to stay at different levels to permit data to be incorporated and thus to ensure that data is protected from hacking, window dressing etc. This study thus helps to explore how blockchain technology, coupled with data science, can play a pivotal role in generating proper financial reports and making them available to its stakeholders in real time

title: ডিজিটাল গোপনীয়তা ও মানহানি সুরক্ষা : সাইবার সুরক্ষা আইন ২০২৬-এর শরয়ী মূল্যায়ন|Digital Privacy and Defamation Protection: A Shariah Evaluation of the Cyber Security Act 2026
venue: ইসলামী আইন ও বিচার | Islami Ain O Bichar
abstract: In this dynamic era of technological advancement, the advent of Generative Artificial Intelligence and the subsequent proliferation of deepfakes have triggered a profound crisis of digital trustworthiness by fundamentally threatening human dignity and the right to privacy. Legal measures aimed at curbing cybercrime in Bangladesh have long been perceived as instruments for suppressing political dissent. Although the newly introduced Cyber Security Act 2026 attempts to amend these previous harsh measures, this research paper highlights its lack of a robust ethical foundation or explicit definitions necessary to safeguard freedom of speech while effectively addressing the very real threats posed by AI-driven defamation. Employing a qualitative and normative legal research methodology, this study conducts a comparative analysis between the provisions of the Cyber Security Act 2026 and Islamic jurisprudence (Fiqh). The research contends that conventional legal frameworks are inadequate for meeting the challenges of the AI era, thereby proposing the integration of Islamic legal principles. By codifying digital defamation, the state can establish precise and objective boundaries for cyber offenses. Furthermore, the application of discretionary punishments (Tazir) can redirect legal focus toward restorative justice aimed at recovering the honor and dignity of victims of synthetic media. Ultimately, this Shariah-based framework can supply the evidentiary standards required to severely punish malicious deepfake creators while simultaneously ensuring the active protection of legitimate Nasiha (sincere counsel) or constructive political criticism, and freedom of expression within the digital public sphere. সারসংক্ষেপ: প্রযুক্তির উৎকর্ষের গতিময় এই সময়ে জেনারেটিভ আর্টিফিশিয়াল ইন্টেলিজেন্সের আবির্ভাব এবং পরবর্তীতে ডিপফেক-এর ব্যাপক বিস্তার ডিজিটাল নির্ভরযোগ্যতার ক্ষেত্রে এক গভীর সংকটের সৃষ্টি করেছে, কেননা এগুলো মৌলিকভাবে মানবিক মর্যাদা এবং গোপনীয়তার অধিকারকে হুমকির মুখে ফেলে দিয়েছে। বাংলাদেশে সাইবার অপরাধ দমনের জন্য আইনি পদক্ষেপগুলো বহুদিন যাবৎ রাজনৈতিক ভিন্নমত দমনে ব্যবহৃত হয়ে আসছে বলে অভিযোগ রয়েছে। নবপ্রবর্তিত সাইবার সুরক্ষা আইন ২০২৬ এ পূর্ববর্তী কঠোর ব্যবস্থাগুলো সংশোধনের চেষ্টা করলেও, এই গবেষণাপত্রটিতে চিহ্নিত করা হয়েছে যে, বাকস্বাধীনতা রক্ষা করার পাশাপাশি কৃত্রিম বুদ্ধিমত্তা-চালিত মানহানি বিষয়ক অত্যন্ত বাস্তব হুমকি মোকাবেলা করার জন্য প্রয়োজনীয় শক্তিশালী নৈতিক ভিত্তি বা সুস্পষ্ট সংজ্ঞা নেই। একটি গুণগত ও নীতিগত আইনি গবেষণা পদ্ধতি অনুসরণের মাধ্যমে এই অধ্যয়নটিতে সাইবার সুরক্ষা আইন ২০২৬ এর বিধানের সাথে ইসলামি নির্দেশনার একটি তুলনামূলক বিশ্লেষণ করা হয়েছে। গবেষণায় যুক্তি দেওয়া হয়েছে যে, এআই যুগের চ্যালেঞ্জ মোকাবিলায় প্রচলিত আইনি কাঠামো অপর্যাপ্ত; ফলে ইসলামি আইনের বিধানসমূহের অন্তর্ভুক্তকরণের প্রস্তাব করা হয়েছে। ডিজিটাল মানহানিকে বিধিবদ্ধ করে রাষ্ট্র সাইবার অপরাধের সুনির্দিষ্ট ও বস্তুনিষ্ঠ সীমারেখা প্রতিষ্ঠা করতে পারে। তদুপরি, তাযীর বিবেচনামূলক শাস্তি-এর প্রয়োগ আইনি মনোযোগকে সিনথেটিক মিডিয়ার শিকার হওয়া ভুক্তভোগীদের জন্য মান-সম্মান পুনরুদ্ধারমূলক ন্যায় বিচারের দিকে ধাবিত করতে পারে। পরিশেষে বলা যায়, এই শরিয়াভিত্তিক কাঠামোটি ক্ষতিকর ডিপফেক নির্মাতাদের কঠোর শাস্তি দেওয়ার জন্য প্রয়োজনীয় প্রমাণ্য মানদ- প্রদান করতে পারে এবং একই সাথে, এটি ডিজিটাল জনপরিসরে গঠনমূলক রাজনৈতিক সমালোচনা এবং মত প্রকাশের স্বাধীনতাকে সুরক্ষিত রাখতে পারে।

title: Cybersecurity, Public-Private Partnership, and the Protection of Critical Information Infrastructure in Bangladesh: A Comparative Study
venue: Beijing Law Review
abstract: This article explores the importance of public-private partnerships in enhancing cybersecurity for critical information infrastructure in Bangladesh, while also providing a comparative analysis of the experiences of the US, UK, and EU. In 2013, hackers successfully infiltrated the Sonali Bank of Bangladesh, leading to the theft of US$250,000. The cyber theft at Bangladesh Bank in 2016 reaffirmed the pressing need for robust cybersecurity legislation to protect key infrastructure. This incident was not the first of its kind; in the last week of August 2025, a coordinated fraud scheme targeted the credit card holders of Standard Chartered Bank, unlawfully extracting approximately BDT 27 lakh through a series of unauthorized transactions. The proliferation of personal computers, mobile phones, tablets, and digital sensors has significantly improved network connectivity and transformed global operations. However, these advancements have also resulted in an increase in the volume of data generation and storage.

title: Biography of Farhad Mazhar: Poet, Philosopher and The Radical Imagination of Bangladesh
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Farhad Mazhar was born on August 9, 1947 in Noakhali, during the final days of British India and the partition that created East Pakistan. This landscape of communal violence and ecological richness shaped his lifelong skepticism toward the state and his deep engagement with the syncretic Baul and Fakiri traditions of the Bengal delta. He studied pharmacy at the University of Dhaka in the 1960s, then moved to New York City where he worked as a pharmacist and studied political economy at the New School for Social Research. There he encountered Western Marxism, the Frankfurt School, and postcolonial theory, developing a heterodox Marxism that refused dogma and took seriously the philosophical dimensions of Marx’s early writings on alienation and species-being. After returning to Bangladesh, Mazhar founded the magazine Chinta and the research organization UBINIG, and co founded the Nayakrishi Andolon (New Agriculture Movement). His poetry, especially the collection Ebadatnama (Book of Devotions), uses Islamic devotional forms to express radical political and philosophical ideas, earning him the controversial label “Communist Mullah.” He draws centrally on Fakir Lalon Shah’s concept of the Moner Manush (the person within the mind) and distinguishes bhav (a relational mode of being) from bhakti (devotional hierarchy). His philosophy of roohaniath (spirituality) synthesizes Ibn Arabi’s Wahdatan al Wujud, Marxist critique, and Foucault’s political spirituality to challenge both secular nationalism and political Islam. The Nayakrishi Andolon, involving over three hundred thousand farming families, practices ecological agriculture based on ten principles including a ban on chemical pesticides, farmer managed seed systems, and the cultivation of uncultivated biodiversity. It maintains thousands of traditional rice varieties through community seed banks led by women, and advances the concept of food sovereignty as a constitutional right. Mazhar argues that the Green Revolution destroyed agro biodiversity and peasant knowledge, and that seed saving is a sophisticated form of practical epistemology. He connects the agrarian question to the theory of constituent power: genuine popular sovereignty requires control over seeds, land, and ecological resources. Mazhar’s constitutional theory, developed in his 2023 book Gono Ovyutthan o Gathan (Mass Uprising and Constitution), argues that Bangladesh’s 1972 constitution lacked genuine constituent legitimacy because it was drafted by a body elected for a different purpose. He traces the erosion of democracy through amendments like the Fifteenth Amendment (2011) and the use of the Digital Security Act to suppress dissent. The mass uprising of July and August 2024, which overthrew Sheikh Hasina’s government, was deeply influenced by Mazhar’s framework. Students and activists used his concept of constituent power to demand not just a change of government but a new constitutional order through a genuine constituent assembly. After the uprising, Mazhar remained critical, arguing that the transition remained incomplete and that both secular fascism and emerging religious nationalism threatened the revolution. Mazhar has paid a high personal price for his intellectual independence. He was arrested in 1995, triggering international protests from Nadine Gordimer, Jacques Derrida, and Mahasweta Devi. In 2017 he was forcibly disappeared for several days under circumstances that pointed to state security forces. Throughout his career he has refused alignment with any political party or ideological camp, maintaining a position of frank speech (parrhesia) that has made him a controversial figure equally attacked by secular nationalists, Islamists, and orthodox Marxists. His intellectual legacy spans multiple domains: a philosophical synthesis of Bengali spiritual traditions with Western critical theory; a constitutional theory of constituent power that helped shape the 2024 uprising; an agrarian philosophy that has preserved thousands of rice varieties and demonstrated the viability of ecological agriculture; and a model of public intellectual practice rooted in institutional independence, theoretical seriousness, and political courage. The February 2026 general election and constitutional referendum, in which the BNP won a two thirds majority and voters approved a reform package, represents both a partial vindication of constituent politics and a continuing test of whether the uprising’s aspirations will be fully realized. Mazhar continues to insist that the struggle against all forms of fascism, whether secular or religious, remains unfinished and that genuine democracy requires ongoing exercise of constituent power by the people.

title: Safety and Security Concerns of Journalists during the COVID-19 Pandemic in Bangladesh
authors: Pradip Kumar Panday; Mamun Abdul Kaioum; Shuvo Karmakar
venue: Athens Journal of Mass Media and Communications
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has caused increased safety and security challenges for journalists around the globe. However, in many developing nations, like Bangladesh, there is a dearth of knowledge regarding these adverse consequences of the journalism profession. This study intends to explore the safety and security issues faced by journalists in covering the COVID-19 pandemic for major newspapers, radio stations, television channels, and news portals. A total of sixty In-depth interviews (IDIs) using a semi-structured interview questionnaire and two Focus group discussions were conducted among journalists in person interview questionnaire and two Focus group discussions were conducted among journalists in-person in sixteen districts under two divisions of Bangladesh. The data were audio taped, transcribed, and later analysed utilizing the hierarchy of influence model. The study revealed four major dimensions of journalists such as physical, psychological, digital, and financial safety concerns. The data showed that most journalists faced financial hardship and mental distress due to a lack of regular salary, health insurance, and fear of infection and prosecution under the Digital Security Act for news reporting. They also suffered from obtaining safety equipment such as personal safety equipment (PPE), hand sanitizer and facemasks. The data indicate that, several safety and security challenges impacted news coverage and the overall state of journalism in Bangladesh during COVID-19 pandemic. Keywords: COVID-19 pandemic, safety and security, journalists, Bangladesh

title: Gender Equality and Women's Empowerment in Bangladesh: Progress, Challenges, and Policy Implications
venue: Econstor (Econstor)
abstract: This research aims to explore the developments, challenges, and prospects of gender equity and women empowerment in Bangladesh in the broader framework of national development and international commitments. While tremendous progress has been made in education, economic empowerment, political empowerment, and legislative measures, gender inequality still persists. The research is qualitative in nature and is based on secondary data sources, including government publications, international sources, and existing literature, to assess the status of women in education, economic empowerment, political empowerment, digitalization, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The study reveals tremendous progress in female enrollment in schools, microfinance services, and the symbolic representation of women in politics. However, high dropout rates, informal employment, financial exclusion, political powerlessness, and the digital divide continue to challenge women’s empowerment. The patriarchal system, discriminatory laws, and unequal distribution of productive resources also contribute to women’s vulnerability. The COVID-19 pandemic has intensified unpaid work, unemployment, and violence against women, raising concerns about sustaining these gains. Opportunities are identified in the digital revolution and women’s participation in STEM despite cyber harassment and digital exclusion. Achieving gender equality requires a holistic, rights-based, and gender-responsive approach emphasizing education, productive work, economic empowerment, political participation, digital empowerment, and social inclusion.

title: Islamic Law and Digital Evidence: Comparative Perspectives from Bangladesh, Malaysia, and the UAE
venue: Al-Arfa Journal of Sharia Islamic Economics and Law
abstract: The developments in digital technology has revolutionized the approach of modern judicial systems to collect, authenticate and present evidence. Nowadays, electronic evidence (comprising digital documents, emails, video files, metadata and forensic digital images) is a core part of litigation. Regrettably, there is a great deal of dispute over whether it is in line with the Koran. This research explores the admissibility of digital evidence in Bangladesh, Malaysia and the UAE under Islamic law. This article examines with a comparative and religious legal method some recent constitutional impacts, namely the UAE Cybercrime Law 2021, Malaysia’s Evidence Act 1990 (S. 90A), and Bangladesh’s Evidence (Amendment) Act 2022, discussing adherence to traditional fiqh principles qarīnah (circumstantial evidence), iqrār (confession), bayyinah (proof), and shahādah (testimony). The results indicate that the digital evidence meets these standards of authenticity, justifiable acquisition, certainty and integrity can be Shariah compliant. The Shariah-Compliant Digital Evidence Framework (SCDEF) that the study will proposes is an integration of forensic science and Islamic law to make justice compatible with maqāṣid al-Sharīʿah if it is based on protective factors such as moral purity, justice and factuality.

title: Effect of cybersecurity awareness on online safety behaviour among university students in Bangladesh
venue: Theseus (Ammattikorkeakoulujen)
abstract: This study examines cybersecurity of university students and also awareness of online safety for the students, with a primary focus on Bangladesh and a comparative perspective from Finland. The motivation for this analysis is the growing exposure of students to online security risks such as data breaches, phishing, and malware, as advanced digital systems are becoming part of personal and academic life. Even though cybersecurity is important, it does not always lead to the practice of safe online behaviour. This study is based on a quantitative research design, and the data were collected from 204 university students using an online questionnaire, which includes 37 respondents from Finland and 167 from Bangladesh. Awareness and online safety behaviour were measured through Likert scale items. Pearson correlation, descriptive statistics, and exploratory data analysis were used for data analysis to examine associations and patterns between the variables. The results of the students revealed that online safety behaviour is low (M = 3,86), and cybersecurity awareness is high (M = 4,17). There are some aspects, such as password management and the use of two-factor authentication, which also indicate that students are more consistent. Overall, however, they don't have as consistent a behaviour when it comes to software updates, maintaining security tools and managing privacy settings. A strong positive correlation (r = 0,73) was observed, indicating that higher awareness is associated with safer behaviour. It is concluded that awareness of cybersecurity is not satisfactory to ensure consistent safe online behaviour. The study highlights the importance of practical cybersecurity with focus on user behaviour, particularly in strengthening applied digital safety practices.

title: Regulatory Control and Self-Censorship in Social Media: Stifling Freedom of Expression in Bangladesh
venue: Journal of Asian and African Studies
abstract: This article examines the impact of regulatory control and self-censorship on social media in Bangladesh, focusing on the Digital Security Act (DSA). The regime employed the DSA to suppress dissent, monitor online activity, and stifle freedom of expression, creating an atmosphere of fear and self-censorship among citizens, journalists, and activists. Social media platforms became tools for political control, with users facing legal consequences for criticizing the government. This regulatory environment undermined democratic participation and restricted the diversity of public discourse, impeding the free exchange of ideas essential to democratic governance. By exploring the legal frameworks and user behavior, the article highlights the tension between protecting national security and safeguarding free speech, questioning how these regulations align with international human rights standards. The findings emphasize the broader implications for democracy and freedom of expression in Bangladesh.

title: Securing Digital Services in Bangladesh: A Decentralized Identity Verification Framework Using Blockchain and Cryptography
authors: Md. Sakibul Islam Sheikh; Md. Dipu; Maksudur Rahmand; Kazi Riadul Islam; Naeem Shahriar; Md Mahedi Hasan; Md Zahurul Haque
venue: International Journal of Computer Applications
abstract: In today's digital environment, secure and trustworthy identity management is critical as centralized systems remain vulnerable to data breaches, identity theft, and unauthorized access.This paper presents a blockchain-based decentralized identity verification framework that enhances data security, privacy, and user control by eliminating reliance on centralized authorities.The proposed system integrates smart contracts, decentralized identifiers (DIDs), and cryptographic security to enable tamper-resistant and transparent identity verification.Sensitive user documents are encrypted using AES-256-GCM and stored off-chain on IPFS, while only cryptographic hashes and verification records are recorded on the blockchain to preserve privacy and data integrity.Key management is strengthened through HKDF-based derivation, and users can selectively disclose identity attributes using privacy-preserving techniques.Experimental analysis indicates that the system significantly reduces identity fraud, improves verification accuracy, and enhances auditability and scalability.The solution is well-suited for applications in finance, healthcare, e-governance, and secure third-party authentication platforms.

title: The State–Corporate Nexus in Cyber Surveillance and Its Impact on Civil Liberties: A Comparative Study of Bangladesh and India
authors: Md. Saiful Islam; Ashiq Iqbal Jishad
venue: World Affairs
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the state‐corporate nexus of digital surveillance and its impacts on civil liberties through a comparative analysis of Bangladesh and India. It seeks to investigate how the states enable monitoring, censorship, and state‐controlled surveillance by partnering with corporates, enacting strict laws, and securitizing discourses. Private firms in both countries harness state power with new technology to erode privacy and democratic values, and to establish a “controlled” society. Similarly, by introducing laws such as the Digital Security Act (2018) and Cyber Security Act (2023) in Bangladesh, and by implementing digital regulations and Aadhaar initiatives in India, both states justify institutional surveillance within a legal framework. The study also scrutinizes the state‐corporate nexus through securitization theory, the influence of surveillance capitalism, endorsing surveillance through judicial provisions, and the impacts of securitization efforts of states over civil liberties.

title: From Registration to Financial Agency: A Five-Stage Pathway and A Gender-Responsive Scorecard for Women’s Digital Financial Inclusion in Bangladesh
authors: Niger Sultana; Md. Shahed Alamm; Ummey Sumaiya; Md. Baharul Hasan; Md. Aminul Islam
venue: International journal of human research and social science studies.
abstract: Purpose: Bangladesh counts more than 239 million registered mobile financial service (MFS) accounts, yet registration alone says little about whether women can control and use digital money for their own purposes. This paper reframes women’s digital financial inclusion as financial agency and asks where the pathway from registration to agency breaks down. Design/methodology/approach: The study is a structured policy review combined with a secondary-data descriptive analysis. It draws on Global Findex indicators for Bangladesh (2017, 2021 and 2024 survey waves), Bangladesh Bank statistics and regulations (MFS data, no-frill account reports, e-KYC guidelines, the National Financial Inclusion Strategy 2021–2026) and peer-reviewed research on mobile money, intrahousehold control and digital fraud. Findings: Women’s account ownership fell from 43.5% in 2021 to 33.4% in 2024 while the gender gap widened slightly to 20.2 percentage points. Only 49.3% of women had a SIM card registered in their own name and 21.4% could change a phone PIN without help, against 74.0% and 38.7% of men. Bangladesh Bank recorded 101.02 million female and 137.88 million male registered MFS accounts in February 2025, but publishes no sex-disaggregated activity data. The paper organizes barriers along five stages (access, activation, regular use, productive use and resilience) and proposes a Gender-Responsive Digital Finance Scorecard that pairs each volume indicator with a control or protection indicator. Originality/value: The paper moves measurement from counting accounts to auditing control, safety and remedy. Implications: Regulators and banks can adopt the scorecard to standardize sex-disaggregated activity, credential-control and complaint data.

title: Forensic Accounting Adaptation in Professional Courses Benefits, Challenges, Tools, and Framework — A Bangladesh Perspective
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Forensic accounting has emerged as an essential discipline for combating financial fraud, corruption,money laundering, cybercrime, and corporate misconduct. In Bangladesh, rising concerns over bankingfraud, tax evasion and weak corporate governance have heightened the demand for forensic accountingprofessionals. This paper examines the adaptation of forensic accounting into professional accounting andbusiness education and evaluates its benefits for professional sectors and industries. The study exploreschallenges, technological tools, implementation frameworks, and strategic recommendations. A mixedconceptual–empirical method is adopted, combining secondary literature with an illustrative survey (n =220) and an OLS regression linking awareness, curriculum adequacy, and analytics skill to perceivedfraud-detection capability. Findings indicate that integrating forensic accounting into CA, CMA, ACCA,MBA and university programs can significantly strengthen fraud detection, audit quality, transparency andstakeholder confidence in Bangladesh.Keywords: Forensic Accounting, Bangladesh, Fraud Detection, Professional Education, CorporateGovernance, Audit, Financial Crime, ACCA, ICAB, ICMAB

title: “We are like brothers”: Free Fire, masculinity, and neoliberalism in semi-urban Bangladesh
venue: International Journal of Adolescence and Youth
abstract: This paper explores why semi-urban Bangladeshi youth play Free Fire and how the game affects them. The game's popularity among semi-urban youth from middle- and lower-middle-income families, alongside real-life violent events, rationalized this study. Over 1.5 years, digital ethnography was conducted with 28 semi-urban Free Fire-playing youth in Rajshahi, revealing that players were driven by peer pressure, a desire for belonging, low hardware requirements, and cross-border interaction. While playing the game increased players’ self-confidence and fostered a sense of community, it also led to disengagement from studies, aggression, cyberbullying, and financial stress. These outcomes, driven by class-based aspirations, religious identity, and masculinity, have introduced neoliberal governmentality among gamers, normalizing self-investment and participation in the global market. This research addresses a gap in studies of the emerging mobile-based gaming culture among non-affluent, non-urban youth in the Global South and explores how unique contextual factors shape this culture.

title: Effectiveness of National ID as a Unique Identifier for Customer Onboarding in Financial Services in Bangladesh: A Survey
authors: Muhammad Shakil Pervez; Md. Nasim Adnan; Ismat Rahman; Moinul Islam Zaber; Sarker Tanveer Ahmed Rumee
venue: Computer and Information Science
abstract: National identity systems lie at the heart of every government’s identity management infrastructure. In Bangladesh, the National Identification Number (NID) has emerged as the primary credential for citizen identification, yet its integration with the financial sector—particularly for electronic Know Your Customer (e-KYC) compliance—remains fragmented, inconsistent, and vulnerable. This study investigates the effectiveness of the NID as a single authentication identifier for customer onboarding in Bangladesh’s banking and non-banking financial institution (NBFI) sector. We conducted semi-structured interviews with ICT heads and technically responsible personnel across 61 banks and 35 NBFIs, supplemented by a structured questionnaire survey covering six key dimensions: single authentication ID usage, e-KYC service operations, onboarding challenges, personally identifiable information (PII) handling, identity theft exposure, and agent banking practices. A mixed-methods analytical approach was applied, combining quantitative survey responses with qualitative thematic coding. Our findings reveal sixteen distinct vulnerabilities and operational gaps grouped into three categories: identity theft, privacy vulnerabilities, and technical vulnerabilities. Notably, the majority of institutions rely on manual, paper-dependent verification processes; the Bangladesh Election Commission (BEC) API constitutes a single point of failure for onboarding verification across hundreds of organizations; and a significant proportion of banks retain NID data beyond its intended purpose. Despite these challenges, we demonstrate that a Federated Identity Management (FIM) system built on the existing NID infrastructure is technically feasible and would substantially reduce administrative burden, improve security, and enable seamless cross-sector identity federation.

title: Digitalization without Confidence: The Role of Institutional Transparency in Shaping Youth Involvement in Bangladesh's Financial Market
authors: Ashiqun Nabi; Hasib Ahmed; Jannatul Ferdaus; Asif Abdullah; Ashrafun Nahar; Akilama Akter Srity
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The paper focuses on the role of institutional transparency in encouraging the youth to participate in the financial market of Bangladesh amid the high financial digitalization. Despite the increased access to financial activities by mobile banking and online platforms, which are digitized financial services, young people are still underrepresented in formal investment markets. The paper fills this gap by investigating the connection between digitalization, institutional transparency, trust, and youth involvement in a financial market.A mixed-methods research design was identified. The survey questionnaires were used to gather quantitative data and 94 youth respondents provided survey questionnaires and 91 valid responses were subjected to SPSS to conduct analysis. The qualitative data were gathered in a form of semi-structured interviews with 8 participants and analyzed using thematic analysis with NVivo. According to the results of the survey, there is a high representation of digital financial use by young people as 76.6% of the surveyed use digital financial services on a regular basis. Nevertheless, investor confidence is low with only 40.7% of the respondents confident in the financial market of Bangladesh with 35.2% being neutral and 24.2% unconfident. The research also reveals that 70.3 of the respondents said that the absence of transparency makes them reluctant to invest and the majority of 56.1 said that they do not invest because they do not trust.The survey results are corroborated by the interview results which indicate that digitalization has made things more convenient and more accessible but it has not made serious investment engagement. According to the respondents, unclear information, poor accountability, corruption, risk of fraud, market manipulations, and financial illiteracy are some of the greatest obstacles to youth participation. The research finds that meaning youth participation can be guaranteed only through digitalization, but only backed up by institutional transparency, greater regulation, dependable disclosure, investor protection and financial literacy. The research adds to the financial inclusion knowledge, demonstrating that access to digital financial services does not necessarily generate confidence in financial markets. It suggests that financial institutions, the regulators, and educational institutions should collaborate to establish a more transparent, safe, and youth friendly financial sector in Bangladesh.

title: Coping with Digital Risk in Urban Bangladesh: Fintech Adoption Across Different Levels of Usage Experience
authors: M. Sirajul Islam; Tawsif Shafayet Ali; Suntu Kumar Ghosh; Md. Mahfuz Ashraf
venue: FinTech
abstract: Fintech adoption increasingly takes place in digital environments where users must balance the convenience of financial technologies against persistent risks of fraud, scams, account misuse, and unauthorized access. This study examines the associations of cybersecurity literacy, perceived fintech security, and institutional trust with fintech adoption among urban users in Bangladesh, with particular attention to secure user behaviour and differences across levels of fintech usage experience. Data from 357 respondents were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), including indirect effects and multi-group analysis. Cybersecurity literacy, perceived fintech security, and secure user behaviour have significant positive associations with adoption, although their individual effect sizes are small. Institutional trust has no significant direct association with adoption. The indirect association through secure user behaviour is significant for cybersecurity literacy but not for perceived fintech security or institutional trust. Measurement invariance checks support standardized path comparisons across the three tenure groups, but none of the nine focal comparisons is significant using two-sided bootstrap MGA at the 5% level. A four-band sensitivity analysis does not establish robust differences after adjustment for multiple comparisons. The model accounts for 61.0% of the in-sample variance in adoption; out-of-sample predictive performance was not assessed. The findings therefore support a cautious, association-based account of security-related fintech use among existing users, without establishing causal effects or developmental changes with experience.

title: Public Figures, Criminal Defamation, and Free Speech: The Missing Public Figure Doctrine in Bangladesh Law
venue: Dhaka University Law Journal
abstract: Defamation law balances free expression and the protection of individuals' reputations. But in Bangladesh, all defamation claims are treated alike and remain criminalised, with no distinction between public officials and private persons or higher proof standards for public figures. Provisions in the Penal Code 1860 and the Digital Security Act 2018 have been used against journalists and critics, chilling democratic debate to silence them. This article argues for reform through decriminalisation, a serious-harm requirement, and a public figure doctrine based on “actual malice.” Drawing inspiration from U.S., U.K., and Indian jurisprudence, it highlights constitutional and policy reasons for stronger protection of speech about public power and concludes with practical legislative and judicial recommendations. title: Growth-Trends of Bank-Led Digital Transactions: A SWOT Analysis of Voluntary Insurance as a New Product in Bangladesh Economy
venue: Journal of Financial Risk Management
abstract: Bank-led digital banking is an important service in today’s economy country-wise where Bangladesh is no exception. But this development faces severe drawbacks, being its insecurity where psychological risk factors in multi-faucets dominate a customer’s or a probable customer’s decision not to use it. It has resulted in slow growth trends of bank-led digital services in economy. Focusing on the issues underpinning Akim’s Model, Voluntary Insurance (VI), can be introduced as a low-cost or fixed-price new product. It can enhance consumer surplus, bank profits, and overall transaction volume. When VI-product is on market, it will spread from bankers to banking-customers. The growth-trend (S-curve) of VI-products will capture revenue-growth against time. In return, it will ensure higher transaction numbers of e-banking. With the prospect, this study brings the VI new product to Bangladesh policymakers’ attentions for its efforts. The SWOT Analysis clearly shows that VI can mitigate perceived risks (hacking, fraud, errors) for users, thereby increasing trust, accelerating adoption of cashless services. It will function as a risk-transfer mechanism for on-the-go or bank-led digital banking transactions, which is crucial for digital-forward economies. It can ensure cashless society soon.

title: Understanding online violence against women in Bangladesh: Sociocultural drivers, legal awareness, and institutional responses
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of digital technology and widespread internet access in Bangladesh have created new opportunities for communication, education, and engagement, particularly for women. However, these developments have also led to new forms of crime, including digital gender-based violence. This study examines the perceived prevalence, sociocultural dimensions, and legal aspects of online violence against young digitally active women in Bangladesh. Using a quantitative research design supported by qualitative findings, the study found that online violence against women is perceived to be highly prevalent among internet users in Bangladesh. Many participants reported that they experienced multiple forms of abuse, including harassment, impersonation, hate speech, stalking, sextortion, and doxing. The findings further showed that harassment is not limited to anonymous online offenders, as perpetrators were also perceived to include acquaintances, friends, and intimate partners, reflecting offline power dynamics in digital spaces. Participants also reported serious psychological effects, including anxiety and emotional distress. Despite existing legal frameworks, respondents expressed limited confidence in institutional responses. Fear of social stigmatisation, lack of awareness of legal remedies, and mistrust of enforcement mechanisms were identified as major barriers to reporting. The study concludes that online violence against women may be reduced through stronger legal enforcement, improved reporting systems, greater public awareness, and gender-sensitive institutional support, helping to create a safer online environment for women.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Trust and Uninterrupted Usage Intention in AI Financial Service: Evidence from Bangladeshi Consumers
venue: Journal of Economics Finance and Management Studies
abstract: In the case of financial services, AI is transforming the industry by offering automated support, one-on-one recommendations, digital payments, fraud detection, and decision-assistance based on data. Nevertheless, the long-term effectiveness of the AI-based financial services relies on consumer trust and the intention to use it constantly. This paper discusses the impact of perceived AI ability, AI visibility, AI customization, perceived security and privacy safeguard, and perceived risk on trust and continuance intention among the consumers of Bangladesh. Quantitative survey design was employed and 630 valid responses were examined using the partial least squares structural equation modelling. The measurement model yielded strong reliability, convergent, discriminant and acceptable collinearity. It is represented in the structural results that the perceived AI capability, AI transparency, AI personalization, and security and privacy protection are positively related to trust, whereas perceived risk is negatively related to trust. Trust is a significant predictor of continuous usage intention and shows mediating relations to all suggested indirect relationships. There also exists moderate explanatory power, predictive relevance, predictive power and acceptable supplementary fit in the model. The conclusions are that sustainable AI-oriented financial services must have effective systems, good explanations, responsible personalization, robust privacy protection, and risk mitigation measures. The research has implications to financial institutions, fintech providers, and regulators interested in retaining consumers in the emerging digital finance markets and inclusive digital transformation in Bangladesh today.

title: Constitutional Pathologies and Popular Sovereignty: Bangladesh's Journey from the 1972 Founding to the July Charter
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This book tells the story of a promise written in blood and broken by power. In 1972, after a savage liberation war that cost three million lives, the newly born nation of Bangladesh adopted one of the most ambitious constitutions in the post‑colonial world. Its architects, led by the country’s founding father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, inscribed four sacred pillars into the document: nationalism, socialism, democracy, and secularism. They believed that a carefully crafted text could forever prevent the horrors of 1971, the mass killings, the systematic rape, the state sponsored terror that they had just escaped. That belief was shattered in less than three years. By 1975, the same founding leader had used the constitution’s own amendment procedure to abolish parliament, ban all political parties except his own, and turn the presidency into a dictatorship. The Fourth Amendment of 1975 was not a coup from outside. It was a constitutional revolution from within. It replaced the Westminster style parliamentary system with a one party state called BAKSAL. The free press was strangled. The Prime Minister’s unchecked power became the template for every future strongman. What followed is a dizzying cycle of martial law, military coups, and constitutional laundering. General Ziaur Rahman seized power in 1975, ruled under martial law, then passed the Fifth Amendment of 1979 to retroactively validate every single decree he had issued. General Hussain Muhammad Ershad did the same in the 1980s, using the Seventh and Eighth Amendments to scrub his own coup from legal memory and even insert Islam as the state religion. The constitution became a rag doll, pulled apart by generals and civilian autocrats alike, each one adding patches to suit their survival. The book does not just narrate events. It puts you inside the courtroom battles that tried to save the constitution. You will learn about the landmark Anwar Hossain Chowdhury case of 1989, where the Supreme Court of Bangladesh bravely adopted the basic structure doctrine from India, ruling that even a constitutional amendment cannot destroy the essential features of the constitution like judicial independence and democratic governance. You will then witness the heartbreaking betrayal of that doctrine in 2011, when the same court, now packed with loyalists, upheld the Fifteenth Amendment that abolished the caretaker government system and inserted the infamous Article 7B, an eternal clause that declared one third of the constitution unamendable forever. The narrative then turns to the brutal 2009 to 2024 era of Sheikh Hasina. You will see how her government weaponized the Digital Security Act of 2018 to imprison journalists and activists for Facebook posts. You will read about the 2014 and 2018 elections, where the opposition was either boycotted or crushed, and the ruling party won 96 percent of parliament seats in results that international observers called a sham. You will follow the case of Chief Justice S.K. Sinha, who dared to strike down the Sixteenth Amendment that would have made judges removable by parliament. His reward was a campaign of state intimidation, forced resignation, and exile to Australia. The judiciary, once a guardian, became a captive. The climax of this textbook is the July 2024 uprising. It started as a student protest against a 30 percent job quota for descendants of freedom fighters, a system that had become a tool of patronage for the ruling party. The government responded with live ammunition, mass arrests, and a nationwide internet shutdown that lasted days. Hundreds of students were killed. But the protests did not stop. They swelled into a tsunami of millions, from rickshaw pullers to garment workers to doctors. On August 5, 2024, Sheikh Hasina fled the country on a military helicopter. The constitution had been suspended not by generals but by the people. What followed is the most fascinating and uncertain part of the story. An interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus took power in a constitutional vacuum. It created eleven reform commissions. The Constitutional Reform Commission, headed by Professor Ali Riaz, produced a January 2025 report calling for a radical rewrite of the constitution. The July Charter of 2025 was born from months of tense negotiation between 24 political parties, though the Awami League was excluded and the BNP had reservations. The charter proposed a bicameral parliament with a 100 seat Senate elected by proportional representation, two term limits for the prime minister, the abolition of Article 70’s anti defection clause, the restoration of the caretaker government system, and the recognition of all mother languages as state languages alongside Bengali. In February 2026, Bangladesh held a historic referendum alongside its general election. Voters approved the July Charter with 61 percent in favor on a 60 percent turnout. But the moment of triumph quickly turned into a new constitutional crisis. The newly elected BNP government, which won a two thirds supermajority, refused to take the second oath that would have formed the Constitution Reform Council mandated by the referendum. Opposition parties, led by Jamaat e Islami and the National Citizen Party, boycotted parliament. The BNP argued that the council was not approved by parliament and that any amendment must follow Article 142. Its opponents cried betrayal, saying the referendum mandate was being ignored. This textbook takes you deep into that crisis. You will read about the Supreme Court’s role, including its explosive November 2025 ruling that reinstated the caretaker government system and called the earlier abolition the judicial murder of democracy. You will examine the proposed new National Constitutional Council, a multipartisan body designed to appoint election commissioners, anti corruption chiefs, and human rights commissioners, insulating them from executive capture. You will grapple with the fate of Article 7B, which has now been declared unconstitutional by the apex court, opening the door to amendments that were previously frozen. The book also expands beyond Bangladesh’s borders. It examines the extraordinary International Criminal Court jurisdiction over the Rohingya deportation, where Bangladesh’s territory became the legal hook to prosecute Myanmar’s generals. It scrutinizes the International Crimes Tribunal, originally built to try 1971 war criminals, now expanded to prosecute the July 2024 killings, and the serious fair trial concerns that still haunt it. It analyzes the gap between Bangladesh’s treaty obligations under CEDAW, the ICCPR, and the Convention Against Torture, and the domestic laws that routinely violate them. More than anything, this book is a philosophical and political education. It explains why Article 70 turned MPs into zombies. It shows how the first past the post electoral system manufactured supermajorities that did not reflect the popular vote. It dissects the political economy of centralization, why every government, regardless of party, has preferred weak local councils and strong Dhaka rule. It explores the forgotten promise of the 1997 Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord and the indigenous peoples still waiting for land rights and autonomy. It ends with a sobering question: can Bangladesh break its cycle of constitutional hope and authoritarian relapse? The author writes with urgency and clarity, drawing on comparative cases from South Africa, India, Germany, and Indonesia. Each chapter is a deep dive into a critical institution: the judiciary, the election commission, the anti corruption commission, the ombudsman that was never appointed, the human rights commission that was starved of funds. The final part, titled The Constitution in the Crucible, confronts the present moment directly. It weighs the prospects of the BNP government honoring the referendum, the role of the courts as a check on executive power, and the enduring power of the people who proved in 2024 that they are the ultimate guardians of the constitution. This is not a book for passive reading. It is a call to understand how a nation’s supreme law can be both a shield and a weapon, and how ordinary citizens, armed with nothing but courage, can force a new beginning.

title: Social Media Start-Ups: Barriers and Possibilities for Rural Women in the F-Commerce Space of Bangladesh
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
abstract: Over the past decade, the proliferation of social media platforms has opened new avenues for micro-entrepreneurship in Bangladesh, most significantly through Facebook-based commerce (F-commerce). This study examines the structural challenges and coping strategies of rural women entrepreneurs engaged in F-commerce, with particular attention to how digital opportunities intersect with gendered social structures and informal market conditions across selected districts of northern Bangladesh. Employing a qualitative research design, the study draws on in-depth interviews (IDIs) with 25 rural women business operators and four key informant interviews (KIIs) with individuals holding professional expertise in women’s entrepreneurship and digital business environments. The findings reveal that entry into F-commerce was predominantly driven by income insecurity, particularly in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, and further facilitated by exposure to other women-led online businesses. While F-commerce reduced entry barriers and enabled flexible, home-based income generation, participants encountered persistent structural challenges. These included delivery-related fraud and customer refusal in cash-on-delivery (COD) transactions, the absence of consumer and seller protection mechanisms, restricted access to formal financial services, and conditional household support shaped by patriarchal norms. The compounding burden of domestic responsibilities and emotional stress associated with online harassment further jeopardised business sustainability. The study concludes that F-commerce functions principally as an adaptive livelihood strategy rather than an assured pathway to economic empowerment for rural digital entrepreneurs. Sustainable digital entrepreneurship for rural women requires structural interventions that extend well beyond digital access and skills training to encompass platform protection, financial inclusion, recognition of gendered labour burdens, and coherent institutional support mechanisms.

title: Institutional Fragility and Cross-Border Cyber Risk in Financial Systems: Insights from the 2016 Bangladesh Bank Heist
venue: Computers
abstract: This paper investigates how institutional fragilities shape cross-border cyber risk in financial systems, using the 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist as an illustrative case from a developing-country context. Drawing on a scoping review of the multidisciplinary literature on cybersecurity governance, financial cybercrime, and cross-border cyber risk, combined with an exploratory case study, the Bangladesh Bank heist is explored through a multi-level analytical lens encompassing macro-level institutional and geopolitical factors, meso-level ecosystem interdependencies, and micro-level organizational vulnerabilities. The analysis suggests that the 2016 heist was not solely a technical intrusion but was also associated with broader governance, regulatory, infrastructural, and organizational weaknesses. Fragmented governance arrangements, digital dependencies, limited operational resilience, inadequate cybersecurity controls, and human-factor vulnerabilities emerged as important dimensions of risk. Comparison with selected incidents from other developing and emerging economies indicates that similar patterns may occur across different institutional settings, although their manifestation remains context dependent. Rather than advancing a general theory, the highlights the importance of strengthening governance capacity, regulatory coordination, and cyber resilience within globally interconnected financial systems.

title: The Role of Social Media and Digital Marketing in Bangladesh's Fashion Market: A Study of Young Women Entrepreneurs
venue: Pacific Journal of Business Innovation and Strategy
abstract: The shift of digital technology and social media platforms in developing economies has revolutionized the market's dynamics and presented unparalleled opportunities for the growth and development of micro and small businesses. The purpose of this study is to explore the importance of social media and Digital Marketing in the fashion and garments industry of Bangladesh where 18–35 age group female entrepreneurs are working as a micro, small enterprises in the field of clothing and garments. The study uses qualitative mixed methods design that involves 20 In-depth Interviews (IDIs) with young women entrepreneurs, four Focus Group Discussions (FGDs), eight Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) with SME support officers, digital marketing experts, representatives from the fashion industry, women entrepreneur association leaders, managers of ecommerce platforms, and development practitioners from NGO.The study uses qualitative mixed methods design, which includes 20 In-depth Interviews (IDIs) with young women entrepreneurs, four Focus Group Discussions (FGDs), and eight Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) with SME support officers, digital marketing experts, representatives from the fashion industry, women entrepreneur association leaders, managers of ecommerce platforms, and NGO development practitioners in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Thematic analysis of primary data indicates that four major platforms are used by young women entrepreneurs for creating brand visibility, customer interaction and sales – Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and WhatsApp. The results also show that there is a positive relationship between digital marketing strategies and business growth, customer trust, and market expansion. There are still many challenges, such as digital illiteracy, lack of affordable internet connection, gender norms, cyberbullying and lack of financial resources. The study concludes that there is a clear need for specific digital marketing training, gender-inclusive policy frameworks, mentorship ecosystems, and the involvement of government, NGOs and private sector actors by collaborating with each other to provide support. Results are added to the body of literature on digital entrepreneurship, gender and development as well as SME promotion in the South Asian context.

title: GAPS AND SHORTCOMINGS IN THE CYBER SECURITY POLICY OF PAKISTAN (2021): A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS WITH THE NATIONAL CYBER SECURITY POLICY OF BANGLADESH
venue: Policy Research Journal
abstract: National cyber security policy has emerged as a critical instrument of state governance in an era defined by accelerating digital transformation, increasingly sophisticated threat actors, and expanding critical infrastructure dependence on networked systems. This study examines the gaps and shortcomings in Pakistan’s National Cyber Security Policy (2021) through a systematic comparative analysis with Bangladesh’s National Cyber Security Strategy (2023). Employing a qualitative comparative policy analysis methodology grounded in document analysis, the study applies a structured evaluation framework derived from established scholarly criteria for assessing national cyber security strategies. Five comparative dimensions are examined: research and development orientation, cyber security education and capacity building, risk assessment and incident response mechanisms, cybercrime governance and institutional frameworks, and public-private partnership architecture. The findings reveal that while Pakistan’s policy acknowledges the principal dimensions of modern cyber security governance, it exhibits structural deficiencies in implementation specificity, institutional coordination, educational integration, and stakeholder engagement breadth relative to Bangladesh’s more operationally detailed and comprehensively scoped strategy. Key gaps include the absence of a funded national cyber security research agenda, underdeveloped public-private collaboration mechanisms, limited integration of cyber security competencies into national educational curricula, and inadequate victim protection frameworks for individuals and e-commerce participants. The study concludes with evidence-grounded recommendations for policy revision aligned with international cyber security governance standards including the ITU Global Cybersecurity Agenda and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, and contributes to the comparative cyber policy literature on South Asian developing economies

title: Prevalence and Associated Risk Factors of Suicidal Tendencies Among Bangladeshi Public University Students: A Mixed‐Methods Exploration
authors: Nurul Islam Uzzal; Md. Al‐Mamun; Md. Majnur Rashid; Abul Kalam
venue: Health Science Reports
abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Aims This study investigates the prevalence and associated risk factors of suicidal tendencies among public university students in Bangladesh. Methods This study design was employed with a total of 200 participants (male: 118; female: 82). Data collection utilized a mixed‐methods approach, combining online and offline surveys with in‐depth interviews. The survey instrument captured socio‐demographic characteristics, risk factors for suicidal tendencies, prevalence, perception levels, and potential mitigation strategies. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS 26 and NVivo 12 software. Results Multinomial logistic regression identified significant associations between suicidal tendencies and age ( p < 0.002), screen time ( p < 0.047), and the interaction of prevalence level with age ( p < 0.004). Additional findings revealed strong relationships between cyberbullying and suicide with income ( p < 0.02), media contagion effect with income ( p < 0.024), and age with suicidal cases inducing suicidal tendencies ( p < 0.034). Correlation analyses highlighted cyberbullying, stressful life events, media contagion, screen time, and easy access to suicide‐related information as key contributors to suicidal behavior (mean = 0.364). Conclusion This study underscores significant associations between suicidal tendencies and factors such as age, income, cyberbullying, media contagion, online platforms, and access to suicide‐related information. The findings emphasize the need for targeted interventions addressing these determinants to mitigate the rising incidence of suicidal tendencies among university students.

title: Cyberbullying Victimization and Offending Dataset
venue: Figshare
abstract: Background: The rapid expansion of digital communication has intensified concerns about cyberbullying, particularly within medical education where students face unique vulnerabilities due to heavy internet use and hierarchical training structures. This study investigated the prevalence and correlates of cyberbullying among medical students at Sirajganj Medical College, Bangladesh. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional survey in January 2026 among 311 students using the Cyberbullying Victimization and Offending Scale. Analytical approaches included Firth's penalized-likelihood logistic regression and quadratic regression. Results: Findings revealed that 17.0% of students reported victimization, while 10.3% admitted to offending behaviors. Male students were disproportionately involved in offending (19.2% vs. 4.7% among females). Quadratic regression identified a curvilinear, inverted U-shaped relationship, indicating that offending peaked at moderate levels of victimization but declined at higher levels. Given sparse subgroup sizes, Firth's penalized-likelihood logistic regression was used for multivariable analysis. Reflecting a victim–offender overlap rather than a directional exposure–outcome relationship, victimization and offending were each strongly associated with the other (victimization associated with offending: OR = 33.04; 95% CI: 12.21–107.11; p < 0.001; offending associated with victimization: OR = 35.40; 95% CI: 12.94–114.22; p < 0.001). Victimization was independently associated with rural residence (OR = 2.53), living with family (OR = 4.45), and higher household income (OR = 3.17; all p < 0.05), while male sex and marital status showed positive, borderline-significant associations with offending (female OR = 0.39, p = 0.056; married OR = 4.36, p = 0.053). Conclusion: This study underscores a pronounced victim–offender overlap in cyberbullying, whereby victimization and offending were strongly associated with one another; the cross-sectional design precludes conclusions about temporal or causal direction. Contextual factors, including rural residence, living arrangement, and household income, were independently associated with victimization risk, while male sex and marital status showed borderline associations with offending that warrant further investigation. Institutional strategies should prioritize digital safety education, psychosocial support, and policy frameworks to address this overlap and foster safer online environments within medical training contexts.

title: GIS-based hybrid modelling for sustainable tourism planning and service quality gap assessment in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh
authors: Md Ashrafuzzaman Pramanik; Muhammad Ariful Islam; Abu Nayem Md. Kayes; Md. Hasan Mahmud; Kazi Mst. Hurajannat Tuba; Tayub Bin Shahajahan
venue: Next Sustainability
abstract: The tourism industry is integral to a country’s GDP, for Bangladesh as well. It is apparent that Cox’s Bazar is lagging behind in proper planning, environmentally friendly approaches, and service quality. It is a paradigm of haphazard development and Infrastructure-dependent over the environment. This study aims to identify quality gaps, key planning factors for eco-tourism development, and suitable sites using GIS-based hybrid modelling in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Primary data were collected from 386 tourists through a semi-structured questionnaire survey using gender-stratified sampling. The survey was conducted during the peak tourist season; therefore, the reported satisfaction levels primarily reflect the perceptions of peak-season visitors and may not fully represent visitor experiences across different seasons or demographic and travel-purpose groups. Secondary data were collected from Landsat 8, the weather and climate website, and the Cox’s Bazar Development Authority. This study employed PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses), Multicriteria Satisfaction Analysis, Fuzzy logic, Random Forest, K-means clustering, and Radial Basis Function Neural Network methods for data analysis. Cox’s Bazar performs well in hotel cleanliness (72.30%), staff behaviour (75.83%), and Regional transport affordability (68.56–68.94%), reflecting strong core tourism potential (overall satisfaction: 62.17%). However, very low satisfaction with scam control (21.45%), public toilets (20.65%), beach shower facilities (18.23%), and night safety (41.78%) highlights critical gaps that limit the visitor experience. Along with this study, the area was delineated into five zones from the backshore to 900 m, with the most inappropriate area being the Central Business District of Cox’s Bazar. This study suggests strengthening transport governance with regulated fares, licensed vehicles, monitoring systems, and a fixed-route electric tram, alongside improved basic facilities. Promote sustainable tourism through decentralization, eco-tourism development, and enhanced safety measures.

title: From Cyber Security to Digital Control: A Comparative Analysis of Speech-Regulating Cyber Laws in Bangladesh and Southeast Asia
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract This policy brief examines the evolution of speech-regulating cyber laws in Bangladesh from 2006 through late 2026, comparing the country's regulatory trajectory with three Southeast Asian models: Singapore's executive correction regime, Malaysia's platform licensing system, and Indonesia's criminal defamation framework. The analysis evaluates statutory provisions across six criteria: clarity of offences, procedural safeguards, content-blocking mechanisms, platform obligations, accountability of enforcement authorities, and proportionality of penalties. It investigates whether legislation justified through national security and cybersecurity objectives functions primarily as protection against digital threats or creates broader mechanisms of executive control over political discourse. The brief addresses three questions: What procedural and substantive safeguards did Bangladesh's Cyber Security Ordinance 2025 introduce, and which of these could be weakened or removed under the proposed October 2026 draft amendment? How do the regulatory approaches of Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia compare in balancing regulatory objectives with freedom of expression and civil liberties? What legislative safeguards could address legitimate online harms, including malicious AI-generated deepfakes and severe cyber abuse, while reducing the risk of disproportionate restrictions on expression? The comparative assessment is benchmarked against international human rights standards, particularly Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the UN Human Rights Committee's General Comment No. 34, and the Rabat Plan of Action. The brief advances the hypothesis that cyber laws framed around broad security imperatives can expand executive discretion over online expression unless offences are narrowly defined, restrictions meet explicit harm thresholds, and content-blocking decisions are subject to independent prior judicial review. Digital control is therefore treated as an analytical proposition to be evaluated against statutory provisions, procedural safeguards, and documented enforcement practices, rather than as an assumed conclusion. Scope and status: This analysis covers the legal and policy position examined up to 1 November 2026. It is a comparative legal-policy assessment and policy brief, not a peer-reviewed journal article.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Post-Flood Security and Resource Planning in Bangladesh: A Review and Conceptual Framework
authors: Rahim Ahmed Druba; Ahsan Habib Shihab; Aman Mussa; Мадина Мансурова
venue: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence & Networking (QPAIN)
abstract: Bangladesh is highly vulnerable to floods, with around 70 million people living in flood prone areas and a large share of the population exposed to high flood risk. Disaster response increasingly depends on detailed household data for forecasting, evacuation, and aid distribution. When this data is collected and stored centrally, it exposes vulnerable groups, especially women, children, and displaced families, to theft, harassment, trafficking, and gender based violence through misuse or data breaches. We review federated learning applications in disaster management and propose a simple conceptual framework for privacy preserving post flood security and resource planning in Bangladesh. The framework model is structured into 04 layers, namely, local data collection, federated training, secure aggregation, and personalized deployment. A structured review of 45 studies covering federated learning algorithms, privacy mechanisms such as secure aggregation and differential privacy, and disaster related applications shows that existing work performs well technically in flood forecasting, disaster detection, and infrastructure monitoring while keeping data local. However, most studies still focus on accuracy and efficiency without addressing human security risks during aid operations. The suggested conceptual framework combines the ideas of federated optimization, Byzantine robust aggregation, fairness systems, personalized learning, and multi stakeholder governance to safeguard the vulnerable groups in post flood response. It considers system heterogeneity, the communication constraints, and the organizational capacity variation. The framework extends evaluation criteria to include human-centered indicators such as reduction of security incidents and fair distribution of aid. This work outlines future directions for deploying federated learning in disaster settings where beneficiary data collection creates direct protection risks.

title: Exploring the association between bullying and depression symptoms among adolescents in Bangladesh: Findings from nationally representative survey
venue: PLOS mental health.
abstract: Bullying victimization is an important public health concern that has been linked to adverse psychological outcomes among adolescents. The study used mental health well-being data collected in the most recent Bangladesh Adolescent Health and Wellbeing Survey (2019-2020) (BAHWS). A total of 9,116 adolescents aged 15-19 years with complete depression data were included in the analysis. A three-level linear mixed-effects model was employed to account for the hierarchical structure of the survey, with adolescents nested within primary sampling units and districts. Additional analyses examined gender and marital status interactions, subgroup differences, and the cumulative association between multiple forms of bullying and depressive symptoms using a composite bullying measure. The findings revealed that verbal bullying (β = 1.39, p < 0.001) and cyberbullying (β = 1.15, p = 0.012) were independently associated with higher depressive symptom scores. The association between physical bullying and depressive symptoms differed significantly by gender, whereas interactions of gender with verbal and cyberbullying were not statistically significant. Exploratory subgroup analyses showed variation in the magnitude of estimated associations across ever-married females, unmarried females, and unmarried males. A graded association was observed for cumulative bullying exposure: compared with adolescents reporting no bullying exposure, those exposed to on (β = 1.25), two (β = 2.61), and three (β = 4.99) bullying types had progressively higher depressive symptom scores (all p < 0.001). Adolescent Age, Current school or college attendance and higher household wealth were associated with lower depressive symptom scores. Bullying victimization, particularly verbal bullying, cyberbullying, and exposure to multiple forms of bullying, was associated with higher depressive symptoms among Bangladeshi adolescents. These findings highlight the need for comprehensive bullying prevention strategies and accessible psychosocial support services, with particular attention to adolescents experiencing multiple forms of bullying and other vulnerable groups.

title: Smartphone Addiction and Consequential Decline of Library Use and Reading Habit of the Youngsters of Bangladesh: A Cross-Sectional Study
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
abstract: Over the last decade or so, the use of smartphones has exploded in growth, impacting not just on communication and how people access information but also overuse is becoming a challenge, especially for the younger generation, who are reading less, using libraries less, and engaging in the academic process less as well. This study finds out the impacts of smartphone addiction on the usage behavior and reading practices of adolescents and youth in the Bangladeshi library and what factors can contribute to solve the problems. It was a cross-sectional study using qualitative method and purposive sampling technique, a total sample of 310 respondents comprising 200 students (ranged from 14-25 years, median age 19 years) and their corresponding teachers (60) and parents (50). Structured questionnaires were used to collect the data, and descriptive statistics were used to analyze the data. The findings showed that 68% of the students were smartphone addicted students and 74% of students experienced issues in their daily functioning because of using the smartphone. Smartphone addiction was associated with anxiety, depression, insomnia, poor concentration and cyberbullying, irritability, and academic decline etc. Students themselves reported that overall, 62% were unwilling to use the library, while 38% used it, mainly university students. All teachers (100%) agreed that student reading and library usage was impacted by the overuse of mobile phones. It also revealed that 80% of the institutions surveyed had libraries, and many of these institutions were deficient of basic facilities particularly in secondary institutions. Even so, 68% of parents reported that their children were interested in smartphones more and 32% reported that their child preferred to read or play. Students’ excessive interest in smartphones is highly detrimental to their academic performance. It has proposed a few provisions regarding the proper use of smart phones, improvement of library infrastructure, integration of the regular activities of the libraries in the academic curriculum and making the Digital Literacy programs more effective in revitalizing reading culture and accelerating overall intellectual development of the youth of the country.

title: "Deprived of support because we're born women": Emerging Socio-Technical Pathways and Evolving Struggles for Women Entrepreneurs in Bangladesh
authors: Manika Saha; MISITA ANWAR; Md Khalid Hossain; Tanjila Kanij; Umme Humayra; Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed; Gillian Oliver; Stephen Lindsay
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
abstract: Women’s entrepreneurship is a key driver of socio-economic empowerment in the Global South, yet patriarchal sociocultural contexts limit entrepreneur’s autonomy and, despite increasing attention to gender issues in HCI, shifting digital infrastructures cause privacy, security, and logistical challenges. We conduct 15 interviews with women entrepreneurs in Bangladesh who rely on digital technology, offering insight into who they are, their business and supply chains, technology use, and the gendered challenges of balancing work with family. We present women’s accounts of navigating in-person and online harassment and crime, including through payment platforms, and banking tools that legally enforce gender discrimination. We discuss how digital technology design must adapt to these pervasive issues and propose digital interventions to support developing their businesses and achieving financial independence. Our work contributes to understanding how HCI can take a transformative role in overcoming barriers and advancing mechanisms for women’s financial empowerment in the Global South.
