title: Body image disturbance and body dysmorphic symptoms among Bangladeshi university students: associated factors and Bayesian network analysis
authors: Firoj Al‐Mamun; S. M. Rakibul Hasan; Susmita Hossain; Tasnim Tamanna; Faria Tasmin; Monim Abdullah; Farzana Akter; Asif Ahammed; Md. Al Mamunur Rashid; Rayhadul Islam
venue: BMC Psychiatry
abstract: BACKGROUND: Body image disturbance and body dysmorphic symptoms are important appearance-related mental health concerns among university students, yet evidence from Bangladesh remains limited. This study examined factors associated with body image disturbance and body dysmorphic symptoms among Bangladeshi university students and explored their conditional dependency structure using Bayesian network analysis. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1,401 residential students at Jahangirnagar University, Bangladesh, between December 2024 and January 2025. Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire assessing sociodemographic, behavioral, psychosocial, mental health, eating-related, appearance-related, and body image variables. Bivariate analyses, multiple linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors, and theory-informed conditional Gaussian Bayesian network analysis were performed. The Bayesian network used 1,297 complete cases, 23 nodes, and 1,000 bootstrap replications. RESULTS: Mean body image disturbance was 12.00 (SD = 5.39), and mean body dysmorphic symptoms were 3.37 (SD = 2.76). In adjusted models, female gender, traditional bullying, cyberbullying, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, eating disorder risk, and several appearance-specific discomfort variables were associated with higher body image disturbance and/or body dysmorphic symptoms. BMI was not independently associated with either outcome. The regression models explained 24.3% of the variance in body image disturbance and 21.4% of the variance in body dysmorphic symptoms. The averaged Bayesian network retained 13 arcs, including stable dependencies between body image disturbance and body dysmorphic symptoms, cyberbullying and body image disturbance, and anxiety symptoms and body dysmorphic symptoms. CONCLUSIONS: Body image disturbance and body dysmorphic symptoms among Bangladeshi university students were associated with psychological, interpersonal, eating-related, and appearance-specific factors. Bayesian network analysis suggested exploratory conditional dependency patterns among these variables. Findings should be interpreted as cross-sectional associations rather than causal pathways and may inform integrated university-based mental health, body image, and anti-bullying support strategies. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: Strategic Factors of Gen Z's Leadership in Technology-Mediated Student Protests: Empirical Insights from the July Movement in Bangladesh
authors: Muslima Zahan; Atikur Rahman Khan; Golam M. Mathbor
venue: South Asian Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities
abstract: This study investigates how Generation Z (Gen Z) exercised leadership during technology mediated student protests in Bangladesh (July–August 2024), focusing on the communication strategies that enabled collective action for Justice and Institutional Strength. Drawing on survey data from 2,120 participants across schools, colleges, and universities, ten leadership dimensions were assessed using a five-point Likert scale. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) and confirmatory factor analysis were employed to examine the relationships between leadership traits and digital mobilization tactics. Findings indicate that Adaptive and Resilient Leadership (ARL) serves as the central mechanism driving effective protest leadership, with key contributors including Emotional and Value-Based Leadership (EAVBL), Crowdsourcing and Collective Intelligence (CCI), Global Connectivity and Networked Leadership (GCNL), Rapid Information Dissemination and Crisis Management (RIDCM), and Transparency via Digital Platforms (TATDP). Digital tools such as hashtags, viral campaigns, and narrative storytelling were found to mediate collective action through crowdsourced intelligence, highlighting how technology facilitates decentralized coordination, rapid mobilization, and emotionally resonant leadership. The study develops a conceptual framework integrating leadership strategies and technological engagement, offering empirical insights into how Gen Z leverages digital tools to orchestrate effective, socially transformative protest movements. These findings contribute to scholarship on digital-era leadership, youth activism, and technology-mediated collective action, providing actionable insights for policymakers, educators, and scholars interested in participatory, digitally driven social change.

title: Marginalizing Messages, Emotional Impacts, and Coping Strategies: Exploring the Experiences of Bangladeshi Female Gamers in Online Multiplayer Gaming Spaces
venue: Cornerstone (Minnesota State University, Mankato)
abstract: This study explores the experiences of Bangladeshi female gamers in online multiplayer gaming spaces, focusing on the marginalizing messages they encounter, the emotional and social impacts, and the coping strategies they use. Although online gaming is often seen as an open and inclusive digital space, for many women it remains shaped by sexism, exclusion, and cyberbullying. In Bangladesh, these experiences are further influenced by patriarchal norms, moral policing, and gendered expectations. Using a qualitative research design, this study employed in-depth semi-structured interviews with Bangladeshi female gamers who actively participate in online multiplayer games, along with cyber-ethnographic observation of gaming-related Facebook groups and online interactions. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns across participants’ experiences. The findings reveal that female gamers frequently encounter sexist jokes, verbal abuse, body shaming, stalking, trolling, exclusion from teams, moral judgment, and financial exploitation. Participants reported emotional distress, anxiety, stress, anger, low self-esteem, and self-doubt, with these effects often extending into offline life and personal relationships. To cope, participants used strategies such as muting voice chat, hiding gender identity, avoiding random teams, blocking users, relying on trusted people, and selective confrontation. The study argues that online gaming spaces reproduce broader patriarchal power structures, forcing women to constantly negotiate between participation and protection. This research contributes to understanding gendered digital harassment in Bangladesh and highlights the need for safer and more inclusive gaming environments.

title: Systemic Corporate Collapse in Bangladesh: Governance Failure, Political Economy, and Banking Fragility a Comparative Study of Bismillah Group, Destiny Group, and Hallmark Group
authors: Sabrina Ashraf Mumu; Fahima Akter; Kazi Saiful Islam; Anup Kumar Saha
venue: Journal of Economics Finance and Management Studies
abstract: This paper undertakes a rigorous comparative analysis of three of Bangladesh's most consequential corporate fraud cases: the Bismillah Group export fraud, the Destiny Group multi-level marketing pyramid collapse, and the Hallmark Group banking scam involving Sonali Bank. Drawing on institutional theory, political economy frameworks, and governance literature, the study examines the structural, regulatory, and systemic conditions that enabled these collapses to occur and persist over extended periods without effective intervention. The analysis reveals a pattern of converging pathologies — namely, politically captured regulatory institutions, deficient corporate governance, weak banking oversight, and an enabling culture of rent-seeking — that transformed isolated organisational misconduct into systemic financial crises. The three cases collectively expose the fragility of Bangladesh's financial architecture and demonstrate how governance deficits at the firm, sectoral, and state levels interact to amplify financial risk. The paper proposes a multi-tier reform agenda addressing institutional independence, banking supervision, corporate accountability, and anti-corruption enforcement, with contextualised recommendations for the Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU), Bangladesh Bank, and the Securities and Exchange Commission of Bangladesh (BSEC).

title: Exploring Self-Supervised Embeddings for Effective Bangla Cyberbullying Detection Using ML Methods
authors: Akash Rahman; Rimon Kanthi Devnath; G M A Ehsan ur Rahman; Chowdhury Mohammad Mehedi; Sanjida Akter; Muhammad Sadman Alam; Tanjim Mahmud
venue: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence & Networking (QPAIN)
abstract: Cyberbullying is a growing concern in Bangladesh, driven by the widespread use of social media platforms where harmful online behavior often goes unchecked. Such incidents can lead to severe psychological and social consequences, particularly among youth. However, detecting cyberbullying in the Bangla language remains challenging due to limited linguistic resources and the informal nature of online communication. To address this issue, this research proposes a framework that integrates Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) and Machine Learning (ML) for Bangla cyberbullying detection. Using a publicly available dataset containing 44,001 samples across five classes, the text was preprocessed and encoded through SSL approaches such as SimCLR, MoCo, SwAV, BYOL, and MAE to generate rich contextual embeddings. These representations were then used to train ML models for classification. Experimental results demonstrate that the BiLSTM model using SimCLR embeddings achieved the highest accuracy of 95 %, confirming the effectiveness of SSL in enhancing Bangla text understanding for cyberbullying detection.

title: TRACE-Graph: Multi-Source Suspect Link Visualizer
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract TRACE-Graph is an investigation-support tool for law enforcement agencies in Bangladesh (CID, DB, CTTC, Cyber Crime Unit). It combines digital data from multiple sources such as SIM/CDR, mobile financial services (MFS), social media identifiers, and device logs. The system creates a clear visual connection graph to help investigators quickly understand suspect networks. TRACE-Graph reduces manual work, improves evidence clarity, and generates case reports faster. Introduction Cybercrime investigations in Bangladesh often involve data from many separate sources. Investigators must manually compare phone records, wallet transactions, social media activity, and device traces. This process is slow and may miss important links. TRACE-Graph helps investigators by organizing and visualizing these connections in one system.This Idea is Presented and become the Champion at the Cyber Security Awareness Day 2025 (CSAD 2025) Idea Presentation competition held at Daffodil International University.

title: CYBERBULLYING DETECTION FROM BANGLA TEXTS EXTRACTED IN SOCIAL MEDIA IMAGES USING MACHINE LEARNING ALGORITHMS
authors: MD. TOFAEL AHMED; SAMINA TASNIM SINTHY; Pintu Chandra Paul; Kashmi Sultana
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract As the number of people using social media grows, so does the rate of cyberbullying in Bangladesh. Cyberbullying can take several forms, one of which is text in images. To address this problem, we conducted research in which we utilized OCR to extract text from photos and then used NLP and Machine Learning to detect the existence of Cyberbullying in those texts. 1003 images were gathered from Facebook, and textual data was extracted using OCR. The texts were then preprocessed, and features were extracted before being fed through four Machine Learning algorithms to train. Accuracy, precision, recall, f1-score, training and prediction time, and roc area were all included in the final performance analysis. Finally, the decision Tree algorithm had the highest accuracy of 94% for the test data. Linear SVC (94%), Random Forest (90%), and KNN (88%) came in second, third, and fourth, respectively.

title: BTTC - A Bangla Tri-class Text Corpus for Spam, Ham, and Promotional Messages
authors: Labib Tahmid; Istiak Abedin; Kawsar Ahmed; Zinedin Hassan Chowdhury; Babe Sultana
venue: Mendeley Data
abstract: --------------------------------------------------------------------- 1. DATASET DESCRIPTION --------------------------------------------------------------------- BTTC (Bangla Tri-class Text Corpus) contains 10,283 unique labeled Bangla messages collected from various SMS users and public Telegram channels in Bangladesh. Unlike traditional binary datasets (Spam vs. Ham) in other languages, BTTC introduces a third category—"Promotional" (PROMO)—to distinguish legitimate marketing messages from malicious spam messages and normal ham messages. This dataset is designed to facilitate research in Bangla language spam detection, phishing identification, and linguistic analysis of promotional messages. It captures the linguistic shift from traditional SMS to modern messaging platforms like Telegram. --------------------------------------------------------------------- 2. CLASS DISTRIBUTION (Total: 10,283) --------------------------------------------------------------------- 1. HAM (3,904 messages): - Legitimate personal conversations. - Transactional notifications (Bank, Mobile Financial Services). - Government alerts and public service announcements. 2. PROMO (3,695 messages): - Marketing and promotional offers from telecom operators (GP, Robi, Airtel, Banglalink, Teletalk). - Focused on data packs, voice minutes, and bundle offers. 3. SPAM (2,684 messages): - Fraudulent messages and phishing attempts. - Online gambling and betting promotions. - Financial scams and fake prize offers. --------------------------------------------------------------------- 3. FILE STRUCTURE & COLUMNS --------------------------------------------------------------------- File Name: BTTC.csv Columns: A. Text: The raw messages, preserved in the same state as when they were collected (masked for privacy). B. Text_Clean: Cleaned version of Text, by removing line breaks (CHAR(10) and CHAR(13)), non-printable characters, and extra spaces in Excel. C. Label: The classification tag (HAM, PROMO, SPAM). D. Source: Platform origin (SMS or Telegram). E. Annotation_Process: - MANUAL: These messages were manually annotated by 3 annotators. - ANNOTATOR-REVIEWED: These messages were pseudo labeled using manually labeled data, then reviewed and fixed by 3 annotators. *PRIVACY NOTE:* All Personally Identifiable Information (PII) has been masked using a regex algorithm. - Phone Numbers: Last 5 digits are replaced with 'XXXXX'. - URLs: Domain kept (e.g., t.me), path masked (e.g., https://t.me/XXXXX). - Emails: Local part (before the @) is masked with 'XXXXX'. - Transaction IDs: Replaced with 'XXXXX'.

title: A Scientific Advisory on Reinforcement Learning in Cashless and Mobile Financial Systems for Inclusive Finance and Equity Support in Developing Economies
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This advisory explores the integration of Reinforcement Learning (RL) into Mobile Financial Services (MFS) to advance inclusive finance and equity in developing economies, with a focus on Bangladesh and Nigeria. RL, an adaptive AI paradigm that trains agents through dynamic interactions and rewards, offers transformative potential beyond traditional models by enabling real-time decision-making in volatile financial environments. Key applications include alternative credit scoring using digital footprints and psychometrics, adaptive fraud detection via algorithms like DQN and PPO, and multi-agent systems for entrepreneurship, such as gamified financial literacy tools. A comparative analysis contrasts Bangladesh's centralized, bank-led MFS ecosystem— dominated by players like bKash and featuring AI-powered MSME lending—with Nigeria's decentralized, innovation-driven landscape, supported by regulatory sandboxes and fostering competition among fintechs like OPay. Despite promising opportunities for poverty alleviation aligned with UN SDGs 1 and 8, challenges persist, including the digital divide (e.g., gender gaps in access and literacy), computational hurdles in data-scarce regions, ethical risks like algorithmic bias from flawed reward designs, and pitfalls in public-private partnerships. Also available on Academia.edu: https://www.academia.edu/attachments/125041986/download_file?s=portfolio

title: Reputation Arbitrage and the Crisis of Institutional Trust: Defending Organisations When Genuine Identities Perform Fraudulent Actions
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence has restructured the threat landscape for institutional security, shifting the locus of attack from technical infrastructure compromise to the instrumentalisation of legitimate insiders. This paper, the second in a three-part series, introduces the Action Authentication Model to describe how reputation arbitrage, the systematic exploitation of borrowed credibility signals, operates at the institutional level. Drawing on principal-agent theory, normal accidents theory, highreliability organisation theory, and sociotechnical systems analysis, the paper argues that identity-centric security architectures are insufficient when adversaries can manipulate genuine employees into authorising fraudulent transactions. Through analysis of four independently documented institutional failures, the 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist, the 2020 Twitter bitcoin scam, the 2024 Hong Kong deepfake video-conference fraud, and the 2025 Hong Kong voice-cloning cryptocurrency fraud, the paper proposes a three-layer defence architecture: Identity, Context, and Consequence, each operationalised through enumerated controls including consequence-weighted authentication, intelligent friction, trust-path forensics, and distributed security authority. The analysis extends calibrated trust, the individual disposition proposed in Part I of this series, into structured trust, its organisational analogue: the property that emerges when consequence-weighted verification is built into process design rather than left to individual judgement. The answer to reputation arbitrage, the paper argues, is not “better authentication” but “better trust architecture.”

title: An Image Dataset for Automated Identification and Rice Quality Analysis
authors: Md Mijanur Rahman; Hasan Iftakhar; Ferdous Alam Khan; Hasan Al Banna
venue: Mendeley Data
abstract: Rice is one of the most widely cultivated and essential crops in Bangladesh. However, there are wide varieties of rice, and the rice grains are so small that not only general people but also the local sellers often cannot distinguish the variety or quality of rice, which causes a scam to the buyers. To tackle this challange we have introduced a raw photobased dataset of fifteen Bangladeshi rice varieties. They are BRRI Ataish, Durga Ataish, Aman(Less fibre), Manikganj Aman(Full Fibre), Bangla Moti(Kushtiya), Biroi(Mymensingh), Black Rice(Sylhet), Guti Shorna(Dinajpur), Haski 29, Biroi(Sylhet), Lal Gutishorna, Miniket, Nazirshail, Paijam, and Utshob Nazir are captured under diverse conditions. The dataset contains a total of 4922 high-resolution images. To ensure robustness and diversity, all images were originally captured in PRO format using Samsung Galaxy S24 mobile phone cameras under different lighting environments. After capturing, these images were converted into JPG format, and the size was 3060*4080 to maintain all the image quality. This rice grain image database is designed to support research in machine learning and computer vision, particularly for automated rice type identification and quality analysis.For upcoming deep learning models in rice identification, quality assurance, and enhanced market transparency across Bangladesh, it will serve as a standard.

title: PhishBD_2026
authors: Abrity Paul Chowdhury; Mohammad Masudur Rahman Khan; Fernaz Nur
venue: Mendeley Data
abstract: PhishBD_2026 is a phishing URL detection dataset for Bangladeshi web infrastructure. It contains 131,167 URLs (91,817 phishing, 39,350 legitimate), each represented by 73 engineered features, the raw URL string, and a binary label. Phishing samples were drawn from threat intelligence feeds and incident records provided by a Bangladeshi financial institution. Legitimate samples combine standard sources (Tranco, ISCX, Majestic Million) with manually verified Bangladeshi websites spanning government, banking, mobile financial services (MFS), telecom, education, media, e-commerce, and healthcare. These regional samples were added because global URL datasets underrepresent Bangladeshi domain and brand patterns, which limits the transferability of models trained only on standard sources. The 73 features are organized into six categories: lexical (length, character composition), structural (subdomain and path depth), encoding-related, statistical (entropy, token distributions), security indicators (HTTPS usage, IP-literal hosts, punycode), and features specific to the Bangladeshi context (local brand detection, typosquatting edit distance, BD-TLD identification, government keyword matching). Some features are correlated by construction (for example, slash_count and path_depth, or token_count and special_char_count). These were retained rather than removed, since redundant representations can be useful for some models and are easily filtered out during feature selection for others. The phishing-to-legitimate ratio is approximately 70:30, reflecting the composition of the source feeds and institutional records rather than an artificially balanced sample. Users training classifiers on this dataset should select evaluation metrics accordingly (e.g., precision, recall, or PR-AUC rather than accuracy alone).

title: Cybersecurity and Human Rights in South Asia: A Legal and Governance Perspective Through Case Studies
venue: IGI Global eBooks
abstract: South Asia, encompassing countries like India, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh, has witnessed rapid digital growth, driven by high mobile penetration and the adoption of digital financial services. As of December 2024, India alone had 970 million internet subscribers, with a 54% annual data consumption growth rate, while Bangladesh reported 50% household internet penetration. However, this digital transformation has been accompanied by a surge in cyberattacks, posing significant challenges to governance, human rights, and privacy. This chapter examines three major cyberattacks in South Asia, the 2022 AIIMS ransomware attack in India, the 2023 Sri Lankan government cloud system attack and the 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist, through a legal and governance lens, analyzing their implications for human rights and privacy. By providing descriptive and historical analyses, the chapter aims to contribute to the discourse on cybersecurity, ethical considerations and human rights in the region.

title: Biography of Mahfuj Alam: Revolutionary Mind, State Power and The Unfinished Republic
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This 2026 textbook is a comprehensive scholarly analysis of the life, political philosophy, and governmental role of Mahfuj Alam, a central figure in the July 2024 student-led revolution that overthrew Bangladesh's long-serving Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. The book uses Alam's biography as a case study to explore the broader themes of democratic transition, constitutional reform, media governance, and generational political change in a post-authoritarian context. It is divided into five interconnected parts. Part One: The Making of a Revolutionary Intellectual establishes the historical and personal context. It details Alam's origins in a rural madrasa family in Lakshmipur and his intellectual formation at the University of Dhaka's law faculty, where he synthesized Islamic jurisprudence with secular constitutional thought. The book traces the history of Bangladesh's state, from its 1971 independence through military rule, the flawed two-party democracy, and the 15-year "architecture of autocracy" under Sheikh Hasina (2009-2024), characterized by electoral fraud, judicial capture, and the use of the Digital Security Act to suppress dissent. The trigger for the July 2024 revolution was a High Court ruling reinstating a 30 percent quota for government jobs for descendants of 1971 freedom fighters. Alam emerged as a key strategic coordinator of the Anti-Discrimination Students Movement. Following a brutal state crackdown and the military's withdrawal of support, Hasina resigned. An interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was formed, with Alam initially serving as Special Assistant and later, in November 2024, as Adviser for Information and Broadcasting. Part Two: Information, Law, and Power focuses on Alam's tenure as Information Adviser. It analyzes the deeply compromised media landscape he inherited: concentrated ownership by Awami League-affiliated conglomerates, state media as propaganda tools, and the weaponization of the Digital Security Act (DSA) and its successor, the Cyber Security Act (CSA). The book examines the work of the Media Reform Commission, which recommended measures like a "One House One Media" policy to break up monopolies, a journalist protection ordinance, and the transformation of state TV (BTV) into an independent public service broadcaster. Alam's implementation record is presented as mixed. He achieved some progress, including a 16-place improvement in Bangladesh's World Press Freedom Index and the partial repeal of the CSA's most repressive provisions. However, he failed to enact the journalist protection law, reform the opaque television licensing process, or overcome deep bureaucratic resistance. The book also candidly addresses major controversies of his tenure, including allegations of nepotism in licensing, a diplomatic incident over a shared map depicting Indian territory as Bangladeshi, and his role in advocating for the exclusion of the Awami League from politics. Part Three: The Constitutional Architecture of a New Bangladesh examines the post-revolution constitutional moment. It details the work of the Constitutional Reform Commission, which proposed sweeping changes including prime ministerial term limits, a bicameral parliament with a proportionally elected upper house (Senate), the restoration of the neutral caretaker government system for elections, and the constitutional entrenchment of internet access as a fundamental right. The book analyzes the jurisprudential revolution led by the Supreme Court, which reinforced the "basic structure" doctrine (holding that certain core features of the constitution cannot be amended). It discusses the controversial February 2026 referendum, where a bundled "Yes" vote (61 percent) approved the July Charter of reforms, held simultaneously with a parliamentary election. The election resulted in a landslide victory and two-thirds supermajority for the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), while the Awami League was banned from participation. The student-led National Citizen Party won only six seats. The book explores the legitimacy tensions arising from this process: the exclusion of a major party, the constitutionally dubious nature of the interim government's Implementation Order, and the risk that the BNP's supermajority could be used to dilute or reverse the very reforms designed to constrain executive power. Part Four: The Political Philosophy of Mahfuj Alam reconstructs Alam's ideology from his public statements and actions. It frames him as an "organic intellectual" of his generation, using Gramsci's framework. Alam's philosophy is identified as a distinctive synthesis: a "post-Islamist" vision that accepts democratic pluralism and constitutional governance while drawing ethical resources from Islamic jurisprudence (concepts like shura, consultation; maslaha, public interest; and zulm, oppression). His central demand is a "new political-economic settlement" based on substantive anti-discrimination and civic nationalism, rejecting both the dynastic politics of the Awami League and BNP and the identity-based politics of religious extremism. The book explores the tension in his thought between a commitment to consensus-based politics and a confrontational "anti-fascist" stance that justified the Awami League's exclusion. It also examines his ethics of political action, navigating Max Weber's distinction between the "ethics of conviction" and the "ethics of responsibility." Part Five: Bangladesh in the World places the country's transition within the global context of democratic backsliding and autocratization. It compares Bangladesh's July Revolution with other democratic transitions: the successful model of South Korea's 1987 student movement, the cautionary tale of the Arab Spring, and the pacted transitions of Eastern Europe. The book analyzes the geopolitics of the transition, particularly the complex relationship with India, which gave sanctuary to the ousted Prime Minister Hasina. It also addresses the ongoing Rohingya refugee crisis as a humanitarian and diplomatic challenge. The concluding chapters assess Alam's legacy, acknowledging his significant intellectual contribution to synthesizing Islamic and secular democratic thought, his partial institutional achievements in media reform, and his role in building a democratic political culture. It also honestly accounts for the criticisms against him, including his role in the controversial exclusion of the Awami League and the questionable due process of the International Crimes Tribunal that sentenced Hasina to death in absentia. The book concludes that Bangladesh remains an "unfinished republic," with the long-term success of its democratic transition dependent on sustained institutional reform, political culture, and the choices of a new generation of leaders.

title: Digital Economy and the Transformation of Rural Markets in Tripura: A Study of Emerging Opportunities and Challenges.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract: The 'Digital India' program, driven by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, is a landmark step in India's governance and economic history. Formally launched on July 1, 2015 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, this mega-project is not any single isolated law [Digital India Journey]; rather, it was a modern upgraded version of the previous 'National e-Governance Plan' (NeGP-2006). To legally protect and make this system effective, the 'Information Technology Act, 2000' (IT Act, 2000) and subsequently passed 'Aadhaar Act, 2016' have acted as core pillars. The core objective of this program was to make India's governance cashless, paperless, and faceless. It was basically built in a systematic way based on three main vision areas or perspectives: building digital infrastructure for citizens, delivering demand-driven online government services, and universal digital empowerment. To fulfill this goal, 9 key pillars (9 Pillars) were specified, among which establishing rural broadband connectivity through BharatNet and reaching government services at the grassroots level through Common Service Centres (CSCs) and e-Kranti are notable [Common Services Centres Expansion, BharatNet Restructuring]. Although this is an all-India comprehensive program, due to India's diverse geographical and social realities, its implementation has not been the same in all states. In this context, the hilly state of Tripura in North-East India is a very important case study for evaluating the impact of Digital India. Real challenges like Tripura's difficult hilly terrain, border regions with Bangladesh and Mizoram, remote tribal (Bru/Reang) settlements, and poor internet connectivity test the real effectiveness of this central program at the grassroots level. Although e-governance, digital banking, and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) have arrived in Tripura's rural markets, bottlenecks like weak network, language barrier (dominance of English/Hindi and lack of Kokborok language), and cyber crime still exist. Therefore, the main focus of this report is—the success of Digital India in Tripura does not depend only on the statistics of opening online portals; rather, to uncover the actual picture of how freely, securely, and affordably common people of marginal markets like Damcherra can use this technology. People's practical digital literacy is very low. The biggest obstacle is language—since most banking apps or government e-marketplaces are made in English and Hindi, simple rural people speaking Kokborok or Bengali cannot use them independently. Taking advantage of this, the graph of OTP (One Time Password) fraud and cyber crimes is increasing rapidly in rural Tripura, which has created a kind of deep distrust about technology in people's minds and they are being forced to return to the old 'cash' dependent economy. Therefore, the main goal of this research is—not just the number of online services, but to evaluate the actual digital freedom of common people in Tripura.

title: Strategic Convergence in the Algorithmic Age: Sovereign AI, Shepherding Architectures, and the Mitigation of AI-Induced Financial Instability
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: As artificial intelligence transitions from experimental technology to global foundational infrastructure, its governance demands a shift from basic adoption to complex geopolitical, ecological, and macroeconomic statecraft. This report analyzes critical paradigms shaping digital governance: the dichotomy between jurisdictional AI Sovereignty and physical Sovereign AI; the operationalization of AI Ethics through algorithmic Explainable AI (XAI); and the necessary transition from rigid, static governance to dynamic, bio-inspired 'algorithmic shepherding.' Furthermore, it highlights how deep reinforcement learning models within AI-induced financial systems create systemic risks of extreme, synchronized liquidity hoarding (modeled via Roy's safety-first criterion)—a fragility amplified by real-time synced instruments and deepfakes. Synthesizing these concepts, the report outlines five actionable, ecologically and economically grounded recommendations tailored under Bangladesh's incoming UNGA 81 presidency. title: Digital Behavioral Analysis, Computer Crime, and Investigations: Persona ex Machina
venue: Routledge eBooks
abstract: Digital Behavioral Analysis, Computer Crime, and Investigations integrates digital forensic methodology with behavioral profiling, criminological theory, and the legal and ethical frameworks that govern admissibility for instruction and practice in equal measure. Behind every digital crime is a human being, and the technical sophistication of modern computer crime has not eliminated the behavioral evidence that has always grounded criminal investigation – where that evidence lives and how investigators recognize it has simply changed. From the Silk Road takedown to the Bangladesh Bank heist, from the Stagg investigation to the Hong Kong deepfake fraud, this book works through the cases that define the field and develops the frameworks that practitioners need to navigate the next generation of digital offenses. Each chapter opens with learning objectives and a key terms section that defines technical vocabulary in non-specialist terms, develops its analytic content through case illustrations drawn from documented investigations, and closes with practical takeaways and discussion questions calibrated for both classroom use and field application. C. R. Johnson establishes operational frameworks for evidence triage, hypothesis development, behavioral cluster analysis, case linkage analysis, and capability assessment, and treats each within the constraints of Federal Rule of Evidence 702 and the Daubert standard for expert testimony. Written for advanced undergraduate and graduate students in criminal justice, criminology, digital forensics, and cybersecurity programs, as well as for practitioners working in digital investigation, behavioral analysis, and the prosecution or defense of computer crime cases, this book is usable as both a course text and an active investigative reference.

title: Voices of the Bar and the Barricade: Fuad's reform, Majumdar's rights, Hajjaj's business, Suman's fall, Manir's courts, Farhana's defiance, Andaleeve's design; the seven doctrines
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: An extraordinary work of critical legal scholarship has emerged from the crucible of Bangladesh’s most turbulent period since the 1971 Liberation War. This textbook, written by S M Nazmuz Sakib and published in 2026, presents a daring and meticulous examination of seven Bangladeshi legal political figures whose careers embody the profound tensions between law as a rational constraint on power and law as a weapon wielded by the powerful. The book arrives at a moment of unprecedented constitutional crisis and transformation following the student led popular uprising of July and August 2024, an uprising that toppled a government, left approximately 1,400 people dead, and set the nation on a path toward comprehensive institutional reform. The seven figures at the heart of this study are not ordinary politicians or lawyers. They are barristers, members of parliament, constitutional architects, and diaspora advocates who have stood on both sides of the divide between legal principle and political expediency. Barrister Asaduzzaman Fuad emerges as the institutional reformer whose third force politics challenges Bangladesh’s entrenched binary party system. Nijhum Majumdar represents the diaspora lawyer and human rights internationalist whose scholarship on international criminal law collides with the political realities of post uprising accountability. Bobby Hajjaj, the Oxford MBA holder and Texas educated reformer, transitions from grassroots activism to a ministerial position in the new government, testing whether reform rhetoric can survive the machinery of power. Barrister Suman, the public interest litigator who built a career fighting financial crime, finds himself caught in the very accountability mechanisms he once championed. The textbook does not shy away from controversy or complexity. It dissects the dual oath crisis that paralyzed the new parliament in February 2026, when BNP lawmakers refused to take a second oath for a proposed Constitutional Reform Council while opposition members embraced it. It analyzes the International Crimes Tribunal’s unprecedented prosecution of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina for crimes against humanity, including the death sentence imposed in November 2025. It examines the deep structural failures of the Digital Security Act and its successor the Cyber Security Act, laws that criminalized online speech in ways that violated Bangladesh’s international treaty obligations. And it confronts the persistent exclusion of women from meaningful political representation, even as two female prime ministers dominated the country’s politics for decades. The book is structured across seven parts, each building on the last to create a comprehensive jurisprudential framework. Part One establishes the constitutional history of Bangladesh, the fractured legacy of its 1972 constitution, and the theoretical tools needed to analyze the seven subjects. Part Two plunges into the transitional controversies of the post August 2024 period, examining accountability debates, internal party conflicts, and the question of individual integrity under political pressure. Part Three delivers a detailed technical analysis of specific constitutional provisions, case law, and the July National Charter’s 47 proposed amendments. Part Four confronts the structural politics of gender and minority rights, documenting the systematic vulnerability of Hindu, Ahmadiyya, and indigenous communities despite formal constitutional guarantees. Part Five expands the frame to international law, examining the India extradition controversy, the Rohingya crisis, and Bangladesh’s navigation of great power competition between China, India, and the United States. Part Six analyzes the new parliament’s legislative agenda, including anti corruption reform, freedom of expression, labour rights for the garment sector, and the design of a proposed bicameral legislature. Part Seven offers comparative perspectives from South Africa, Indonesia, Tunisia, Turkey, and India, synthesizing theoretical conclusions about the seven subjects’ jurisprudential legacies. What makes this textbook remarkable is its refusal to treat its subjects as heroes or villains. The author applies a demanding standard of integrity, asking whether each figure’s actions cohere with their stated principles across changing political contexts. Rumeen Farhana, the only woman directly elected to parliament as an independent after being expelled from the BNP, emerges with the strongest claim to principled consistency, yet even her career reveals the structural limits of individual virtue in a system designed to reward partisan loyalty. Mohammad Shishir Manir, the constitutional lawyer who has defended Jamaat e Islami’s right to political participation and advocated fiercely for judicial independence, faces the tension between procedural consistency and substantive justice in cases like the Abrar Fahad murder trial. Andaleeve Rahman, the barrister and legal educator who comes from a family of zamindars and ministers, represents the dynastic dimension of Bangladeshi politics while contributing systematically to comparative constitutional design. The author draws on an extraordinary range of theoretical frameworks. H L A Hart’s concept of the rule of recognition illuminates the contested foundations of Bangladesh’s legal order. Hans Kelsen’s Grundnorm theory helps explain whether the August 2024 uprising constituted a revolutionary change in the basic norm of the legal system. Ronald Dworkin’s rights jurisprudence provides a lens for evaluating public interest litigation and the enforcement of fundamental rights. Jurgen Habermas’s discourse ethics offers a standard for assessing the quality of Bangladesh’s public sphere and the legitimacy of its legislative process. Philip Pettit’s republican theory of non domination supplies the most demanding benchmark for constitutional reform: whether the new institutional arrangements genuinely reduce the capacity of political actors to exercise arbitrary power over citizens. Pierre Bourdieu’s field theory illuminates the competition for legal, social, and symbolic capital among the seven figures as they navigate the permeable boundary between law and politics in Bangladesh. The textbook also serves as a primary source document for a constitutional moment still unfolding. It includes analysis of the February 2026 election that produced a BNP supermajority with 209 seats, the simultaneous referendum in which 60.26 percent of voters endorsed the July National Charter, and the early legislative battles of the new parliament. It documents the death of former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia in December 2025 and the succession of Tarique Rahman as Prime Minister. It examines the contempt conviction of Sheikh Hasina for an alleged licence to kill recording and the subsequent death sentence for war crimes related to the 2024 uprising. It tracks the positions of each of the seven subjects as they navigate the new political landscape, from Farhana’s independent parliamentary role to Fuad’s extra parliamentary influence following his electoral defeat in Barisal 3. The book is unflinching in its assessment of Bangladesh’s structural pathologies. It documents the persistent failure of the legal profession to maintain independence from partisan politics, the capture of judicial appointments by executive power, the systematic misuse of blasphemy laws against religious minorities, the weaponization of defamation cases to silence critics, and the winner takes all political culture that has frustrated every previous attempt at institutional reform. Yet it also finds grounds for guarded optimism in the extraordinary mobilizing capacity of the July 2024 uprising, the genuine if incomplete reforms of the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus, and the emergence of a more active civil society and a more independent judiciary than at any time in recent memory. The author concludes with a philosophical reflection on the kind of person that Bangladeshi legal political practice tends to produce. The answer is both encouraging and sobering. All seven subjects demonstrate genuine intellectual engagement with jurisprudential questions, developing coherent frameworks that guide their public conduct. Yet all have also experienced moments where political accommodation has taken priority over principled consistency, reflecting the structural conditions of a polarized and often violent political environment where the costs of independence are high and the rewards of loyalty are great. The institutional reform agenda of the post August moment is therefore not merely a matter of constitutional design but a project of character formation, an attempt to create practices that form a different kind of legal political character, one shaped by accountability, independence, and the internalization of constitutional values. This textbook is essential reading for anyone seeking to understand the intersection of law and politics in contemporary South Asia. It is a work of critical scholarship that holds its subjects accountable to the highest standards of legal ethics and democratic theory while remaining grounded in the specific empirical realities of Bangladesh’s extraordinary constitutional experiment. The voices of the bar and the barricade, the barristers and the student protesters, the parliamentarians and the civil society advocates, all find a place in this ambitious and intellectually rigorous volume. The constitutional future of Bangladesh remains uncertain, but the analytical resources needed to engage with that future are now available in a single compelling text.

title: Digital Resilience Within a Hypermediated Polycrisis
authors: Marc Esteve Del Valle; Ansgard Heinrich; Anabel Quan‐Haase
venue: Media and Communication
abstract: This thematic issue examines digital resilience within an increasingly complex landscape of hypermediated, overlapping crises. Situated at the intersection of several research areas—including digital literacy, platform studies, Indigenous media studies, journalism studies, and political science—the thematic issue explores the complexities of digital resilience and seeks to advance its conceptualization and understanding. The issue brings together 15 articles spanning more than 17 countries and addressing a wide range of digital resilience phenomena, from Bangladeshi women’s responses to disinformation and online harassment, to community-led technologies countering environmental injustices in Brazil, to the navigation of digital surveillance in later life in Spain. Together, this issue offers an interdisciplinary, multimethod, and global approach that highlights both the opportunities and challenges involved in fostering digital resilience. In the context of a hypermediated polycrisis, critically assessing how digital resilience can empower people to confront digital threats is especially urgent, particularly for marginalized populations in both the Global North and the Global South.

title: Digital Spaces, Structural Inequalities: Rethinking TFGBV in South Asia’s Legal and Socio-Cultural Context
venue: The Informal South Asian Journal of Human Rights and Social Justice.
abstract: This article explores the growing prevalence of technology-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV) in South Asia within the context of rapid digital expansion and persistent structural inequalities. While increased internet penetration across Nepal, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka has enabled greater access to information, freedom of expression, and economic participation, it has simultaneously amplified gendered forms of harm in digital spaces. Manifestations of TFGBV, including cyberstalking, doxxing, image-based abuse, and online sexual harassment, reflects a spillover of entrenched patriarchal violence into How to Cite this Article digital spaces rather than a completely new phenomenon. Adopting a triangulated qualitative methodology, the study combines doctrinal legal analysis with a comparative and socio-legal approach to assess the adequacy of legal frameworks and their enforcement mechanisms. The findings suggest that legal responses across the region remain fragmented, morality-driven, and heavily reliant on criminalization, often failing to address the consent-based, intersectional, and rapidly evolving nature of digital harms. Legal ambiguities, weak enforcement mechanisms, and limited institutional capacity further widen the gap between formal protections and the lived realities of survivors.The article further underscores how socio-cultural barriers, including victim-blaming attitudes, honor-based social norms, and unequal access to digital technologies, restrict reporting and impede access to justice. It argues that TFGBV not only inflicts harm on individuals but also restricts women’s participation in public and digital spaces, thereby undermining democratic engagement and civic inclusion. It calls for a shift toward survivor-centered, rights-based approaches integrating legal reform, platform accountability, digital literacy, and broader processes of social transformation.

title: An Investigation into Digital Citizenship Behaviour of Generation-Z Using Mediation and Moderation Models
authors: A. S. M. Asaduzzaman; Saiful Hoque; Md. Alamgir Hossain
venue: Social Science Review
abstract: This study investigated the digital citizenship of Generation Z in Bangladesh. Although digital devices have become available across the country keeping up with the rapid growth of internet use, a serious lack of digital literacy prevails among the users, particularly among the youth. Consequently, poor level of digital citizenship is seen, which entails using hate speech, cyber bullying, irresponsible social media use, and a general lack of knowledge about safe use of the Internet. The primary objective of this project was to measure their knowledge and awareness level of digital citizenship which refers to respectful online behaviour and online civic engagement. We conceptualised that four dimensions of social media competence (SMC) i.e., social media experience, effort expectancy, performance expectancy and social influence have positive influence on civic engagement and digital citizenship behaviour. We also hypothesized that civic engagement (CVEe) has positive influence on their digital citizenship behaviour (DCB). In order to examine these objectives and proposed hypotheses, we analysed survey data using mediation and moderation models which are part of structural equation modelling (SEM). Adopting a quantitative research design, the study analysed survey responses of a total of 393 students from six universities including four public and two private universities. It was found that SMC significantly influences both digital citizenship behaviour and civic engagement. Additionally, when tested using mediation model, it was found that the four dimensions of SMC have mediating effect on students’ digital citizenship behaviour through civic involvement. Lastly, while ‘gender’ of the students was considered as an independent variable, it was found that these dimensions have significant effects for both male and female groups. In contrast with majority of the research on digital citizenship done in the context of the West, this sociological investigation for empirical pieces of evidence in Bangladesh provides a non-Western account of the phenomenon. This study contributes to a developing field of research that seeks to explore the dimensions and possibilities of young users’ digital citizenship. title: CYBERSECURITY AWARENESS AMONG UNIVERSITY STUDENTS: A SOCIAL AND TECHNOLOGICAL STUDY
venue: Journal of Social Sciences Development
abstract: Although it is true that university students are more and more involved in digital technologies, they are also highly vulnerable to cyber security threats because of the lack of consistency in awareness and protective behaviours. This article is a combination of the latest empirical studies on the Cybersecurity awareness of Higher Education students, with a focus on social and technological components, and the latest systematic reviews on the subject. The surveys in Indonesia, Turkey, India, Bangladesh, Bahrain and the United States showed that students have the ability to report these same threats (phishing and malware), but those reports don't necessarily result in protection. Moreover, there are a number of reports that despite the fact that many students are aware about threats in cyber space, only a small number of them are formally trained in cyber security. The findings also suggest that perceived behavioural control is a factor affecting students' cybersecurity intentions, and that social learning is an important factor in shaping students' cybersecurity behaviour outside of the classroom. The article identifies the disconnect between the technical education in cybersecurity, which is mainly associated with the computing fields and the education in cybersecurity to all children/young people as an interdisciplinary field. The results indicate that structured cybersecurity training in the curriculum and the use of interesting pedagogical approaches like gamification and simulation can be implemented in universities.

title: A machine learning framework for enhancing threat detection in core banking systems
authors: Subodh Kumar Bhowmick; Bodhi Chakraborty; Hirak Mazumdar; Sunil Kumar Singh
venue: Scientific Reports
abstract: Abstract One of the biggest issues around using machine learning (ML) for cybersecurity in commercial banking is the gap between proof-of-concept and in production. Not every model that has a high accuracy score on a benchmark dataset is the same model as one that is operating in a live transaction pipeline, subject to the multiple regulatory regimes including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI-DSS), New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) Part 500, Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act (GLBA), NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF), Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) operational resilience principles and the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act), which has requirements that go far beyond predictive accuracy. In this paper, a twelve-month experience of designing, deployment, and operation of an ML-based security framework has been reported, that serves more than one million Customers of Midland Bank Plc, Dhaka, Bangladesh on its Core Banking System (CBS) platform. The created detection stack consists of two models, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for spatial anomaly detection and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network for sequential patterns analysis, and two other methods, namely the Autoencoder (AE) for anomaly scoring via reconstruction errors and the Random Forest (RF) and Gradient Boosting (GB) ensemble for final decision making. Evaluation is based upon dataset of 4,286,530 anonymised events (6 categories of threat instances partitioned in a stratified manner as 70/15/15) with 5-fold cross validation approach. During production, the system had 98.0% ± 0.7% (95% confidence interval [97.4%, 98.6%]) detection accuracy with a false-positive rate of 2%. FPR and a mean response time of 5 min and Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.98. There is evidence of a decrease in FPR from 32% to 2%, a decrease in mean response time from 45 min to 5 min and an increase in composite resilience score from 55 to 94, as proven by before and after metrics from Midland Bank Plc. Through ablation analysis, we verify the contributions of the complementary components, and are able to keep competitive accuracy versus 2024–2026 state-of-the-art Graph Neural Network (GNN), transformer and federated-learning approaches while reducing inference latency by 2–3× and estimated deployment cost by 3–7×. From the 1,100 incidents identified during deployment, 30.9% of were phishing/malware incidents, 18.2% DDoS attacks and 16.4% Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs). Finally, consolidated, audit-tested guidance for banks implementing ML-based security under various multi-jurisdictional mandates is provided in the paper.

title: An End-To-End Deep Learning Framework for Multi-Font Urdu Handwritten Character Detection and Recognition in Unconstrained Images
authors: Nida Zainab; Faria Bibi; Muqaddas Yousaf; Assad Iqbal; Yousra Rehman; Sohair Sultan Fayyaz Jeelani
venue: Journal of Engineering and Computational Intelligence Review
abstract: Detection and recognition of handwritten characters is the process of finding the area in an image where text is written and drawing a bounding box around it, with the label containing the text within the bounding box. It has widespread applications, including postal address reading, recognizing Persian vehicle number plates as the Persian language has similar digits to the Urdu language, digitizing and preserving old manuscripts, making handwritten documents in digital format, automatically reading house numbers, and also providing a way for creating apps for kids which will help them in writing and pronouncing Urdu characters properly. Urdu is a cursive language, so it is difficult to apply state-of-the-art handwritten character detection and recognition models developed for other languages to Urdu. The current state-of-the-art techniques cannot handle font style variations, complex backgrounds, illumination, stroke variations, and multiple characters simultaneously due to handcrafted feature extraction. A dataset with such kinds of variations is rare. Very few have used deep learning techniques for Urdu due to the lack of rich datasets. Moreover, the detection and recognition of Urdu handwritten characters are challenging due to variations in stroke sequence, font size, color, style, illumination, background, overlapping, and orientation. YOLO v3 is used for the detection and recognition of Urdu handwritten characters after some fine- tuning. Furthermore, a rich dataset is developed for the training and validation of the proposed technique. The performance of the proposed model is compared with state-of-the-art Urdu handwritten character detection and recognition models. The results show that the proposed technique outperforms the state-of-the-art Urdu handwritten character detection and recognition techniques, both qualitatively and quantitatively. REFERENCES [1] M. title: Green HRM Practices and Organizational Performance-Related Outcomes in Pakistan's Hospitality Sector: The Mediating Role of Perceived Organizational Support and the Moderating Role of Spiritual Leadership in Employee Retention
venue: Journal of Business Insight and Innovation
abstract: This study examines the relationship between green human resource management (GHRM), perceived organizational support (POS), spiritual leadership (SL) and employee retention in the hospitality and tourism sectors of Pakistan. Employee retention is treated as a workforce-related outcome relating to organizational performance, rather than as a direct measure of organizational performance. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 300 employees in Islamabad and Rawalpindi in 2023, using simple sampling, five-point questionnaires, and SPSS-based descriptive, reliability, correlation, regression, mediation, and moderation analyses. GHRM was positively associated with POS (b = .7567, p < .001) and employee retention (b = .4421, p < .001), while POS was positively associated with retention (b = .5139, p < .001). Spiritual leadership was neither a significant direct predictor of retention (b = −.0045, p = .8396) nor a significant POS × SL interaction (b = −.0394, p = .2218). The positive indirect effect is consistent with partial mediation by POS. These findings identify organizational support as a potential explanatory mechanism linking environmentally centred HR practices to employee retention, with appropriate limitations on leadership and general organizational performance claims.
