title: Cybercrime in India under the New Criminal Laws: Emerging Challenges in Investigation, Digital Evidence and Criminal Justice
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
abstract: The rapid growth of digital technology has changed the way people communicate, conduct business, access financial services and interact with government institutions. At the same time, this transformation has created new opportunities for criminal activity. Cybercrime today includes online financial fraud, identity theft, unauthorised access to computer systems, cyberstalking, impersonation, data theft, social media offences and technologically facilitated forms of traditional crime. The investigation and prosecution of such offences present difficulties that differ from those associated with conventional crimes because electronic evidence can be easily altered, deleted, transferred and stored across multiple jurisdictions. The introduction of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 represents a significant transformation of India's criminal justice framework. This paper examines the implications of the new criminal laws for cybercrime investigation, digital evidence and criminal justice administration. It also considers the continuing importance of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the constitutional protection of privacy and due process. The paper adopts a doctrinal and analytical methodology based on legislation, judicial decisions and authoritative legal materials. It argues that legislative reform by itself cannot adequately address the complexity of cybercrime. Effective enforcement requires trained investigators, modern forensic infrastructure, rapid preservation of electronic evidence, coordination between investigative agencies and service providers, and appropriate safeguards for individual rights. The paper further examines emerging challenges associated with artificial intelligence, deepfakes, digital impersonation and sophisticated online fraud. It concludes that India's new criminal laws provide an important foundation for dealing with cybercrime, but their success will ultimately depend upon effective implementation, technological capacity and a careful balance between criminal enforcement and constitutional liberties.

title: Analyzing Decadal Cyber Crime Trends In India: A Data Driven Approach Using Clustering And Predictive Modeling
authors: Manisha M. More; Mayuri More; Varsha Gidde; Sheetal Sandeep Patil
venue: International Journal of Science Engineering and Technology
abstract: The proposed study explores the NCRB i.e. National Crime Record Bureau data for the period of 2012 To 2022 and assessed the trends cybercrime across the states, the metropolitan cities, and the sectors such as IT and IPC. The analysis is conducted using Power BI for data visualization and statistical methods in Python looking for any trends or correlations. In addition, clustering techniques were utilized in grouping states and sector data observation into three groups, i.e., low risk, medium risk and high risk. The analysis showed that most states were classified as low risk and only a few instead showed an extremely high intensity of Cyber Crime suggesting a degree of geographical concentration for Cyber Crime. The authors also used two types of machine learning model (Linear Regression and Random Forest) to identify any trends based on time. However, both machine learning models displayed limited success in their predictability meaning that Cyber Crime occurrences cannot simply be explained by reference to time alone. The overall findings of this study then align with the conclusion that while some Cyber Crime occurrences are similar and concentrated to a particular location or point in time, they are also dissimilar based upon when they occur and where they occur. As a whole the study illustrates a methodical analytical technique of using both data visualization through statistical methods and explorative AI methods to provide better insight into Cyber Crime trends.

title: FROM VICTIM TO VILLAIN: A FORENSIC AND LINGUISTIC INQUIRY INTO THE CONSTRUCTION OF CRIMINAL IDENTITY IN THE AGE OF DEEPFAKES
venue: LawFoyer International Journal of Doctrinal Legal Research.

title: Regulating AI in Criminal Justice: A Study on Surveillance Technologies, Predicative Policing, Cybercrime Enforcement, and Human Rights Protection
venue: Advances in Social Science, Education and Humanities Research/Advances in social science, education and humanities research
abstract: In this fast-changing digital era, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transitioned contemporary criminal justice systems through its migration into surveillance networks, predictive policy methods, and regulatory cybercrime enforcements.This technology ensures greater operational efficiency, real-time monitoring of threat detection and prevention analytics, and enhanced investigative capabilities.However, on the other hand, these rapid technology adoption raises complex legal, ethical, and human rights concerns that our regulatory frameworks fail to recognize.This research paper will examine the development of AI in criminal justice by focusing on predicating algorithms, risk assessment, AI driven cybersecurity tools, automated facial recognitions etc., my study will further evaluate how Indian legal governance framework such as Indian Constitution, IT Act[1], Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023[2], regulate or lack in governing the AI enabled law enforcement processes.The paper further examines how international regulatory bodies approach AI, specifically UN OHCHR regulations on human rights-centered AI, the European Union AI Act, and International cybercrime governance standards, evaluating the best practices and identifying gaps that are relevant to India's perspective.Will further assess in detail ethical concerns in algorithm bias, privacy infringements, risk of over-criminalization, and discriminatory profiling.Additionally, the paper will also emphasize how AI-AI-generated evidence are automated investigations have reshaped the legal policy-making process, courtroom proceedings, and access to justice, which requires enhancing judges, lawyers, and investigators.

title: Deepfakes and Cyber Law: Is India's Legal Framework Ready?
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This article examines whether India's legal framework has kept pace with the rapid growth of deepfake technology. It surveys the pre-existing toolkit under the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Sections 66C, 66D, 66E, 67, 67A) and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and shows how each provision applies only awkwardly to deepfakes, since none was drafted with synthetic media in mind. It then examines the 2026 Amendment to the Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code Rules, which for the first time defines "synthetically generated information," mandates labelling and embedded metadata, and compresses takedown timelines to three hours for content flagged by a court or government order. The article situates these obligations alongside the Delhi High Court's personality-rights jurisprudence (Amitabh Bachchan v. Rajat Nagi, Anil Kapoor v. Simply Life India) and the constitutional right to privacy recognised in Puttaswamy, while testing the new takedown regime against the free-speech safeguards affirmed in Shreya Singhal. It identifies persisting gaps — anonymous and cross-border creators, metadata stripped on re-sharing, imperfect detection tools, and the absence of a standalone statutory right over one's likeness — and argues that India, while now possessing one of the more detailed regulatory frameworks for synthetic media, must move beyond platform-facing obligations toward enforceable individual rights, faster victim-facing remedies, and public media literacy.

title: Cybercrime, Complaint Attrition and Enforcement Outcomes in Cyberstalking and Online Harassment: Analysis of National and Haryana Official Statistics, 2019–2025
venue: Enterprise Development and Microfinance
abstract: Background: Cyberstalking and online harassment are widely reported to be under-recorded in India, but the size of the gap between victimisation, complaint, registration and conviction has rarely been quantified from official sources. Objective: To analyse national and Haryana official statistics for 2019–2025 to describe trends in recorded cybercrime and in the cyber stalking/bullying head, to measure the attrition between complaints and registered cases, and to assess enforcement outcomes. Methods: A descriptive analysis of secondary data from the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) Crime in India reports, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (NCRP), parliamentary replies and Haryana Police statements, using growth rates, compound annual growth rates, shares, conversion ratios and rates per lakh population. Figures that could not be reconciled across sources were excluded or tested in sensitivity checks. Results: NCRB-registered cyber crime rose from 44,735 cases (2019) to 86,420 (2023), an increase of 93.2% (17.9% a year), while the cyber stalking/bullying head rose only from 771 to 1,305 (69.3%), and its share of all cyber crime fell from 1.7% to 1.5%. Cyber fraud and cheating together rose from 21.5% to 42.1% of recorded cases. Only 8–15 convictions a year (0.9–1.6% of registered cases) were recorded under the stalking head in 2019–2021. NCRB cases equalled 11.7% of NCRP incidents in 2021 and 5.4% in 2023; in 2024 only 2.43% of 20,33,316 portal complaints became FIRs. In Haryana, complaints rose from 1,362 (2019) to 66,784 (2022) and about 1.15 lakh (2023), while NCRB cases rose from 564 to 751, so the ratio of cases to complaints fell from 41.4% to 1.0% and 0.7%. Haryana's 2023 rate of 2.6 cases per lakh was far below that of Telangana (52.1) and Karnataka (35.9), and only 103 women-centric cyber crimes were registered against 15,758 crimes against women. Conclusion: Official statistics record the visible tip of cyberstalking. Registration capacity, not incidence, appears to be the binding constraint, and it is weakest where complaint volumes grow fastest. Separate counting of cyberstalking, reporting of outcomes and investment in registration and forensic capacity are needed.

title: CYBERCRIME AND DATA PROTECTION LAWS IN INDIA: EMERGING LEGAL CHALLENGES
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research and Multidisciplinary Trends (IJARMT)
abstract: The digitization of governance, business, banking and social interaction in India has been happening at an unprecedented speed and with it, the rise of the cybercrime and the need for a robust data protection law. This paper explores the statutory landscape of cyberspace in India over the past two decades, first the Information Technology Act, 2000 and then the Information Technology (Amendment) Act, 2008, until the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the country's first comprehensive personal-data law, was enacted. The paper is divided into five thematic sections, respectively addressing the statutory framework of cyber law, the data protection regime, cybercrimes against individuals, cybercrimes against property and the State and new challenges created by artificial intelligence, cross-border data flows and cloud jurisdiction. A separate chapter then examines key court rulings such as that in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, Justice K.S. Puttaswamy's decision in its favour and other privacy, intermediary liability and electronic evidence cases, that have influenced the application of these laws. The paper states that while India has constructed a reasonably developed legal structure, there are still several areas of enforcement, cooperation, victim redressal and regulation of emerging technologies which remain unaddressed. Finally, it provides recommendations on the strengthening of the institutional capacity, harmonisation of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act with sectoral regulation and reform of criminal procedure in order to address the challenges posed by the fast-changing digital environment.

title: CYBERCRIME AND THE LAW: AN ANALYSIS OF LEGAL FRAMEWORKS FOR COMBATING DIGITAL OFFENCES IN INDIA
authors: Arun Kumar; Dr. Vinay Kumar Katiyar
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the Indian legal framework for fighting digital crimes. It looks at the link between rising cybercrime rates and new legal or institutional responses. The research uses a quantitative secondary methodology. It uses data from the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) from 2019 to 2023. The Ministry of Home Affairs reported this data. The study uses other official legal and institutional sources alongside this data. Registered cybercrime cases rose from 44,735 in 2019 to 86,420 in 2023. This is a 93.18% increase. Cases rose by 31.15% between 2022 and 2023 alone. Karnataka, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, and Maharashtra recorded the highest numbers of registered incidents among Indian states. The legal analysis covers several legislative texts. These include the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. The analysis includes the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, CERT-In, and the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C). The findings show that India changed how it handles cybercrime. It moved from just using laws to creating a full institutional system. This system integrates substantive offenses, criminal procedures, and electronic evidence. It covers incident response, data protection, and specialized cybercrime coordination. This change shows that the main challenge is not a lack of laws. India needs better implementation and stronger technical skills. It needs better digital forensic tools and better coordination between agencies. India must finish investigations faster. Keywords: cybercrime, cyber law, India, Information Technology Act, electronic evidence, I4C, CERT-In, quantitative research

title: Reconstructing India’s Cybercrime Law: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and the Emerging Architecture of Digital Criminal Justice
authors: Regoti Ajay Kumar; S S L Shyam Kishore P
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
abstract: The rapid digitisation of economic, social and governmental activity in India has produced a corresponding expansion in the scale, sophistication and transnational character of cybercrime. The replacement of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 marks a significant reconfiguration of substantive criminal law. This paper undertakes a doctrinal examination of the adequacy of the new Sanhita, read together with the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, to address contemporary cyber threats. The research purpose is to evaluate whether the technology-neutral drafting of the Sanhita, the express inclusion of cyber-crimes within the organised-crime provision, and its extraterritorial reach supply a coherent and enforceable framework, or whether structural gaps persist in definition, evidence, jurisdiction and institutional capacity. The methodology is primarily doctrinal, drawing upon statutory text, parliamentary materials, leading Supreme Court authorities on electronic evidence and free speech, and comparative insights from international instruments. The findings indicate that while the Sanhita improves coverage of cyber-enabled fraud, stalking, forgery and syndicate-level activity, it does not create a dedicated cybercrime regime; dual charging with the Information Technology Act continues to generate interpretive friction; evidentiary certification requirements remain a frequent point of failure; and cross-border investigation continues to confront mutual-legal-assistance delays. The paper concludes that the Sanhita constitutes a meaningful incremental advance rather than a comprehensive solution, and that adequacy ultimately depends upon coordinated interpretation, enhanced forensic capacity, clearer guidance on emerging technologies such as deepfakes, and stronger institutional coordination between special cyber legislation and general criminal law.

title: A Critical Study of Digital Arrest Scams and the Erosion of Online Trust: A Socio-Legal Analysis of Cybercrime Regulation in the AI Era

These scams involve cybercriminals impersonating law enforcement agencies, judicial authorities, telecom regulators, or financial institutions through video calls, AI-generated voices, forged digital documents, and deepfake-assisted communication to create fear and compel victims to transfer money under the false pretext of legal action. title: Cyber Bullying, Online Hate and Harassment: Emerging Challenges and Legal Protections to the Victim
venue: Social Prism
abstract: Cyber bullying, hate speech via the internet, and harassment that is enabled by technology are quickly relying the point of harm not only to physical geography but also to networked environments where abuse can be scaled, sustained and hard to get rid of. In Pakistan, the concept of victim protection is rooted in constitutional rights to dignity and privacy (Article 14) and a broad interpretation of life and liberty (Article 9) with statutory protection under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016 (PECA). But the legal difficulty is dual: (i) under-enforcement and procedural drag that will deter reporting and a slowing of relief, (ii) there is the danger of over-extensive regulation of content that will suppress legitimate speech and political dissent. Workable thresholds are determined with the help of comparative jurisprudence. The constitutional weakness of vaguely charging crimes of offensive speech as seen in Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) points to the striking down of vague online restrictions on speech in India, whereas its privacy jurisprudence in K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) compounds claim regarding doxxing and non-consensual dissemination. The case law of DPP v Collins 2006 and Chambers v DPP 2012 to establish the distinction between grossly offensive communication and defensive expression and the cases of defamation and harassment in digital media characterise the UK attitude to reputational harm. The US constitutional framework provides the most robust safeguard of hateful speech, but nonetheless authorizes it to be limited to subjective threats and stalking-like behaviors, which has been narrowed down more recently in Counterman v Colorado (2023).

title: Deepfakes and Indian Laws: Is India Ready for the Next Digital Threat?
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Deepfakes have emerged as a significant digital threat with the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence and advanced digital technologies. By manipulating or generating realistic images, videos, and audio, deepfakes can imitate individuals with remarkable accuracy, making it increasingly difficult to distinguish authentic content from fabricated material. While deepfake technology has legitimate applications in entertainment, education, accessibility, and creative industries, its misuse has raised serious concerns relating to privacy, defamation, identity theft, misinformation, cybercrime, and electoral integrity. India has witnessed several deepfake incidents involving celebrities, politicians, journalists, and ordinary individuals, highlighting the urgent need for effective legal safeguards. This paper examines the existing Indian legal framework dealing with deepfakes, including provisions relating to cyber offences, privacy, defamation, and intermediary liability. It further analyses the limitations and challenges of the present framework and explores whether existing laws are sufficient to address rapidly evolving AI-generated threats. The paper concludes by suggesting the need for stronger regulation, technological detection mechanisms, and greater public awareness to ensure responsible use of Artificial Intelligence.

title: Understanding Silence: A Sociological Exploration of the Challenges Faced by Elderly Cybercrime Victims in Approaching Formal Reporting Channels in India
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Indian society is digitizing at a rapid pace. This development has resulted in new opportunities for senior citizens to utilize technology but, at the same time, has also exposed them to severe cybercrime threats. This paper examines the socio-cultural barriers that prevent senior Indians from coming forward to report their experiences of victimization due to hacking. Previous studies have already pointed out the knowledge gaps, decreased intentions to report, inefficiencies in the reporting system, and vulnerabilities intersecting with digital literacy, gender, and socio-economic factors. We have discovered that senior citizens are struggling to navigate digital environments because of insufficient awareness about online cyber threats and risky online practices, which are further worsened by the hindrances created by institutions to make complaint filing easier. The significance of this paper is threefold: it belongs to the growing literature on digital gerontology and the victimology of cybercrime by highlighting an impediment in the Indian socio-cultural setting. The findings suggest that the need for immediate action to safeguard this vulnerable group in a rapidly digitizing environment is imperative.

title: Gendered Victimization and Institutional Response to Cybercrime: Evidence from Faisalabad, Punjab, Pakistan
venue: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
abstract: Research into cybercrime in Pakistan notes that women are less likely than men to report cybercrimes to authorities and organisations, but does not explain why women’s reporting remains low even when they do come forward. In this paper, we examine the importance of gender in a larger qualitative study conducted on cybercrime in Faisalabad, in Punjab, through a gendered lens looking specifically at girls’ and women’s experiences of cybercrime. Our findings based on semi-structured interviews with 28 participants (victims of crime, FIA officers, lawyers and civil-society workers) and analysis of case files suggest three key issues contributing to the disadvantage women experience. Specifically, gender creates unjust conditions for women in the context of cybercrime in three interrelated areas: 1) women have far less freedom of movement compared to men, and thus use private platforms where predators operate; 2) family reactions to female victimisation are primarily aimed at hiding the fact of victimisation instead of seeking justice; and 3) complaints regarding problems related to cybercrime are dealt with by the male-dominated cybercrime department which does not adequately respond to complaints.We understand these findings in accordance with Routine Activity Theory’s concept of guardianship, Braithwaite’s categorization of reintegrative shame and stigmatising shame, and Lonsway and Archambault’s ‘justice gap’ approach. We argue that gendered victimisation is produced and sustained in Faisalabad through the interplay of family, community and state institutions, rather than by any one of the institutions alone.

title: LEGAL CHALLENGES OF DEEPFAKE TECHNOLOGY IN INDIA
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In the age of artificial intelligence, seeing is no longer believing. Within just a few years, AI has advanced from a tech-hobbyist's playground into a highly sophisticated factory capable of cloning voices, generating photorealistic images, and altering video footage with terrifying precision. For a long time, we treated these "deepfakes" as harmless entertainment—a viral video of a celebrity dancing, or a deceased actor "brought back to life" for a film cameo. But that innocent phase is officially over. Today, deepfakes have weaponized digital media, leaving a trail of compromised elections, ruined reputations, targeted cybercrimes, and an unprecedented violation of women's privacy. This threat hits with unique force in India. As home to one of the largest and fastest-growing digital populations on the planet, millions of Indians are logging onto the internet for the first time every month, often via cheap smartphone data. This rapid digital expansion has outpaced public awareness, creating a massive, vulnerable ecosystem where synthetic misinformation spreads like wildfire across messaging apps before anyone thinks to fact-check it. Ultimately, the deepest crisis we face isn't just the existence of fake content itself. It is the creeping, systemic collapse of trust in all digital evidence. When anything can be perfectly faked, authentic proof can easily be dismissed as a hoax, leaving our legal system, our media, and our public discourse stranded in a world where truth itself becomes a matter of opinion.

title: Cybercrime Preparedness and the Digital Economy: Empirical Evidence in MENA and South Asia Using Driscoll-Kraay
authors: Gulnar Sadat Mulla; Mark P. Doblas; Laurence P.Bazan .; Liza Mae Maganding
venue: CRC Press eBooks
abstract: This paper focuses on analyzing determinants of cybercrime preparedness using a panel data econometrics approach among 48 countries based in the MENA and South Asia regions from 2018 to 2022. By using data available in the World Development Index hosted at the World Bank site, this research utilizes a panel analysis with Driscoll and Kraay standard errors to correct for cross-section dependence. The study shows that when countries are more digitally penetrative and when better governance standards for fighting corruption and rule of law are achieved, there are substantial gains toward safeguarding against cybercrime attacks. However, this study finds no evidence for literacy as a factor for preparedness against cybercrime. This clearly indicates that a broader conceptualization of cybersecurity covers more than purely technical parameters and must therefore include governance factors especially those that pertain to public integrity.

title: Understanding Cyber Crime Awareness Levels Among School Students: A Quasi-Experimental Study in Dehradun
authors: Raj Vishnoi; Sangam Sharma; Kusum Lata; Diksha Bahuguna
venue: Adolescencia e Saude
abstract: Background: Children and teenagers face growing exposure to severe digital risks, including cyberbullying, privacy intrusions, and financial fraud, the latter of which accounted for 69% of all cybercrime instances in India in 2023. Because young people are highly susceptible to online abuse and digital threats, incorporating age-appropriate cybersecurity education is a vital requirement to close the gap in digital safety. Methods: A quantitative, one-group pre-test/post-test quasi-experimental study was conducted among school students aged 12 to 18 in Dehradun. Using a demographic interview schedule and a self-structured multiple-choice questionnaire, researchers evaluated a sample of 60 students. Participants completed a baseline pre-test, attended a 45-minute interactive audio-visual awareness session on cybercrime prevention, and completed a post-test on the seventh day to measure knowledge retention. Results: Baseline assessments indicated a severe lack of digital literacy, with 65.0% of respondents exhibiting inadequate awareness, 31.7% showing moderate awareness, and only 3.3% demonstrating adequate awareness. Following the intervention, awareness levels shifted significantly: inadequate awareness dropped to 6.7%, moderate awareness rose to 71.7%, and adequate awareness climbed dramatically to 21.7%. The intervention yielded a highly significant increase in the mean knowledge score, moving from 13.55 in the pre-test to 20.83 in the post-test (p < 0.001). Furthermore, baseline awareness levels showed no statistically significant associations with demographic variables such as age, gender, educational standard, digital exposure, or primary device used. Conclusion: School students exhibit a severe baseline lack of cybercrime awareness, independent of their demographics or daily digital habits. However, a structured 45-minute audio-visual intervention significantly improved their knowledge, drastically reducing the rate of inadequate awareness from 65% to 6.7%. This demonstrates that formal, school-based cybersecurity education is highly effective and an essential requirement for equipping youth with proactive digital defense mechanisms.

title: DEEPFAKES AND THE LAW: A GROWING LEGAL CHALLENGE
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Deepfakes are AI-generated synthetic media that convincingly depict a person saying or doing things they never did. Though they have lawful uses in entertainment, education and accessibility, their misuse for impersonation, fraud, harassment, non-consensual sexual imagery and disinformation threatens autonomy, privacy, consent and reputation. This article examines how deepfakes are created, the harms they cause and the Indian legal framework that applies to them: Article 21 of the Constitution, the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the IT Rules, 2021, as amended in February 2026 to cover synthetically generated information. It argues that these laws punish the consequences of deepfakes but do not regulate deepfakes themselves. It proposes stricter penalties, quick and affordable remedies, stronger personality and likeness rights, careful scrutiny of digital evidence and greater public awareness, so that individual rights are protected without stifling legitimate uses of AI.

title: Cybercrime and criminal law: Navigating the digital battlefield
authors: Alok Verma; Pushpendra Kumar Anuragi; Sampada Jagannath Kangane
venue: International Journal of Criminal Common and Statutory Law
abstract: The exponential proliferation of internet connectivity and digital technologies has engendered a complex and rapidly evolving landscape of criminal activity that transcends conventional geographical and jurisdictional boundaries. Cybercrime, encompassing offences ranging from hacking and data breaches to cyberterrorism and online financial fraud, poses unprecedented challenges to existing criminal law frameworks that were designed for a pre-digital era. This paper undertakes a comprehensive analytical examination of cybercrime through the lens of criminal law, focusing on the jurisprudential, legislative, and enforcement dimensions of the digital battlefield. Drawing upon Indian statutory frameworks principally the Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended in 2008) and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [37] alongside comparative analysis of international instruments such as the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime, 2001, and legislative models from the United States and European Union, this study critically evaluates the adequacy of existing legal responses. The paper further explores doctrinal tensions including jurisdictional conflicts, evidentiary challenges posed by digital forensics, the attribution problem inherent to anonymous cyber actors, and the emerging threat paradigm of artificial intelligence-enabled cybercrime. The authors argue that effective criminal law responses to cybercrime necessitate not merely legislative amendments but a fundamental reconceptualisation of criminal liability, jurisdictional doctrine, and international cooperation frameworks. Recommendations for law reform and policy innovation are advanced, with particular attention to the Indian context.

title: An Examination of Cybercrime in India
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The term "cybercrime" describes crimes committed through the use of a communication channel or device, such as a watch, laptop, desktop computer, PDA, mobile phone, or car, either directly or indirectly. In the "Global Risks for 2012" research, cyberattacks are expected to be among the top five worldwide threats to the government and corporate sectors. Cybercrime is a kind of crime that gradually damages victims' life and is hard to detect and stop once it has occurred. Because online banking and shopping are becoming more and more popular and entail sensitive financial and personal data, we hear this phrase in the news a lot. In this paper, the various forms of cybercrime, their evolution, case studies, majors that focus on prevention, and the departments that fight them are briefly summarized.

title: Cyber Harassment and Victim Blaming on Women: A Perception Study
venue: International Journal of Engineering Development and Research
abstract: The study examines how victim blaming remains an ongoing issue in India through its examination of female victims who face online harassment. The study examines how people who have experienced victimization develop mental health issues and social problems and legal problems because of their belief in victim-blaming. The research used a quantitative survey which involved 204 participants to determine that cyberstalking and cyberbullying represented the most common types of cyber harassment. The results show that people who believe in traditional gender roles together with those who think of personal responsibility as the main cause of victimization tend to develop victim-blaming beliefs. The study shows that people with these specific beliefs experience emotional distress and social isolation because they refuse to report incidents which they believe will damage their reputation.

title: Cybercrime Regulation in Pakistan: An Assessment of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016 and the Role of Law Enforcement Agencies in Comparative Perspective
venue: Social science review archives.
abstract: The use of digital technologies has changed the nature of modern societies in many respects, and it has opened up new avenues for cyber criminals to exploit. States are having to establish broad, all-encompassing legal and institutional strategies to prevent, investigate and prosecute cyber-crimes, which are becoming more sophisticated and large in scale. The present study reviews Pakistan's cybercrime legislative framework in detail with a specific focus on Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016 (PECA) and assesses the contribution of the law enforcement agencies in the enforcement and implementation of the cybercrime laws. The study adopts a qualitative doctrinal and comparative legal research approach and examines the cybercrime regime in Pakistan and its comparison with other legal and institutional frameworks of the United Kingdom, the United States, Singapore and the European Union. The analysis shows that PECA offers a fairly broad legislative response to cyber offences, but there are some barriers to effective implementation today, such as a lack of capacity to conduct digital forensic investigations, a lack of certain types of investigators, jurisdictional problems, institutional coordination issues and a lack of public awareness. The comparative assessment highlights how more developed jurisdictions have developed more advanced solutions, including via the use of dedicated cyber security enforcement bodies, a more forward-looking approach to cyber security, greater international cooperation arrangements and institutional and institutional frameworks. Concluding the study, the researchers argue that good governance of cybercrime needs to be more than just a legislative provision and is facilitated by institutional capacity building, technological investments, professional training and cooperation between nations. The article calls for the modernisation of legislation, strengthening of digital forensic tools, creation of a coordinated national mechanism for handling cybercrimes and implementation of international best practices to make the system more effective against the emerging cyber threats to protect fundamental rights and digital security.

title: Comprehensive Systematic Review and Critical Evaluation of AI-Driven Cybercrime Detection, eFIR Systems, and Legal Frameworks in Indian Policing
authors: Vemireddy Prasanth Reddy∗; Jambula Tharun Prasad Reddy†; Kunduru Anil Kumar Reddy‡; Korangi Mahitha Venkata Lakshmie.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: As cyber-threats become increasingly sophisticated in the artificial intelligence (AI) era, law enforcement agencies face severe operational bottlenecks in reporting, triaging, and processing cybercrime complaints [1]. Current literature spans machine learning detection architectures, e-FIR lodging portals, legal framework analyses, and police administrative studies [2, 9]. However, existing research remains highly fragmented: technical threat-detection systems operate in isolation from legal work-flows, while policy and legal studies lack actionable automated implementations [7, 17]. This paper conducts a comprehensive critical evaluation of 20 seminal and contemporary works cover-ing AI cybercrime models, blockchain e-FIR platforms, statutory provisions (IT Act, BNS, DPDP Act), and police operational reports [1–20]. By systematically identifying methodological limi-tations, variables, and procedural gaps across existing studies, we establish the explicit necessity for an integrated, AI-driven Smart FIR system capable of automated complaint triage, evidence extraction, legal mapping, and transparent police workflow integration.

title: CYBERCRIME AGAINST WOMEN IN INDIA: A CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF THE LEGAL FRAMEWORK, ENFORCEMENT GAPS AND ACCESS TO JUSTICE
venue: LawFoyer International Journal of Doctrinal Legal Research.
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technology has transformed communication, education, employment and social interaction, but it has simultaneously created new spaces for harassment, exploitation and abuse.Women increasingly encounter cyber offences such as cyberstalking, impersonation, identity theft, online harassment, non-consensual dissemination of intimate material, morphing, cyberbullying and other forms of technology-facilitated abuse.The nature of these offences makes them particularly challenging because perpetrators may operate anonymously, evidence can be altered or deleted rapidly, and harmful content can spread across multiple jurisdictions within a short period.This paper examines the Indian legal framework applicable to cybercrime against women and evaluates the extent to which existing laws and institutional mechanisms respond to the distinctive difficulties associated with online offences.It studies relevant provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, together with significant judicial decisions concerning online harassment, privacy, intermediary responsibility and unlawful digital content.The paper further examines institutional mechanisms including the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre.Particular attention is given to under-reporting, difficulties in identification of perpetrators, preservation and admissibility of electronic evidence, intermediary cooperation, privacy concerns and the emotional and social consequences experienced by victims.The study adopts a doctrinal methodology supported by secondary literature and government materials.It argues that although India possesses several overlapping legal remedies, the framework remains fragmented and its LawFoyer

title: Digital Panopticon, Algorithmic Bias, and the Law: Cyber-Victimization and Legal Vulnerabilities in 21st-Century Indian Fiction
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper explores the intersecting landscapes of technology, surveillance, and institutional justice within 21st-century Indian fiction, offering a comprehensive analysis of how literature reflects modern legal and digital anxieties. Framing the contemporary digital environment as an advanced "Digital Panopticon," the study investigates how modern Indian narratives depict the systemic vulnerabilities of the individual against corporate data gathering, algorithmic bias, and digital manipulation. Moving deliberately beyond conventional science-fiction paradigms, this research applies critical legal and technological lenses to contemporary prose. It focuses heavily on the phenomenon of cyber-victimization, analyzing how individuals are rendered defenseless against algorithmic framing, systemic data corruption, deepfakes, and relentless trial-by-media. By anchoring its analysis in texts like Prayaag Akbar’s 'Leila' and Samit Basu’s 'The City Inside,' this paper scrutinizes the lived realities of characters whose physical movements, psychological autonomy, and legal rights are stripped away by invisible digital codes. Furthermore, the paper highlights a critical institutional void: the tragic reality that traditional legal frameworks, including the Indian Information Technology Act, often fail to keep pace with rapid technological advancements. This leaves a structural vacuum where digital citizens are uniquely vulnerable to both corporate overreach and state-sponsored technological oppression. Ultimately, the study argues that contemporary Indian fiction acts as a crucial socio-legal critique. It compels readers to acknowledge that the machinery of the digital age is not neutral, and forces a radical re-evaluation of justice, proof, and fundamental human rights in an irreversible, hyper-connected era.

title: AI-GENERATED DEEPFAKES AND THE INDIAN LEGAL FRAMEWORK: A LEGAL ANALYSIS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Artificial Intelligence has changed the way digital content is produced and shared, making it possible to create images, videos and audio that can appear remarkably real. Deepfakes are one such development, where a person's face, voice or actions can be digitally created or altered. While this technology can be used for legitimate purposes in fields such as education, entertainment and media, its misuse can cause serious harm through impersonation, fraud, harassment, misinformation, privacy violations and non-consensual intimate content. These developments have created new legal concerns in India, particularly because many existing laws were framed before such advanced forms of synthetic media became common. This article examines how the Indian legal system deals with deepfake-related harms through constitutional protections, the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and the Information Technology Rules, 2021. It also looks at important judicial decisions concerning privacy and personality rights, along with recent regulatory measures relating to Synthetically Generated Information. The article further considers difficulties in detecting deepfakes, securing their timely removal and providing effective remedies to victims. It concludes that India needs a practical and balanced legal approach that protects individuals from harmful uses of deepfakes while allowing legitimate expression, creativity and technological development. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Deepfakes, Cybercrime, Privacy, Indian Legal Framework.

title: The Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016: Balancing Cybercrime Control and Freedom of Online Expression in Pakistan
authors: Muhammad Tauheed Ahmad; Rao Imran Habib
venue: Pakistan Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences
abstract: To properly manage the burgeoning digital world and cybercrime activities, the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016 (PECA) was enacted in Pakistan. Its primary role was to address serious online offences like cyber harassment, hacking, identity theft, online fraud, hate speech and the misuse of electronic communication. A law like this was needed to safeguard citizens and ensure order in the online world, especially in a nation where the internet is growing in significance. But the use of PECA has caused deep concern particularly in terms of freedom of expression. While the law was intended to protect from real cybercrime, many of its provisions are deemed to be too vague, too broad and lacking in clear boundaries. Given this uncertainty, PECA has been criticized in many cases to be applied to journalists, media personnel, political activists, and people voicing opposing views. This can create the danger that legislation designed to protect becomes a means of abridging free expression and stifling criticism. This paper looks at PECA through the lens of the law and reviews the interpretation and application of PECA in Pakistan. It also explores the attitude of judiciary and underlines the lack of consistency in protection of fundamental rights especially the right to freedom of speech provided under the Constitution of Pakistan. The study also investigates if PECA has instilled fear in citizens to voice their opinions online. It is conducted by doctrinal legal research, which involves careful attention paid to the statute, cases, judicial rulings and scholarly writing. It aims to understand its impact on the internet in Pakistan, and to assess if the law has a good balance between cyber security and constitutional freedoms. The paper ends by suggesting for legal changes to clarify PECA and provide fairer and better protection under the Law.

title: An Evaluation of Cybercrime in India
venue: Advanced International Journal for Research
abstract: Cyber-crime, in its contemporary manifestation, is no longer limited to isolated instances of identity theft, phishing, or financial fraud. It has evolved into a sophisticated, organized and often state-supported phenomenon capable of destabilizing national infrastructure. Modern cyber threats include cyber terrorism, cyber espionage, ransomware attacks targeting critical information infrastructure, large-scale data breaches, disinformation campaigns and hybrid warfare tactics. These activities demonstrate that cyberspace is no longer a peripheral domain of criminal activity but a strategic battleground where power, influence and sovereignty are contested. Globally, cyber-attacks on power grids, healthcare institutions, financial networks and government databases illustrate the devastating consequences of digital insecurity. In the Indian context, incidents involving data leaks, ransomware attacks on hospitals, breaches of financial systems and attempts to infiltrate defence communication networks underscore the gravity of the threat.

title: Deepfakes and AI-Generated Evidence in Indian Criminal Trials
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
abstract: Artificial intelligence has transformed the creation, manipulation and interpretation of digital information. Deepfakes and other forms of AI-generated content can reproduce human faces, voices, movements and conversations with a degree of realism that makes ordinary visual or auditory inspection unreliable. These developments raise important questions for criminal justice, particularly where video recordings, audio clips, photographs, social-media content and digitally generated material are relied upon to establish criminal liability. In India, the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), provides the principal statutory framework governing electronic and digital records, but compliance with the rules of admissibility does not necessarily establish the factual truth of the content presented. This paper critically examines the challenges posed by deepfakes and AI-generated evidence in Indian criminal trials. It analyses the distinction between admissibility, authenticity, attribution and evidentiary weight, with particular attention to Sections 39 and 61–63 of the BSA, the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the constitutional guarantees of equality, personal liberty and fair trial. It also considers the continuing relevance of judicial decisions concerning electronic evidence under the former Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The research adopts a doctrinal and analytical methodology based on statutory provisions, judicial precedents and relevant legal scholarship. It argues that electronic-record certification, hash values and conventional chain-of-custody procedures are important safeguards but cannot independently establish that a recording depicts a genuine event or identifies the correct person. The paper recommends risk-sensitive forensic examination, transparent disclosure of relevant technical findings, effective opportunities for cross-examination, and judicial caution against treating digital recordings as inherently reliable. A balanced framework should protect the integrity of criminal proceedings without allowing unsubstantiated allegations of AI manipulation to undermine genuine evidence.

title: Three Decades of Publications on Hacking and The Law: A Bibliometric Analysis
authors: Ani Munirah Mohamad; Zaiton Hamin; Mohd Bahrin Othman
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
abstract: This study examines three decades of scholarly output on hacking and the law, addressing the growing need to understand how legal, regulatory and ethical dimensions of hacking have evolved in response to rapid technological change. Despite the proliferation of cybersecurity incidents and corresponding policy developments, there has been limited systematic assessment of the intellectual landscape shaping this field. To address this gap, the study employed a structured bibliometric methodology. Data were collected using Scopus advanced searching, covering publications from 1995 to 2025, yielding an initial dataset of 246 documents that was subsequently refined to 236 through the application of inclusion criteria. Statistical trends and distributional patterns were analysed using the Scopus Analyzer, while OpenRefine was used to clean, standardise and harmonise author names, keywords and source information to ensure data accuracy. VOSviewer was then applied to generate visualisations of co-authorship networks, keyword co occurrence structures and thematic clusters, enabling the identification of dominant research themes and collaborative patterns. The results demonstrate a marked increase in publication activity after 2010, with notable peaks between 2020 and 2025, and reveal substantial thematic concentration around ethical hacking, cybersecurity, penetration testing and legal governance of digital intrusions. Co-authorship mapping further highlights the central roles of the United States, India and the United Kingdom, alongside emerging contributions from Malaysia and selected European countries. The analysis shows that research in this domain is expanding, diversifying and becoming increasingly interdisciplinary. The study concludes that bibliometric insights provide a robust foundation for understanding how legal scholarship is adapting to the complexities of contemporary cyber threats and regulatory transformations, while also identifying future research directions in technology law and governance.

title: Cyber Law as a Legal Framework Against Cybercrime
venue: International Journal of Education Modern Management Applied Science & Social Science
abstract: The moment you think you are chatting with your friend privately, stop immediately and reconsider. Noticed, whenever there is news related to cybercrime, the media and news channels sometimes show their chats and records. So, how exactly did their conversation history and records get leaked when such messaging and calling apps claim to be “private, secure and encrypted”? In India, we have stronger cybersecurity than many nations worldwide, but to eliminate cybercrime, staying alert to common threats like financial fraud, phishing, identity theft, deep fake and online scams is essential. In this paper, we will discuss how to prevent cybercrime and be aware of the cyber law.

title: Deepfakes and the Law in India: Copyright, Personality Rights and the Need for a Comprehensive Legal Framework
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The fast growth of artificial intelligence has enabled the creation of deepfakes, which are very realistic audio, video, and images that are made or changed using artificial means. Even though deepfakes can be useful for art, jokes, teaching, and fun, they are now more often used to pretend to be someone else, share fake news, harm people's reputations, steal money, and create unwanted explicit photos or videos without consent. These uses put a person's privacy, dignity, identity, and ability to control their own creative work at risk. This paper looks at how Indian laws deal with deepfakes right now. It looks at the Information Technology Act from 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita from 2023, the Information Technology Rules from 2021 which were updated in February 2026, and the Copyright Act from 1957.It also looks at personality rights and the right of publicity. It also looks at the techniques used to find deepfakes and the challenges of proving who made them, determining responsibility, and helping victims get help quickly. The paper says that the current rules, even though they work to some extent, are broken up into different parts, weren't made with synthetic media in mind, and only give some protection to a person's digital image. Victims continue to have difficulty getting help that comes quickly and really makes a difference. India needs a clear and full plan that brings together changes in laws, better technology, and working with other countries.This plan should balance new ideas and free speech with making sure people's rights are protected.

title: SAKHA: A Chatbot-Based Support System for Legal and Mental Health Aid to Women & Children Cybercrime Victims
authors: Srishti Gupta; Ashwani Kumar; Sourav Kumar Dandapat; Pankaj Kumar; Meha Jain; Tulika Shankar
venue: Northern European Journal of Language Technology
abstract: In a digital world where cybercrimes are on the rise, women and children in India face unique challenges that are often overlooked by existing solutions. The globally available platforms fail to address the nuances of Indian laws and the cultural stigma surrounding sensitive issues like mental health and legal aid. Our chatbot bridges this gap, offering a safe, confidential, and culturally relevant space for victims of cybercrime to seek help. Tailored specifically to the Indian context, the chatbot provides legal guidance based on local laws, empowering users to understand their rights and encouraging them to seek help. It also offers compassionate mental health counselling, addressing the emotional toll of cybercrime without the fear of judgment or taboo. By providing a seamless blend of legal aid and psychological support, this chatbot ensures that women and children affected by cybercrime have a reliable, accessible, and non-threatening resource to turn to.

title: Cybercrime 2.0: Evolving Digital Threats and The Indian Legal Framework
venue: Journal of Law and Legal Research Development.
abstract: The fast growth of technologies has resulted in the development of cybercrimes into technologically complex forms of crimes that go beyond the conventional crimes like unauthorised access and data breach. In fact, the emergence of artificial intelligence, deepfakes, cryptocurrency, connected devices and social engineering is seen as the emergence of Cybercrime 2.0 that is discussed in the current paper. India, as one of the largest digital economies in the world, is faced with a challenge to address the constantly evolving cyber-threats. As for the mechanisms to combat cyber-crime, there is the legislative and institutional framework based mainly on the Information Technology Act, 2000, and supplemented by Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. However, the rate of technological advancement is usually faster than legislative and institutional response. The following research paper sheds light upon the evolving concept of Cybercrime 2.0 and the ability of India's legal system to meet the challenges of new threats in the digital age. Specifically, such problems as jurisdiction, digital evidence, attribution, enforcement, platform protection and individual rights protection will be considered. The paper emphasizes the need for a comprehensive legislative approach based not only on the expansion of criminal offenses but also on the development of flexible legislation, better investigation methods and institutions.

title: Regulating Deepfakes and Synthetic Media under India's New Criminal Laws (BNS)
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence has given rise to deepfakes — hyper-realistic synthetic media capable of fabricating the words, actions, and identities of real individuals. In India, the viral spread of a non-consensual deepfake video of actress Rashmika Mandanna in 2023 exposed the alarming inadequacy of the existing legal framework in addressing AI-generated harm. This article examines how India's newly enacted Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), which replaced the Indian Penal Code with effect from 1 July 2024, approaches the regulation of deepfakes and synthetic media. Through an analysis of relevant BNS provisions including Sections 319, 336, 351, 353, and 354, read alongside the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the article argues that while the BNS provides a fragmented but functional basis for prosecuting deepfake-related offences, it falls significantly short of a coherent regulatory response. The article identifies key gaps including the absence of a standalone deepfake offence, inadequate penalties, and the lack of proactive platform obligations, and concludes with a call for dedicated synthetic media legislation drawing from international models including the EU AI Act and China's deepfake regulations.

title: Criminal Liability for Data Breaches Under Indian Law: Need for a Comprehensive Legal Framework
venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
abstract: The rapid digitalization of Indian society has transformed governance, commerce, communication, and social interaction. However, the increasing dependence on digital technologies has also resulted in growing concerns relating to privacy violations, cyber insecurity, and unauthorized disclosure of personal data. India has witnessed a sharp rise in cybercrimes, including data breaches involving financial institutions, healthcare databases, e-commerce platforms, educational institutions, and government portals. While the Indian legal system addresses certain aspects of cybercrime through statutes such as the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the absence of a comprehensive criminal liability framework for data breaches remains a significant legal challenge. This research paper critically examines the legal dimensions of criminal liability for data breaches in India in alignment with the broader thesis concerning privacy, security, and criminal accountability in Indian digital societies with special reference to Jodhpur. The study analyzes existing statutory provisions, judicial approaches, institutional mechanisms, and comparative international practices. It further explores the limitations of the present legal framework, particularly in relation to corporate accountability, cross-border data breaches, victim compensation, digital evidence, and enforcement challenges. The paper argues that India requires a specialized and comprehensive legal framework that clearly defines criminal liability for negligent and intentional data breaches while balancing innovation, digital governance, and constitutional privacy rights.

title: Cybercrimes and Legal Remedies In India: An Analysis of the Legal Framework and Judicial Approach
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technology has transformed communication, commerce, education and public administration in India. Alongside these developments, cybercrimes have emerged as a significant legal and social concern. India has developed a legal framework to address cybercrimes but the changing nature of technology continues to expose gaps in investigation, enforcement and victim protection. This article examines the statutory framework and discusses judicial decisions that have shaped cyber law. It also considers the legal remedies available to victims and the challenges faced by enforcement agencies. The article argues that effective cybercrime control requires not only legislation but also timely investigation, digital awareness, institutional coordination and safeguards for fundamental rights.

title: GENDER, LAW AND DIGITAL JUSTICE IN INDIA: WOMEN'S RIGHTS IN THE AGE OF AI AND CYBERCRIME
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Cybercrime and Emerging Legal Challenges
venue: Journal for Civil and Criminal Law for Legislative Studies (JCCLLS)
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital connectivity has transformed the nature and scale of criminal activity, giving rise to a category of offences that transcend physical borders, traditional jurisdiction, and conventional modes of investigation. This paper examines the legal response to cybercrime, with particular focus on the Indian statutory and judicial framework, situating it within a broader discussion of emerging challenges such as data breaches, artificial-intelligence-enabled fraud, cross-border jurisdictional conflict, and the tension between digital surveillance and the constitutional right to privacy. The paper traces the evolution of India's cyber law regime from the Information Technology Act, 2000, through its 2008 amendment, the Supreme Court's landmark free-speech ruling in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the recognition of privacy as a fundamental right in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, and the recent operationalisation of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. It further considers institutional responses, including the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre, and evaluates the persistent gap created by India's continued non-accession to the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime. The paper concludes that while India's legal framework has matured considerably, emerging technologies continue to outpace legislative and enforcement capacity, necessitating continuous legal reform, institutional strengthening, and greater international cooperation.

title: Sextortion as an Emerging Cybercrime: An Analysis of Legal Gaps in the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
venue: Iconic Research and Engineering Journals
abstract: Victims often find themselves trapped in financial pressure after being threatened with leaked private photos. That stems from predators using threats of exposure to extract money or demand new content, tactics rooted in emotional manipulation rather than actual data breaches. Even though Indian laws don't name sextortion as its own offense, rules under the information Technology Act, 2000, and the bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, are used loosely to catch similar acts. As it happens, this leads to cases being mislabeled or dropped entirely because the exact nature of the harm isn't clearly defined. The legal system fails to offer clear direction when handling these offenses. So this gap means investigations stall and prosecutors struggle to build strong cases against perpetrators. A recent review shows how courts apply existing sections without creating special procedures for sextortion-specific harms. Without dedicated statutes, victims end up handling a maze of conflicting interpretations instead of receiving consistent support during trials. The article finds that the current laws are incapable of fully handling sextortion issues and strongly advocates for developing a more integrated, clearly articulated, and victim-friendly legal system in India.

title: NAVIGATING THE DEEPFAKE DILEMMA IN PAKISTAN
venue: SSRN Electronic Journal

title: DEEPFAKE PORNOGRAPHY AND GENDER-BASED ONLINE VIOLENCE: A CRIMINAL LAW PERSPECTIVE
venue: Indian Journal of Legal Review
abstract: Deepfake pornography is a serious form of online violence against women. It uses intelligence to create fake but realistic sexual videos or images of women and girls without their permission. These fake videos are often shared online to hurt, blackmail or shame the victims causing pain, loss of reputation and health problems. From a law point of view this issue is studied to see how well current laws can deal with it. Most laws on harassment, privacy or revenge porn were made before deepfakes existed. As a result, they often fail to cover videos properly. It's hard to prove who made the video prove their intention and collect evidence in court. Many victims also face problems because the content spreads quickly across countries. This paper looks at laws introduced in countries like the United States, United Kingdom, India and the European Union. It examines what works what's missing and the challenges in catching offenders and holding websites responsible. The study argues that clear specific laws are needed to treat -consensual deepfake pornography as a serious sexual offence. Stronger rules for media platforms quick removal of fake content better police powers and cooperation, between countries are also essential. The main goal should be to protect victims and stop this growing abuse while balancing free speech and privacy rights.

title: Digital Arrest Scams in India: Doctrinal Analysis of the Legal Framework, Enforcement Challenges and Regulatory Reforms
venue: Journal of Law and Legal Research Development.
abstract: The quick proliferation of technologies of digital communication, online banking services and digitized public services has given rise to new ways of cyber criminals to make use of technological mechanisms and people’s trust. Digital arrest scams are one of the new types of cyber enabled financial scams, which are known as “digital arrests”. In the case of digital arrest, the offenders take the identity of any of the investigating agencies, police, court or any public official and make the individuals believe that they have any involvement in the crime. Through phone calls, video conferencing, false documents, the threat of being arrested and psychological manipulations, the victims are convinced into transferring the amount to bank accounts maintained by the offenders. Notably, there is no concept of digital arrest in the laws of India and any process that does not allow an individual to be arrested or detained via phone call or video call. This paper will carry out a doctrinal analysis of the current Indian legal system in regard to digital arrest scams. In this context, the paper will review the relevant sections of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Information Technology Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, in addition to the institutional measures involved in reporting and investigation of cyber frauds. The paper posits that the criminal law can be utilized in dealing with constituent crimes like cheating, cheating by personation, criminal intimidation and forgery. Nevertheless, challenges still exist in terms of identifying offenders, preservation of electronic evidence, tracing and freeze of the fraudulent money, jurisdiction and inter-agency cooperation.

title: Cybercrimes and Legal Remedies: A Critical Analysis of the Indian Framework
