title: Cybercrime and Cybersecurity Law: Legal Challenges in the Age of Digital Transformation
venue: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
abstract: Digital transformation has fundamentally changed the manner in which individuals, businesses, governments, and financial institutions communicate, transact, store information, and deliver services. The rapid expansion of cloud computing, digital payments, social media, artificial intelligence, Internet of Things devices, blockchain, and interconnected information systems has generated substantial economic and social benefits. At the same time, increasing digital dependence has created new opportunities for cybercriminals and exposed organizations and individuals to sophisticated forms of cybercrime. Cyberattacks can result in financial loss, identity theft, privacy violations, intellectual property theft, disruption of critical infrastructure, reputational damage, and threats to national security. This article examines the legal challenges associated with cybercrime and cybersecurity in the age of digital transformation. It adopts a doctrinal and comparative legal research methodology and evaluates the adequacy of existing legal frameworks in addressing contemporary cyber threats. Particular attention is given to India’s Information Technology Act, 2000, the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the Indian Penal Code/Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita framework as applicable to cyber-related offences, the role of CERT-In, and emerging cybersecurity governance mechanisms. Comparative reference is made to international approaches, including the Budapest Convention, European Union cybersecurity regulation, and international cooperation mechanisms. The study examines major challenges including ransomware, phishing, identity theft, cyber fraud, cyberstalking, cyberterrorism, data breaches, artificial intelligence-enabled attacks, cryptocurrency-related crime, jurisdictional difficulties, digital evidence, attribution, intermediary responsibility, and cross-border enforcement. The article argues that effective cybersecurity law requires an integrated approach combining criminal law, data protection, corporate governance, technical security, international cooperation, digital evidence mechanisms, and victim protection. It proposes a risk-based and technology-neutral legal framework emphasizing prevention, accountability, resilience, rapid incident response, and effective remedies.

title: REGULATING DEEPFAKE TECHNOLOGY UNDER INDIAN CYBER LAWS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: One of the most significant and unregulated risks facing digital society in the twenty-first century is the rise of deepfake technology, which creates artificially synthesised audio-visual content using deep learning algorithms. The rise of deepfakes in India has led to sophisticated financial frauds, AI-generated electoral disinformation, widespread non-consensual intimate imagery targeting women, and serious concerns to national security. India's current legal framework, which is mainly based on the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, does not have any special legislation that addresses synthetic media manipulation in spite of this obvious harm. This study uses comparable international models, such as those of the US and the EU, to critically assess the effectiveness of Indian cyber legislation in regulating deepfakes. It also reveals basic normative and institutional gaps. The European Union, the United Kingdom, and China, and suggests a logical, rights-preserving legal and policy framework for India. The study comes to the conclusion that the necessity of passing specific deepfake regulations is a constitutional requirement based on the fundamental rights to equality, dignity, and free speech rather than just a question of technology governance. Keywords: AI regulation, digital rights, platform liability, non-consensual intimate imagery, synthetic media, deepfakes, Indian cyber law, information technology act, and disinformation.

title: A Study on Rising Cybercrime in India with Technicaland Legal Perspectives
venue: National Journal of Criminal Law
abstract: The expansion of India’s digital economy has transformed lives, yet it has also made the country more vulnerable to cybercrime. The amount of money people is losing on online scams has more than doubled within a year. Why is this happening? Well, it is a mix of a few things. Our digital systems have weaknesses, and our laws just cannot keep up with new threats, like scams, powered by AI and realistic deepfakes. What I want to say is, while the government has done a great job with programsthat stop fraud and help people get their money back, there is a big missing piece. We are not doing a good enough job of catching and punishing the criminals. It is like we are fixing the leak after the flood, but we are not getting the people who broke the dam in the first place. What this paper argues is that to truly fix this, we need a two-pronged strategy. First, we need a legal makeover. This means creating a special court system with judges who actually understand technology. They cannot just beexperts in old laws; they need to get the complexities of things like bitcoin and online hacking. This would make it easier to prosecute and convict cybercriminals. Second, we need to focus on education. We need to make sure every single person in India knows how to protect themselves online. It is about empowering people, so they do not fall for these scams in the first place.

title: Two-Track Justice: How Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) Functions As Political Control Rather Than Cybercrime Prevention
venue: OSF Preprints (OSF Preprints)
abstract: This thesis investigates whether Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) functions according to its stated legislative intent of combating cybercrimes or operates primarily as an instrument of political speech control. Using mixed methods combining quantitative analysis of enforcement statistics with qualitative examination of court judgments and case studies, the research documents systematic disparities in PECA enforcement based on target identity rather than conduct. Between 2020 and 2024, FIA received 639,564 complaints but secured only 222 convictions (0.03% rate), with women's harassment cases achieving just 0.24% conviction rate. This massive attrition for ordinary citizens contrasts sharply with rapid prosecution of journalists: 150+ cases registered in December 2024 alone, representing 28.5 times the monthly caseload of the Counter-Terrorism Wing. The B4U fraud case demonstrates state capacity for complex digital forensics (4+ years, Rs 3.7 billion recovered), while journalist arrests occur within 48-72 hours, proving capacity constraints are strategic choices rather than technical limitations. The January 2026 Mazari-Chattha case, resulting in 17-year imprisonment for social media posts, marks a shift from process-as-punishment to actual incapacitation. The research introduces the "two-track justice" framework, demonstrating how PECA operates through parallel enforcement pathways: strategic inefficiency exhausting ordinary complainants while selective hyper-efficiency rapidly targets political critics. This pattern is traced alongside the turbulent institutional history of Pakistan's cybercrime apparatus — including the establishment of the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) in May 2024, its rules being repealed in October 2024 before it ever became operational, and its formal reconstitution under the 2025 PECA amendments — revealing how institutional instability consistently disadvantages ordinary citizens while leaving enforcement against political targets uninterrupted. The findings validate theoretical predictions from procedural justice theory, process-as-punishment, authoritarian legality, and legal instrumentalism scholarship. The thesis concludes PECA violates Pakistan's ICCPR Article 19 obligations and Pakistani constitutional vagueness standards, functioning as authoritarian legality where formal legal procedures mask systematic political control.Keywords: Pakistan, cybercrime legislation, PECA, digital rights, authoritarian legality, procedural justice, process-as-punishment, two-track justice, freedom of expression, selective enforcement

title: Deepfakes, Digital Identity and Legal Liability: Is Indian Law Ready for the AI Era?
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The pace at which artificial intelligence has been progressing is breathtaking, resulting in what is known as a crisis of authenticity in the digital space. The deepfake technology makes use of neural networks to manipulate audio, video, and visual data in such a realistic manner. This technology, which originated in entertainment, has been transformed into an instrument of deceit and extortion.

title: Online Fraud and Legal Protection Under Indian Law: A Critical Analysis of Legal Remedies and Their Effectiveness in India
authors: Husna Kounain; Hunain Fathima; Huma; Mayuri; M. Misba; Prof . Sumaiya Banu
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Internet has now become a crucial element of daily life, aiding people with conveniences in purchasing, money transaction and communication. However, there has been a rise in online fraud cases in India. Victims are frequently targeted through various forms of cybercrimes including phishing, identity theft and fake online transactions, which cause significant monetary loss and emotional suffering. The current research will evaluate the effectiveness of Indian legislation in tackling online fraud. This paper will analyze essential legislation including the Information Technology Act of 2000 along with other relevant legislation and guidelines. The analysis will be done based on information gathered from scholarly journals, official documents, and online sources. The results show that while there is enough legislation in place to counter the problem of online fraud in India, their efficiency is hindered by issues like lack of awareness among the public and long legal procedures involved. The conclusion states that while India has made substantial progress in combating the issue of online fraud, more needs to be done in order to increase system effectiveness.

title: Online Financial Fraud in India: Legal Remedies and Challenges in Cybercrime Investigation
venue: Research Vidyapith International Multidisciplinary Journal.
abstract: Online financial fraud has emerged as one of the most serious cybercrime challenges in India due to the rapid expansion of digital banking, online payments, mobile financial services, and internet-based transactions. This paper examines the legal framework, investigative mechanisms, institutional responsibilities, and victim-remedy systems governing online financial fraud in India. It analyses the role of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Indian Penal Code, 1860, financial regulations, and other economic laws in addressing offences such as phishing, identity theft, payment fraud, data theft, malware attacks, and cyber-enabled money laundering. The study also highlights major procedural difficulties, including collection and preservation of electronic evidence, maintenance of chain of custody, tracing of digital money trails, jurisdictional conflicts, cross-border investigations, and limited forensic capacity. It evaluates the functions of police agencies, cybercrime cells, financial regulators, and digital forensic institutions in investigation and enforcement. In addition, the paper discusses civil, administrative, compensatory, and restitutionary remedies available to victims. Comparative perspectives are used to identify international best practices. The study concludes that stronger legal definitions, specialized investigation mechanisms, improved inter-agency coordination, enhanced digital forensic infrastructure, public awareness, and effective victim-recovery systems are essential for combating online financial fraud in India.

title: Gender Sensitivity in Cyberspace: A Doctrinal Analysis of Cybercrime and Gender Justice in India
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
abstract: The rapid growth of digital technology has changed the way people communicate, work, study and participate in public life. At the same time, cyberspace has created new opportunities for harassment, exploitation, surveillance and other forms of gender-based harm. Women are particularly vulnerable to cyberstalking, doxxing, online sexual harassment, image-based abuse, morphing, deepfakes, cyber blackmail and sextortion. Men and gender-diverse persons may also experience online threats, harassment, identity misuse and other forms of digital abuse. This paper examines the legal framework governing technology-facilitated gender-based cybercrime in India through a doctrinal and analytical approach. It examines the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, along with relevant constitutional principles and judicial decisions. The study also examines the emerging challenge of content generated or manipulated by artificial intelligence, including deepfakes. The paper finds that Indian law provides several legal remedies, but these remedies remain distributed across different statutes and institutions. Emerging forms of cybercrime often fall between existing legal categories, creating difficulties relating to reporting, investigation, evidence, intermediary responsibility and victim protection. The paper proposes a more coordinated, gender-sensitive and technology-responsive framework supported by stronger digital forensics, rapid content removal, victim-centred mechanisms, cross-platform cooperation and international collaboration.

title: Cybercrimes against women in India and Pakistan: An overview from digital abuse to accountability
venue: VTechWorks (Virginia Tech)
abstract: This report examines how India and Pakistan respond to cybercrime against women and asks whether women who report online abuse obtain justice and protection. Drawing on official statistics from India’s National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and National Crime Records Bureau, parliamentary committee reports, Ministry of Home Affairs data, Pakistani government figures, and civil society research, it traces abuse from the forms it takes through reporting, institutional response and prosecution. The findings point to an accountability gap at different stages in each country. In India, only 2.4% of the 5.39 million complaints filed between 2019 and 2024 became First Information Reports, reported cases against women more than doubled between 2021 and 2025, and court pendency is high. In Pakistan, the 2025 data record 31 convictions against 142,272 complaints. The report finds that the gap is driven by limited technical and forensic capacity, slow platform cooperation, fragmented coordination, and social stigma. Outspoken women, journalists and religious and ethnic minorities are the most frequent targets, and generative AI and platform-based abuse are intensifying the harm. Rather than new laws or portals, the report recommends strengthening existing institutions through training, case prioritization, faster content removal, transparent case data, and victim-centered support. It argues that progress should be measured by the number of women able to seek justice, not by the number of laws enacted or complaints filed.

title: DEEPFAKES AND AI MISUSE: THE NEXT CHALLENGE FOR INDIAN CYBER LAW
venue: Acta Innovations
abstract: Deepfakes and AI-facilitated artificial media have become extremely hard to the Indian cyber law, which implies privacy, identity, reputation, financial stability, evidence reliability, and trust of the population. This paper discusses the technology underpinning and key types of deepfake abuse, the suitability of the current legal system in India, and the judicial and regulatory events of recent years. It takes into account the Information Technology Act, 2000, the rules of intermediary liability, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, data-protection law, personality rights and constitutional protections. Regulatory approaches in the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, as well as China, are also compared in the study. It draws persistent attributional, platform responsibility, and victim remedies, and digital evidence authentication gaps, and presents a coordinated regulation paradigm of prevention, disclosure, provenance, takedown, remedies, forensic capacity and institutional oversight of the digital ecosystem of India.

title: **"The Rise of Digital Deception: Deepfakes, Sextortion, and AI-Driven Financial Fraud in the Digital Age"**
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: --- ### Alternative Titles 1. **"Trapped in the Digital Illusion: Analyzing Deepfake Extortion, Cyber Blackmail, and the Weaponization of Social Media"** 2. **"The Dark Side of the Digital Web: A Comprehensive Study of AI-Driven Sextortion, Financial Scams, and Law Enforcement Countermeasures"** 3. **"Beneath the Likes: How Cybercriminals Exploit Social Media for Deepfake Blackmail and Investment Fraud"** 4. **"Digital Maya: The Escalating Threat of AI-Manipulated Media, Cyber Extortion, and the Urgent Need for Digital Literacy"** 5. **"From Fake Profiles to Financial Ruin: A Case Study on Deepfake Sextortion and AI-Enabled Cybercrime in India"** --- ### Subtitle**"A comprehensive analysis of the escalating threat of AI-manipulated media and cyber extortion—examining the predatory tactics of criminals on social media, the devastating psychological and financial toll on victims, and the critical role of law enforcement and digital literacy in combating this new wave of cybercrime"** --- ### Detailed Description This research paper provides an in-depth analysis of the rapidly evolving landscape of cybercrime, focusing specifically on the malicious use of Deepfake technology, sextortion, and AI-driven financial fraud. Drawing on recent case studies, police reports, and cybercrime statistics from India, the paper examines how the convergence of artificial intelligence, easily accessible image manipulation tools, and the ubiquity of social media platforms has created a fertile ground for sophisticated digital deception. The paper is structured around five core analytical dimensions. **First**, it investigates the mechanics of Deepfake-based extortion. The analysis details the predatory pattern used by cybercriminals: creating fake profiles on platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and Telegram to lure victims, extracting sensitive personal information (photos, contact lists), and using AI tools to morph the victim's face onto explicit or compromising images. These manipulated images are then used as leverage for blackmail, demanding ransom under the threat of public exposure to family and friends. The paper highlights the devastating psychological impact of this crime, noting tragic cases of suicide among victims who felt trapped and stigmatized. **Second**, the paper examines the broader ecosystem of AI-driven financial fraud, including investment scams and phishing operations. It details how criminals use WhatsApp and Telegram to promote fraudulent stock market and cryptocurrency schemes, often creating fake apps and "trading rooms" that display artificially inflated profits to encourage larger investments. The paper cites specific cases involving the siphoning of crores of rupees through complex networks of "mule accounts" and stolen identities, illustrating the sophisticated nature of these operations. **Third**, the paper analyzes the response of law enforcement agencies, particularly the Cyberabad police. It highlights successful operations, including the arrest of individuals involved in selling stolen data and the interception of youths returning from Cambodia who were allegedly forced to work in cyber-slavery conditions running scam operations targeting Indians. The paper also discusses the police's advocacy for AI-based detection tools to identify Deepfakes and track cryptocurrency transactions. **Fourth**, the paper critically evaluates the role and responsibility of social media platforms. It argues that the lax verification processes and anonymity offered by major platforms are being blatantly exploited by criminals. The paper calls for greater accountability from tech companies in monitoring, removing malicious content, and cooperating swiftly with law enforcement. **Fifth**, the paper outlines essential prevention and digital literacy strategies. It emphasizes the need for users to avoid accepting friend requests from unknown individuals, refrain from sharing personal photos online, and exercise extreme caution with unverified investment schemes. The paper strongly advises victims of sextortion to report the crime immediately rather than paying ransom, as capitulation only encourages further demands. The paper concludes that the weaponization of AI and social media represents a paradigm shift in cybercrime. Combating this "digital maya" requires a multi-pronged approach: stringent platform accountability, improved AI detection technologies, robust law enforcement, and a massive, nationwide campaign to educate the public about the dark side of the digital world. **Target readership:** Cybersecurity researchers, law enforcement officials, digital rights advocates, social media policy analysts, psychologists studying cyber-trauma, and the general public. **Methodological note:** The paper is a review and analysis based on reported police cases and journalistic accounts from the source articles. title: Impersonation Scams
venue: Routledge eBooks
abstract: In an increasingly digitalized world, impersonation scams have emerged as a sophisticated form of cyber fraud, exploiting the trust placed in law enforcement through psychological manipulation and technological deception. This chapter adopts a global perspective to examine the transnational nature of such scams, which often involve perpetrators operating across borders using advanced tools such as deepfakes, voice cloning, and spoofed communication platforms. The study undertakes a comparative legal analysis of international conventions, including the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime and the United Nations Convention Against Cybercrime (UNCAC), highlighting both their potential and limitations in addressing AI-enabled impersonation frauds. National legal frameworks of jurisdictions such as the United States, European Union, United Arab Emirates, and India are critically analyzed to illustrate the divergent levels of legislative preparedness and victim protection. The chapter emphasizes the need for harmonized international cooperation, robust cross-border investigative mechanisms, and the development of AI governance models that balance cybersecurity with individual rights. Towards the end, the researcher ultimately calls for the recognition of impersonation scams as a distinct international cybercrime category, advocating for stronger legal, technological, and policy-oriented responses to safeguard victims and uphold global digital trust.

title: Legal Challenges Posed by Emerging Threats in Cyberspace: A Study on Deepfakes, Ransomware and Cyberwarfare
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract: The rapid expansion of cyberspace has led to new and complex threats such as deepfakes, ransomware and cyberwarfare, which have created significant challenges for legal systems across the world. This study aims to explore and understand the legal and procedural responses to emerging threats of cybercrime through a comparative analysis of legal systems in India, the United Kingdom, and the United States of America. Through a doctrinal and comparative method of research, this paper aims to evaluate and analyse various provisions and responses of legal systems to emerging threats of cybercrime. The study found that contemporary legal systems are still in their reactive and fragmented stages and have not yet fully addressed the need for comprehensive regulation of AI-based cybercrimes. Keywords: Cybersecurity, Deepfakes, Ransomware, Cyberwarfare, Digital Governance. JEL Classification Number: K24, K42, O33, L86, K38

title: CYBERCRIME AND DATA PROTECTION LAWS IN PAKISTAN: CHALLENGES, LEGAL FRAMEWORK, AND THE NEED FOR EFFECTIVE DIGITAL RIGHTS PROTECTION
authors: 1Zaheer Iqbal Cheema, 2Muhammad Azeem Farooqi, 3Gul Sher Butt
venue: Policy Journal of Social Science Review
abstract: Digital technologies have revolutionized social, economic and governmental activities in Pakistan. The expansion of the internet, smart phones, online banking, e-commerce sites and digital communication networks have provided positive opportunities for economic development and social interaction. The digital transformation, however, has also yielded new manifestations of criminality, such as those involving cyber fraud, unauthorized use of information systems, ID theft, online harassment, data breach and other crimes that are technology-based. With the rising trend of dependence on digital platforms and low awareness among the public on cybersecurity practices, cybercrime is becoming a major problem for Pakistan. To confront these problems, Pakistan enacted the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), 2016, which is an all-embracing legislation to combat electronic crimes and digital offences. While PECA has laid a solid ground for the regulation of cybercrime, there are also some issues that need to be addressed in relation to enforcement mechanisms, institutional capacity, privacy protection, and balancing cybercrime security measures with basic human rights. The study analyzes the existing legislation related to cybercrime and data protection in Pakistan, highlighting the effectiveness of the laws, implementation challenges, and the need for more robust protection of digital rights. The study calls for a comprehensive data protection regime in the country, enhancement of institutional capacities and a rights-based approach to cybersecurity regulation. Good cyber governance should not only safeguard against digital risks faced by individuals and institutions, but also respect privacy, freedom of expression and due process in compliance with constitutional and international human rights principles. Keywords: Cybercrime, Data Protection, Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016, Digital Rights, Privacy, Cybersecurity, Pakistan, Information Technology Law.

title: Problematic Online Gaming, Cyberbullying Perpetration and Aggression Among Pakistani University Students
authors: Muhammad  Sajjad Shahid; Memona Naz; Rizwana Samreen
venue: Pakistan Journal of Psychological Research
abstract: Problematic online gaming has become an increasing concern among students in recent years.The present study sought to investigate whether cyberbullying perpetration mediates the relationship between problematic online gaming and aggression.Using a cross-sectional correlational design, data were collected through purposive sampling technique from 310 university students aged 18 to 35 years (M = 23.10,SD = 2.89).The study utilized three questionnaires, namely Gaming Addiction Scale for Adolescents (Lemmens et al., 2009), Buss Perry Aggression Questionnaire (Buss & Perry, 1992), and the Cyberbullying Perpetration Subscale of the Cyberbullying Perpetration and Victimization Questionnaire (Lee et al., 2017).Correlational findings revealed that problematic online gaming was positively correlated with cyberbullying perpetration and aggression.Additionally, cyberbullying perpetration was positively correlated with aggression.Further analysis demonstrated that cyberbullying perpetration significantly mediated the relationship between problematic online gaming and aggression.These findings highlight the indirect pathway from problematic online gaming to aggression through cyberbullying perpetration, while the direct effect remained nonsignificant.

title: Navigating the Legal Landscape of Deepfake Technology in Indian Political Dimension
venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning and Data Science
abstract: This paper, Navigating the Legal Landscape of Deepfake Technology in the Indian Political Dimension, discusses how deepfake technology, powered by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), is transforming political communication and creating new challenges to democratic stability in India.Deepfakes distort public perception and spread misinformation, especially during elections, because of their ability to produce hyper-realistic manipulated content.Key incidents, like the use of deepfakes in the 2020 Delhi election, demonstrate the potential for such technology to shape the perception of voters and erode public trust.The proliferation of deepfakes in a pluralistic digital environment with heterogeneity of literacy poses risks of dimensions of significant proportions in India, particularly within regional languages on social media platforms.Presently, the legal framework in India would comprise the Information Technology Act, IT Rules 2021, and Election Commission of India initiatives.The existing paper covers some of the issues with deepfakes, but it lacks full attention to the new threat.Research in this direction proposes legislation that would make malicious use of deepfakes criminal, along with the adoption of preventive measures such as AI-based detection systems, content watermarking, public awareness campaigns, and international cooperation.That, in turn, requires strategies that will save the democratic fabric from pernicious synthetic media effluvia.

title: The Rise of Deepfake Technology and Its Legal Challenges in India
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Deepfake technology, powered by artificial intelligence and machine learning, has emerged as a significant challenge in the digital era. By creating highly realistic but manipulated videos, images, and audio recordings, deepfakes pose serious threats to privacy, dignity, reputation, and democratic processes. This article examines the rise of deepfake technology in India and analyses the legal and ethical concerns arising from its misuse. It evaluates the existing legal framework under the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and other relevant laws, highlighting their limitations in addressing AI-generated manipulation. The article concludes that India requires a comprehensive and balanced regulatory framework that protects individual rights, ensures platform accountability, and promotes the responsible use of emerging technologies.

title: NAVIGATING DEEPFAKES IN TORT LAW
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Deepfake technology, which uses artificial intelligence to synthesize or manipulate audio and visual content, has emerged as a profound legal challenge in the contemporary digital landscape. This paper examines the intersection of deepfakes and Indian tort law, exploring how existing legal frameworks respond to the harms caused by deepfakes. The paper traces the evolution of deepfake technology from early computer-generated imagery to modern Generative Adversarial Networks, and looks the statutory landscape, including the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 and the Copyright Act, 1957. It finds that while these statutes offer partial remedies, they don't directly or comprehensively address harms caused by deepfakes. The paper then analyses how established torts in India such as defamation, intimidation, malicious falsehood, deceit, and passing off can be applied to deepfake-related injuries, drawing on Indian case law such as Anil Kapoor v. Simply Life India, Amitabh Bachchan v. Rajat Negi, Ankur Warikoo v. John Doe etc. It further looks as consumer protection concerns relating to deepfakes under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The paper concludes that India's existing tort law is inadequate to address the novel threats posed by deepfakes and calls for judicial recognition of a distinct deepfake tort, targeted statutory amendments to the Consumer Protection Act and the establishment of a specialized adjudicatory body equipped with both legal and technical expertise.

title: Are India's Existing Law adequate to Regulate Harmful Deepfakes
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper examines the adequacy of India's existing legal framework in addressing harmful deepfakes. It analyses provisions under the Information Technology Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and constitutional privacy protections that may be applied to deepfake-related offences. The paper argues that while existing laws can address several forms of harmful deepfakes, they were not specifically designed for AI-generated content. It emphasises the need for clearer regulation, platform responsibility and digital awareness.

title: Jurisdictional Dilemmas of Digital Arrest in Cross Border Cybercrime in India
authors: Aayush  Verma; Shrikant Ambdkar; Bhavya Mittal
venue: International Journal of Legal Science and Innovation
abstract: “Digital arrest” is a form of cyber-enabled fraud in which offenders impersonate police officers, investigators, regulators, customs officials, or judicial authorities and create the false appearance that a victim is under criminal investigation or custody. Victims may be kept on video or telephone calls for hours and pressured to transfer money to accounts controlled directly or indirectly by the offenders. The distinctive legal difficulty is geographical. The caller may be in another State or another country; the victim may be in Lucknow or another Indian city; the first recipient account may be located in a different State; later transactions may cross several jurisdictions; and the digital infrastructure used for communication may be situated abroad. This article examines whether Indian criminal law can determine the appropriate forum for such a distributed offence. It argues that Indian law possesses substantial domestic jurisdictional capacity: the place where electronic communication is received, the place where the consequence occurs, and the place where property is delivered can connect the offence to an Indian court. The principal domestic difficulty is the multiplicity of potentially competent forums. The cross-border problem is different: Indian law may prescribe jurisdiction over foreign conduct, yet foreign evidence, platforms, and accused persons remain beyond direct coercive reach. The article proposes a “Digital Arrest Jurisdiction Nexus” based on five factors (act, communication, victim, consequence, and evidence) and a six-stage procedure for investigators and courts.

title: Legal Liability for "Deepfake" Media under Digital India Act
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The fast-growing use of deepfake in India has become a pressing issue of concern to the digital governance, privacy rights, and democratic integrity. This paper explores the changing legal environment surrounding the issue of deepfake media covered in the proposed Digital India Act and Information Technology laws. Based on the recent legal rulings, legislative developments, and international precedent, this in-depth discussion of the multi-layered liability regime involving creators, distributors, and digital intermediaries explores various facets of digital travel liability. The paper assesses the overlap of constitutional rights, the provisions of criminal law, the principles of data protection, and the accountability mechanisms of platforms and considers the technological and jurisdictional issues in the regulation of AI-produced synthetic media.

title: The Role of Android Applications in Cybercrime in India
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Role of Android Applications in Cybercrime in India Ashok Kumar* Android applications have emerged as the principal vector for cybercrime in India, driven by the country’s near-universal Android adoption, an open sideloading ecosystem, and the rapid expansion of digital financial services among users with limited digital literacy. This article examines the principal modalities through which Android applications are weaponised for criminal purposes: predatory lending applications that harvest contact lists and photo galleries to enable extortion and blackmail; banking trojans and impersonation malware that abuse Accessibility Services to intercept credentials; fraudulent investment and trading platforms; UPI-linked remote-access fraud; covert spyware; and, increasingly, generative-AI-enabled impersonation schemes such as "digital arrest" fraud. Drawing on official data from the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, the Ministry of Home Affairs, and the Reserve Bank of India, the article documents the scale of this problem, noting the more than fourfold rise in reported complaints between 2021 and 2024 and annual financial losses now exceeding ₹22,000 crore. It then situates this conduct within India’s existing legal architecture, analysing the relevant provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Sections 43, 66, 66C, 66D, 43A, and 69A), the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the Reserve Bank of India’s Digital Lending Directions, alongside platform-level measures adopted by Google. Using the Enforcement Directorate’s multi-year investigation into Chinese-linked loan applications — including the Cashbean/PC Financial Services case and the raids on Razorpay, Cashfree, and Paytm — as an extended case study, the article argues that effective enforcement against app-based financial crime depends as much on money-laundering and foreign-exchange law as on information-technology legislation, since fraudulent applications can be rebranded and relaunched faster than blocking orders can be secured. The article concludes by identifying persistent structural constraints — sideloaded distribution, cross-border operation, resource limitations, and the accelerating pace of AI-enabled fraud — that continue to limit the reach of India’s regulatory and enforcement response. *Assistant Professor, Atal Bihari Vajpayee School of Legal Studies, C.S.J.M. University, Kanpur

title: CrimeScanAI - Cybercrime Reporting Assistant
venue: International Conference on Intelligent and Innovative Technologies in Computing, Electrical and Electronics (IITCEE)
abstract: With the rapid increase in cybercrime cases such as UPI frauds, sextortion, OTP scams, and fake social media accounts, many victims remain hesitant to report incidents due to privacy concerns, low digital literacy, language barriers, and fear of retaliation. Traditional cybercrime reporting portals are often form-heavy, text-based, and available in limited languages, which further discourages reporting. CrimeScanAI is a user-centric, AI-powered cybercrime reporting assistant designed to simplify this process. The system accepts complaints via text, voice, or image input, supports multiple Indian languages, and uses Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) to extract key details like scam type, date, amount, and contact information. CrimeScanAI automatically generates a structured FIR draft and provides a dashboard for law enforcement to review, categorize, and respond to complaints efficiently. By combining accessibility, multilingual support, and AI-driven automation, CrimeScanAI aims to empower citizens, improve reporting rates, and assist authorities in faster and more accurate cybercrime investigations.

title: Deepfakes and Global Legal Regimes
authors: Divyansh Shukla; Mansi Gupta; Meghna Bajpai; Pulatsya Shukla; Diksha Shukla
venue: Routledge eBooks
abstract: The emergence of deepfake technology has presented unprecedented challenges to global legal frameworks. This document explores the multifaceted implications of deepfakes across jurisdictions, examining their misuse in domains such as privacy violations, misinformation, and intellectual property theft. It evaluates regulatory responses from regions, including the European Union, United States, Singapore, China, and India, highlighting legislative measures, such as the GDPR, Digital Services Act, AI Act, NO FAKES Act, and Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act. These laws aim to address the risks posed by deepfakes while maintaining a balance with innovation and free speech. The discussion underscores gaps in existing legal frameworks, emphasizing the need for targeted laws, mandatory disclosure, and international cooperation to mitigate the adverse effects of deepfake technology. By providing a comparative analysis, the document offers insights into best practices and suggests proactive measures like AI-driven detection tools, digital watermarking, and public awareness initiatives to combat the misuse of this evolving technology.

title: Legal and Ethical Dimensions of Digital Arrests Scam: Insights from Indian And Other Countries
venue: Indian Journal of Law.
abstract: Digital arrest scams are an increasingly sophisticated form of cybercrime, leveraging fear, urgency, and advanced technology to deceive victims. These schemes often involve criminals posing as law enforcement or government officials, using tactics such as fake communications, phishing attacks, and forged documents to manipulate individuals into providing money or confidential information. This study examines the growing prevalence of these scams, focusing on their legal, ethical, and societal dimensions, with a particular emphasis on India alongside global comparisons. Real-life cases, including the ₹5.66 crore Hyderabad scam, are analysed to uncover recurring patterns and weaknesses in the existing legal frameworks. The research evaluates laws such as the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) to identify gaps in enforcement and propose reforms. Additionally, the study explores how scammers exploit psychological vulnerabilities, such as victims’ unfamiliarity with digital systems and legal processes. By adopting a comprehensive approach, this research aims to provide practical solutions, including stronger legal frameworks, improved public awareness, and advanced technological safeguards to mitigate the escalating threat of digital arrest scams.

title: Digital Arrest Scams and Existing Legal Remedies
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In 2024, a prominent industrialist reportedly lost ₹7 crore after cybercriminals posing as CBI officers convinced him that he was under investigation for money laundering. For nearly two days, he remained under constant video surveillance, believing he was in the custody of law enforcement officials. In reality, he was the victim of a "digital arrest" scam. Similar incidents have affected retired professionals, senior citizens, and even highly educated individuals across India. The scam succeeds not because victims are careless, but because fraudsters exploit fear, authority, and unfamiliarity with legal procedures.

title: Legal, Ethical, and Governance Perspectives on Deepfakes
venue: CRC Press eBooks
abstract: This chapter provides a critical overview of the evolving legal, ethical, and regulatory frameworks of deepfake technology and how these technologies have created a new “quasi-legal” environment. It focuses on three different jurisdictions (the United States, the European Union, and India) to compare the respective approaches taken by each. The European Union has taken the most definitive stance on deepfake regulation by establishing a specific requirement for every deepfake video to contain an explicit indication that the video is a deepfake under Article 50 of the EU Artificial Intelligence Regulation (2024/1689). Conversely, the US has taken a piecemeal approach to regulating deepfake technology, only criminalizing the use of nonconsensual visual representation of intimate activity through the enactment of the 2025 TAKE IT DOWN Act, with no other types of harm addressed under federal law, but rather relying predominantely on state law to regulate. In India, deepfakes are regulated under three different statutes, namely, the Information Technology Act 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, and the recent amendments to the Information Technology Rules. It discusses topics related to the detection of deepfakes, policies, remedies available to victims of deepfakes, the admissibility of deepfakes in court hearings, cross-border enforcement of deepfake violations, and the ethical considerations surrounding the entire discussion. The conclusion will address the manner in which existing deepfake regulatory gaps can be closed while still preserving and supporting legitimate uses of deepfake technology.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, DEEPFAKES, AND ELECTORALINTEGRITY IN INDIA: LEGAL AND INTELLECTUAL PROPERTYCHALLENGES
venue: PANJAB UNIVERSITY LAW MAGAZINE - MAGLAW
abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed multiple facets of society, including political communication and electoral processes. In India, where digital campaigning increasingly dominates elections, AI-generated content such as deepfakes, manipulated images, and voice cloning poses significant challenges to free and fair elections. These technological innovations can undermine voter trust, distort public opinion, and blur the line between authentic political discourse and fabricated propaganda. Furthermore, AI-driven campaign content frequently intersects with intellectual property rights (IPR), as it may involve unauthorized use of copyrighted material, trademarks, and the likenesses of public figures. This paper examines the legal frameworks governing elections, digital communication, and intellectual property in India, identifying gaps in current regulations. By employing a doctrinal research methodology supplemented with comparative insights from the US, EU, and UK, this study analyzes the implications of AI misuse for electoral integrity. The findings suggest that while existing Indian laws provide partial remedies, specific regulatory measures addressing AI’s role in electoral campaigns are urgently needed. This study adopts a doctrinal research methodology, supported by comparative analysis of regulatory approaches in the United States, European Union, and United Kingdom, to examine the adequacy of India’s existing legal framework on elections, digital communication, and IPR. The analysis finds that current Indian laws offer only partial safeguards, leaving critical gaps in addressing AI-enabled manipulation during electoral campaigns. The research further indicates that India lacks targeted rules for transparency, provenance, accountability, and misuse of AI-generated political content. The paper proposes a multi-pronged reform approach that balances technological innovation with the protection of democratic ideals, ensuring transparency, accountability, and the safeguarding of IPR in electoral contexts.

title: DEEPFAKE AND PERSONALITY RIGHTS IN INDIA: NEED FOR A SEPARATE LEGAL FRAMEWORK
authors: Anju  Bala; Aayush  Verma; Prof. (Dr.) Sudarshan Verma
venue: LawFoyer International Journal of Doctrinal Legal Research.
abstract: DEEPFAKE AND PERSONALITY RIGHTS IN INDIA: NEED FOR A SEPARATE LEGAL FRAMEWORK Anju Bala, BBA LL.B., Student at Department of Law, School of Legal Studies, Babasaheb Bhimrao Ambedkar University (A Central University), Lucknow (India) Aayush Verma, Ph.D. Scholar at Department of Law, School of Legal Studies, Babasaheb Bhimrao Ambedkar University (A Central University), Lucknow (India) The digital revolution and the rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies have fundamentally transformed the landscape of personal identity and its protection under law. Among the most alarming manifestations of this transformation is the emergence of deepfakes hyper-realistic, AI-generated audio-visual simulations that replicate an individual’s voice, likeness, and mannerisms without consent.

title: Cybercrime Awareness, Legal Literacy and Reporting Behavior among Generation-Z in Pakistan: Gendered Patterns and Policy Implications
authors: Muhammad Mohsin Waqas; Husnain Hameed Awan; Makia Nazir; Dr. Muhammad Faisal Khan
venue: Journal of Religion and Society
abstract: The rapid growth of digital technologies has exposed Generation-Z to increased risks of cybercrime, yet their awareness of legal protections and reporting mechanisms remains limited. This study examines knowledge of Pakistan’s cybercrime laws (Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016), reporting behavior and gendered differences in awareness and fear among 350 Generation-Z social media users aged 18–26 years. Findings reveal that only 29.1% of respondents were familiar with PECA 2016 and only 17.4% knew how to file a complaint with the FIA Cybercrime Wing. Female respondents reported higher fear of victimization compared to males, despite slightly higher legal awareness. Awareness of cybercrime laws negatively correlated with fear, indicating that legal knowledge serves as a protective factor. The study underscores the urgent need for targeted digital literacy programs, gender-sensitive awareness campaigns and simplified reporting mechanisms to safeguard Generation-Z in Pakistan. title: Growing Incidence of Cybercrime in India: Causes and Remedies
authors: Abhay Bora; Gayatri N. Nayak; Prem Kulsrestha
venue: Journal of Applied Social Sciences and Humanities
abstract: Over the last ten years, India's digital transformation has dramatically altered its social and economic landscape. At the same time as providing unparalleled opportunity for economic development, it has exposed the Indian population to rapidly emerging and intensifying levels of cybercrime. This study explores the growing prevalence of cybercrime within India using official data from the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Center (I4C). It will examine the multi-faceted dimensions of this issue. The research aims to identify key factors contributing to the dramatic rise in cybercrimes, assess how effective are current institutional frameworks for managing cybercrime, and propose actionable policy options based on empirical data for enhancing prevention of and prosecutions for cybercrimes. Two main hypotheses were tested by this study. Hypothesis 1 states that the growth in cybercrime offenses is directly related to increases in Internet penetration throughout India. Hypothesis 2 states that, despite enactment of the Information Technology Act 2008 and establishment of the I4C mechanism, these have not resulted in reductions in cybercrime offense growth rates. The methodology employed for conducting the analysis was documentary analysis. Registered cybercrime offenses increased at an annualized rate of approximately 35.5% during 2014-24. Offense numbers rose from 9622 in 2014 to 86,420 in 2023. In addition, registered offense numbers rose to 101,928 in 2024, an increase of nearly 18%. Therefore, substantial shortcomings exist regarding mechanisms for recovering lost funds. The low conviction rate of just 2.6 % in 2023 demonstrates that there are serious deficiencies in the criminal justice system which prevent effective prosecution of cybercrime offenders. Both of the above stated hypotheses have been supported by the results of this study. The study concluded with specific and actionable recommendations for enhancing India’s cybersecurity infrastructure and for improvement of prosecution outcomes for cybercrimes.

title: Legal Protection against Non-Consensual Deepfake Content in India
venue: Iconic Research and Engineering Journals
abstract: This dissertation focuses on the newly emerged phenomenon of deepfakes and its intricate legal aspects, analyzing it mostly through the Indian legal system and a comparative perspective of how the legal systems of different countries operate. Deepfakes are generated with the help of the latest artificial intelligence methods, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and allow producing highly realistic and fake audio-visual content, which is associated with grave concerns regarding privacy, reputational concerns, misinformation, and democratic integrity. The paper starts by discussing the conceptual and technological background of deepfakes, their development and the different types and uses of them in entertainment, politics, and cybercrime. It also harshly evaluates the dangers of deepfakes, such as identity theft, defamation, non-consensual explicit content, and mass-disinformation campaigns. The study also assesses the moral issues and social implications of the abuse of such technology. The dissertation dedicates a considerable portion to the analysis of the sufficiency of the current Indian legislation such as the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, to deal with harms caused by deepfakes. It further takes into account intermediary liability in the context of the Information Technology Rules, 2021, and examines the judicial cases that influence the discussion of the privacy and free speech in the digital era. The paper singles out regulatory issues including lack of specific legislation on deepfakes, technological constraints in the detection process, jurisdictional issues, and the conflict between freedom of speech and regulation. In order to give a broader picture, a comparative review of the legal systems in other countries like the United States, European Union and the United Kingdom is also conducted with a focus on best practice and trends in regulation. The dissertation ends by suggesting legal and policy recommendations such as the necessity of specialized legal framework, greater platform responsibility, enhancing technological detection systems, and global collaboration. It stresses the need to adopt a balanced strategy that does not only protect basic rights but also effectively deals with the menace of deepfake technology in an ever-digitalized society.

title: Understanding Cybercrime Evolving Legal and Regulatory Framework for Combating Financial Fraud in India
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In the fast-changing digital era, cyber-enabled money laundering has become a pressing threat to national security and financial integrity. Since the development of the internet and technology, cybercrimes keep increasing. With new technological developments happening, everyday there is something new to add to the crime list. New laws were required to deal with this widespread problem. The purpose of this article is to examine cybercrime in India and the legal frameworks governing it to keep such crimes under control. With the rapid development of computer technology and internet over the years, the problem of cyber crime has assumed gigantic proportions and emerged as a global issue. It has created an entirely new set of problems for law enforcement agencies all over the world. It has equally become cause of serious concern for the legal fraternity to find effective ways and means to combat cyber criminality because of its worldwide devastating effect. Cyber security provides protection to the internet connected networks and system from the cyber-attacks. To stop attacks everyone must know and aware of all cyber law, regulations and compliance to secure the cyber. Cyber security is all about to stop cyber-crime. Cyber security is must and we have to know about all safety measures required to stop cyber-crime. Securing online information is priority where everyone is involved with technology. Whenever anyone talked about cyber security, straight one thing comes in mind that is cyber-crime and what safety measures need to take to be safe from it. title: REGULATING DEEPFAKES IN INDIA: EVALUTING THE ADEQUACY OF EXISTING LEGAL FRAMEWORKS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed digital communications by making possible the creation of incredibly realistic synthetic media known as deepfakes. This is done through the application of machine learning techniques, specifically deep learning techniques, which are used to manipulate or produce audio, video, and images that look real. Despite the fact that there are many legitimate applications of this technology in the fields of entertainment, education, accessibility, and content creation, misuse of deepfakes has raised serious ethical and legal concerns. Deepfakes have increasingly been used for identity theft, fraud, disinformation, deception, blackmailing, and character assassination. This paper analyses the concept of deepfake technology and examines the legal problems surrounding the creation and dissemination of deepfakes. The paper reviews the relevancy of laws existing in India concerning the problem, such as the IT Act of 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita of 2023, the Copyright Act of 1957, and the DPDP of 2023. Moreover, this paper juxtaposes the regulatory practices adopted in India against developments made in areas like the European Union, USA, and China. This paper argues that although the existing laws have little to offer in terms of resolving the problems caused by deepfakes, India is lacking an elaborate law on how to regulate artificial intelligence and synthetic media.

title: Cybercrime Governance in the Digital Age: Contemporary Challenges, Legal Responses and the Need for Reform in India
authors: Lohit Kumar Bimal; Mani Kumar Meena
venue: Journal of Advances and Scholarly Researches in Allied Education
abstract: Cybercrime governance has become an essential component of contemporary public administration, national security, economic regulation and protection of fundamental rights. The digitisation of banking, commerce, government services, communication and critical infrastructure has transformed cybercrime from an isolated law-enforcement concern into a systemic governance issue. Contemporary threats include ransomware, financial cyber fraud, identity theft, digital-arrest scams, phishing, cyberstalking, data breaches, deepfakes, AI-enabled impersonation, malicious synthetic media and attacks upon critical information infrastructure. These offences operate across institutional and territorial boundaries, requiring coordination between government departments, police organisations, banks, telecommunications companies, technology intermediaries, cybersecurity agencies and international partners. India has created a multi-layered cyber-governance architecture centred around the Information Technology Act, 2000, CERT-In, the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, State cybercrime units, intermediary regulations and sector-specific regulators. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 have broadened the legal environment surrounding digital offences and electronic evidence. The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 and Information Technology Amendment Rules, 2026 dealing with synthetically generated information further reflect a transition towards regulation of data security and AI-enabled harms. Despite these developments, India's cyber-governance framework remains institutionally fragmented and continuously challenged by transnational crime, jurisdictional conflicts, rapid technological change, limited investigative capacity, delayed electronic-evidence acquisition and tensions between cybersecurity, privacy and freedom of expression. This article analyses the historical development and contemporary structure of cybercrime governance in India, evaluates regulatory and enforcement challenges and examines international models including the Budapest Convention, United Nations Convention against Cybercrime, NIS2 Directive and NIST Cybersecurity Framework. It argues for an integrated, rights-based and technologically neutral governance model combining prevention, resilience, criminal enforcement, corporate accountability, rapid financial intervention, victim protection and international cooperation.

title: Digital Arrest Fraud in India: Examining the Legal and Investigative Challenges in Combating Emerging Cyber Scams
venue: International Journal of Social Science Research (IJSSR)
abstract: The speedy digitalisation of financial transactions and communication in India has been accompanied by a perceptible escalation in cybercrime, with “digital arrest” scams emerging as one of its near psychologically damaging and financially costly forms. In the scams, perpetrators impersonate law enforcement, judicial, or regulatory officials, often using AI-generated voices, deepfake video calls, and forged digital documents to coerce victims through fear and a false sense of valid urgency into transferring money. This paper examines digital arrest fraud as a different category of cybercrime, situating it within the broader ecosystem of digital payment vulnerability, mule account-based money laundering and organized cybercriminal networks. This study is based on prior research on digital arrest scams, including the psychological tactics used to commit such crimes, such as impersonation of authority, creating a sense of urgency, and instilling fear. It also covers the various technological tools and forensic techniques employed by investigators to track and dismantle such frauds, including those used by Cellebrite (UFED), FTK, EnCase, and others. In addition, the various institutional frameworks created to counter cybercrimes have been covered, including the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (14C) established by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal set up by the National Crime Agency (NCA) of the Ministry of Home Affairs. Several jurisdictional and intermediary liability gaps in the Information Technology Act, 2000 have been identified. These need to be addressed through legal reforms. This paper is written from the socio-legal perspective of technology and law, specifically addressing the technological and regulatory measures for Digital Arrest Scams in India. The paper attempts to strengthen India’s capacity to prevent, investigate and prosecute Digital Arrest Scams and, in the process, safeguard and protect the digital trust of its citizens through a multi-pronged approach of the latest technological safeguards, inter-agency coordination, public awareness programs, and dynamic law reforms to address cyberspace challenges.

title: BREAKING THE FIREWALL: HACKING, INTRUSIONS, AND UNAUTHORIZED ACCESS
venue: Iterative International Publishers eBooks
abstract: In the contemporary digital landscape, hacking, intrusions, and unauthorised access represent some of the most formidable threats to information security, organisational integrity, and national infrastructure. This chapter provides a comprehensive examination of the multifaceted phenomenon of cyber intrusion, tracing its historical evolution from early computer experimentation to the sophisticated advanced persistent threats of the modern era. It critically analyses the legal and ethical frameworks governing unauthorised access across global jurisdictions, including key legislative instruments such as the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and India's Information Technology Act. The chapter systematically categorises attack methodologies, including social engineering, malware deployment, network exploitation, and zero-day vulnerabilities, while also distinguishing the spectrum of threat actors from nation-state groups to hacktivists. Drawing on landmark case studies, it evaluates both the technical and socio-legal dimensions of notable intrusions. Furthermore, the chapter addresses detection, prevention, and incident response strategies, as well as emerging challenges posed by cloud environments, the Internet of Things, and artificial intelligence-enabled attacks. The discussion concludes with an outlook on evolving legal mechanisms and proactive security architectures required to safeguard cyberspace.
