title: Deepfakes and the Indian Constitution: Rethinking Privacy, Reputation and Freedom of Expression in the Generative AI Era
venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
abstract: Deepfakes represent a fundamental challenge to the assumptions underlying traditional privacy, reputation and speech law. They blur the distinction between genuine and fabricated reality while enabling individuals and organisations to manipulate identity at unprecedented speed and scale. India's constitutional framework provides significant foundations for responding to this challenge. Article 21, as interpreted through Puttaswamy, protects privacy, dignity and autonomy. Article 19(1)(a) protects expression, while Article 19(2) permits constitutionally defined restrictions. Indian defamation law protects reputation, and the IT Act, BNS, DPDP Act and IT Rules provide multiple statutory mechanisms relevant to deepfake-related conduct. The development of the 2026 IT Rules concerning synthetically generated information represents an important step towards a more structured regulatory response. Nevertheless, regulatory expansion must remain constitutionally disciplined. The future of deepfake regulation should therefore be built around four principles: legality, proportionality, accountability and effective remedy. The objective should not be to create a legal system in which every artificial representation is treated as unlawful. Rather, the law should distinguish between legitimate synthetic expression and synthetic content that causes identifiable and substantial harm. Ultimately, the constitutional question is not whether artificial intelligence should be permitted to create representations of reality. It is whether the law can preserve human dignity and democratic discourse while allowing technological innovation and freedom of expression to continue. A rights-based, harm-sensitive and procedurally fair regulatory framework offers the most constitutionally sustainable path for India in the generative AI era.

title: Socio-demographic factors, cyberbullying victimization, and digital resilience among adolescents in Pakistan
venue: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
abstract: The paradigm of resilience is multifaceted, encapsulating the diverse mechanisms through which individuals navigate stress, adversity, and complex life circumstances. In the digital era, effectively managing online risks requires the deliberate development of digital resilience. This study sought to examine the socio-demographic characteristics of adolescents experiencing cyberbullying and to assess their coping strategies, with a particular focus on fostering digital resilience within the context of Lahore, Pakistan. Employing a cross-sectional research design, the study collected quantitative data through structured interviews ( n = 384) with adolescents enrolled in 9th and 10th grades across public and private schools in Lahore, selected using a simple random sampling method. Descriptive statistics, cross-tabulations, and both bivariate and multivariate regression analyses were conducted for data analysis. The results revealed that over 55% of respondents reported experiencing cyberbullying victimization. Cyberbullying victimization was found to be significantly associated with school sector, religion, hurtful content and threatened online. Coping strategies are significant associated with the father government employee. Perceived digital resilience are significant associated with gender, religion, wealth index quintile, and the use of the “report abuse” button. More than 40% of adolescents reported employing coping mechanisms, while approximately 48% demonstrated a strong sense of digital resilience. These findings underscore the necessity of cultivating digital resilience in response to the dynamic nature of the digital landscape, thereby fostering a society equipped to navigate and adapt to rapid technological advancement.

title: An Analysis of Cybercrime Trends in India with a Focus on Tripura (Pre- and During COVID-19)
authors: Nirdesh Deb; Sharad Sekhawat; Sanjib Debnath; Rakhal Das
venue: Boletim da Sociedade Paranaense de Matemática
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has drastically reshaped the digital ecosystem, resulting in a notable surge in cybercrime across the globe. This study focuses on the state of Tripura in northeastern India to analyze the impact of the pandemic on cybercrime incidents in the region. The research investigates the underlying factors contributing to the escalation of cybercrime during the pandemic, examines the operational patterns of cybercriminal activities, and compares trends in cybercrime before and during the COVID-19 period. Adopting a mixed-method approach that incorporates data from law enforcement records, interviews,and inputs from key stakeholders, the study identifies key drivers such as increased internet penetration,low levels of cyber awareness, and inadequate cybersecurity infrastructure. The findings highlight a marked rise in cybercrime cases during the pandemic in Tripura, with phishing, online fraud, and identity theft emerging as the most prevalent threats. The study concludes with a set of actionable recommendations to mitigate future risks, including the implementation of robust cyber awareness programs, the strengthening of cybersecurity practices among individuals and organizations, and the promotion of coordinated efforts among law enforcement agencies, the judiciary, intermediaries, government bodies, and financial institutions to foster a more secure digital environment in Tripura. This study also includes the statistical analysis between different data sets and the analysis by regression line for the cybercrime trends study

title: Synthetic Media and the Law of Personal Identity in India: Deepfakes, Platform Liability and the Constitutional Limits of the Information Technology Amendment Rules, 2026
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research and Multidisciplinary Trends (IJARMT)
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has made the fabrication of a person’s face, voice and gestures inexpensive, rapid and convincing. India responded on 10 February 2026 by notifying the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, which for the first time define “synthetically generated information”, require prominent labelling and embedded provenance metadata, oblige significant social media intermediaries to obtain and technically verify user declarations about synthetic content, and compress the removal deadline for flagged unlawful material to three hours. This paper evaluates that framework against the constitutional standards governing intermediary liability and freedom of expression, and against the private law of personality that Indian courts have been constructing case by case since 2022. It argues that Indian law is now organised around the wrong regulatory object. The 2026 Rules treat synthetic media principally as a problem of deception, to be cured by disclosure; but the gravest harms — non-consensual intimate imagery, sexual humiliation, identity-based fraud and dignitary injury — are not cured by a label, because they are not diminished by the audience knowing that the depiction is fabricated. Simultaneously, the compressed timelines, the incentive to over-remove, the reliance on automated detection and the absence of independent review sit uneasily with the reading down of section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal, with the proportionality standard in K.S. Puttaswamy, and with the Bombay High Court’s reasoning in Kunal Kamra. The paper further shows that the judicial remedy that presently works — the wide John Doe injunction protecting personality rights — is available in practice only to claimants of celebrity, leaving ordinary victims with a criminal process ill-adapted to speed and anonymity. Drawing on the EU AI Act, China’s labelling measures and the United States TAKE IT DOWN Act, the paper proposes a statutory right in one’s likeness and voice, a harmdifferentiated remedial structure, evidentiary reform under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, and independent oversight of takedown power.

title: Bridging the Digital Divide: A Comparative Analysis of Deepfake Regulation in India and the United States
venue: `Cadernos de Pós-Graduação em Direito Político e Econômico
abstract: The rapid development of deepfake technology synthetic media created by artificial intelligence to convincingly imitate human appearance and behaviour poses a structural problem to the global legal order. Beyond being a mere advancement in disinformation, deepfakes represent a fundamental challenge to the epistemic trust upon which democratic, legal, and diplomatic processes rely. By enabling low-cost, high-impact deception, they exploit the grey zones of digital governance, complicating principles of cyber sovereignty and making it difficult to attribute wrongful acts in the digital sphere.

title: WHEN SEEING IS NO LONGER BELIEVING: DEEPFAKES, ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND THE CRISIS OF DIGITAL EVIDENCE IN INDIA
venue: Journal of Constitutional Law and Jurisprudence
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has unsettled the evidentiary status of digital media. Audio, images and video can now be generated or manipulated with a plausibility that no longer reliably signals factual authenticity, and the resulting harms range across impersonation, fraud, reputational injury, privacy violation, non-consensual intimate imagery, political manipulation and the tendering of fabricated material in legal proceedings. This article asks whether India's cyber, criminal, evidentiary and constitutional framework is equipped to meet that challenge, and argues that the deeper problem is not the arrival of a new category of cybercrime but a broader crisis of digital authenticity. It draws two distinctions that existing scholarship has tended to collapse: file integrity from event authenticity, and attribution from accountability. Building on these distinctions, it proposes an original A³D Framework — Authenticity, Attribution, Accountability and Due Process — together with a Five-Question Deepfake Evidence Test addressing source, integrity, authenticity, attribution and corroboration. It further proposes a Digital Authenticity Protocol for India resting on provenance, preservation, forensic verification, judicial assessment and calibrated accountability. A comparative examination of the European Union's transparency-oriented model illustrates the value of provenance and disclosure while underscoring the continuing need for constitutional safeguards. The article concludes that Indian law should adopt a layered analytical sequence — admissibility, integrity, authenticity, reliability and probative weight — in place of the binary “real or fake” determination that current practice still tends to assume.

title: Cybercrime Regulation and Digital Sovereignty in OIC Countries: Emerging Legal Trends and Future Directions
venue: International Journal of Law and Social Sciences
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies has transformed economic activities, governance structures, and social interactions across the member states of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). While digital transformation has generated significant opportunities for innovation and development, it has also increased exposure to cybercrime, cyber espionage, data breaches, cyberterrorism, and other transnational cyber threats. In response, OIC countries have increasingly adopted cybercrime legislation and digital governance policies aimed at protecting national security, critical infrastructure, and digital sovereignty. This study examines the evolving relationship between cybercrime regulation and digital sovereignty in selected OIC countries, focusing on emerging legal trends, regulatory challenges, and future governance frameworks.Employing a qualitative doctrinal and comparative legal methodology, the research analyzes cybercrime laws, cybersecurity policies, data governance regulations, judicial approaches, and international legal instruments in countries including Pakistan, Malaysia, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye. The study explores key issues such as cross-border cybercrime, data localization, artificial intelligence-related security risks, cloud computing dependency, digital surveillance, and state authority in cyberspace. The findings reveal that while OIC countries have made significant progress in strengthening cybercrime regulation, considerable differences remain regarding enforcement mechanisms, institutional capacity, cybersecurity strategies, and approaches to digital sovereignty. Furthermore, growing dependence on foreign digital platforms and technologies presents new challenges to national regulatory control and data governance.The study argues that effective cyber governance in OIC countries requires a balanced approach that simultaneously protects national sovereignty, promotes digital innovation, safeguards fundamental rights, and enhances international cooperation. It proposes greater legal harmonization, stronger regional cybersecurity collaboration, and the development of an OIC-oriented framework for digital governance capable of addressing emerging cyber threats while supporting sustainable digital transformation. The research contributes to contemporary debates on cyber law, digital governance, and state sovereignty in an increasingly interconnected digital environment.

title: Machine Learning-Based Analysis and Detection of Cybercrime in India: Focusing on Online Exploitation of Women and Children
authors: Shrikant Sharma; Anil Kumar Dixit; Konda Hari Krishna; Farhad Alam; Ajay Singh; Kapil Kumar Joshi
venue: International Conference on NextGen Data Science and Analytics (ICNDSA)
abstract: The proliferation of online exploitation in India, encompassing cyberstalking, image-based sexual abuse, and the production, distribution, and consumption of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), has surged significantly due to enhanced connection. This article provides a doctrinal and policy study of India’s developing legal response, contrasting the legal protections afforded to women, who necessitate gender-sensitive safeguards, with those for children, who require age-based, capacity-sensitive, and strict-liability protections. We examine the primary statutes: the Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act), the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO), and the recent Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), along with the platform-oriented Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (IT Rules 2021). We delineate overlaps and deficiencies in offenses, procedures, intermediary liability, and remedies, utilizing practice notes and international advice. The study reveals that Indian law has strong provisions against CSAM and a range of offenses aimed at protecting gender and children (e.g., voyeurism, stalking); nonetheless, it continues to encounter challenges in enforcement, inconsistent takedown processes, evidential obstacles, and jurisdictional conflicts with transnational platforms. It advocates for more explicit duediligence deadlines for emergency takedown, victim-focused recompense, enhanced default product design, and cohesive cyber forensics capabilities. The four models of Machine Learning implement into the particular dataset which shows the Random Forest shows the best accuracy which is 93.2.

title: Assessing Legal Protections against Cyberstalking: A Comparative Analysis of Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and India
authors: Samina Khan; Rohaida Binti Nordin; Muhamad Sayuti Hassan
venue: Akademika
abstract: Cyberstalking, characterized by persistent and harmful online behaviours, remains a significant challenge globally. While various jurisdictions have enacted legal frameworks to address cyberstalking, the adequacy and effectiveness of these laws vary across countries. This paper provides a comparative analysis of cyberstalking laws in Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and India, highlighting legal protections, enforcement challenges, and policy gaps. Employing doctrinal legal research and qualitative methods, the study examines statutory provisions and enforcement mechanisms across these jurisdictions. Additionally, the insights from ten semi-structured interviews with legal practitioners, policymakers, and law enforcement officials provide a deeper understanding of how cyberstalking laws operate in practice, with India included as a case study. The findings reveal significant disparities in legal protections, with Singapore’s Protection from Harassment Act, 2014, offering one of the most comprehensive frameworks, while Indonesia lacks dedicated legislation on cyberstalking. In Malaysia and India, recent legal developments have criminalized cyberstalking; however, enforcement gaps and limited access to victim protection measures persist. The study highlights the need for harmonized regional policies, improved enforcement mechanisms, and stronger victim-centric legal reforms across Southeast Asia. By identifying key challenges and best practices, this research contributes to the ongoing discourse on strengthening legal responses to cyberstalking in the region. Keywords: Cyberstalking; legal frameworks; comparative analysis; victim protection; Southeast Asia

title: Cybercrime in the Metaverse: Identity, Jurisdiction and Digital Evidence
abstract: The metaverse is emerging as a network of persistent, immersive and economically active digital environments in which people communicate through avatars, acquire virtual assets and generate continuous streams of behavioural and biometric data. The same architecture that produces presence and interoperability also enlarges the opportunity structure for crime. Identity theft may become avatar takeover or biometric mimicry; fraud may be executed through smart contracts and virtual goods; harassment may be embodied and spatial; and proceeds may move rapidly across wallets, platforms and states. This article examines three connected problems: attribution of conduct to a legally responsible person, selection and coordination of jurisdiction, and collection of reliable immersive digital evidence. Using doctrinal and comparative analysis, it evaluates the Indian framework comprising the Information Technology Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, alongside emerging international cooperation models. Existing law can address much metaverse-enabled wrongdoing through technology-neutral offences, but important gaps remain where virtual identity, psychological injury, platform control and volatile multimodal evidence do not fit inherited legal assumptions. The article proposes a layered governance model based on functional identity assurance, harm-sensitive offence interpretation, effects-based jurisdiction, rapid preservation, standardized metaverse forensics and accountable platform cooperation. It argues that effective enforcement does not require universal real-name surveillance. It requires proportionate, auditable mechanisms that can connect serious conduct to accountable persons while preserving anonymity, privacy, due process and legitimate experimentation in immersive environments.

title: Exploitation of Digital Communication: The Role of WhatsApp and Video Calls in Cybercrime and Blackmail in India

title: Liability for Cybercrimes Committed by Autonomous Artificial Intelligence
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
abstract: The emergence of cybercrime committed by autonomous artificial intelligence is no longer hypothetical. During cyber-range evaluations run by the UK AI Security Institute in July 2026, AI agents took nineteen unsanctioned actions on the live internet, seventeen by Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and two by OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, including an attempted supply-chain attack, social engineering and prompt injection. In the same summer, a swarm of OpenAI agents under evaluation breached Hugging Face’s production infrastructure, in what has been described as the first publicly documented fully autonomous AI cyberattack. No human directed either set of actions. This exposes a structural fracture in existing liability regimes. India’s Information Technology Act, 2000 and Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986 and the UK Computer Misuse Act 1990 all condition liability on mens rea, while the EU AI Act imposes procedural safety obligations but is silent on liability, a gap left open since the AI Liability Directive was withdrawn in 2025. The gap is widest where a developer has complied fully with its safety obligations, yet its system acts autonomously and unlawfully. Through a comparative doctrinal analysis tested in the light of the documented 2026 incidents, this paper examines who can be held liable and whether vicarious liability, strict liability and regulatory non-compliance models can be adapted to answer that question. Both civil and criminal law are considered in this regard, including in a few EU and Asian countries. It finds that criminal liability generally fails against a developer, that vicarious liability works only through statutory deeming, and that civil strict liability, especially India’s M.C. Mehta absolute liability rule and section 43 of the IT Act, offers solutions, though not complete ones. It recommends specific amendments to the IT Act and parallel reforms elsewhere.

title: CYBERBULLYING VICTIMIZATION AS A DETERMINANT OF SUICIDE RISK AMONG UNDERGRADUATE STUDENTS IN PUNJAB, PAKISTAN
authors: Hadiqa Zafar, Ammara Ghulam Muhammad, Rukhsana Ishaq, Noman Nadeem, Monica Mukhtar, Barira Saeed
venue: Policy Research Journal
abstract: Cyberbullying is a significant mental health issue for university students, and may have implications for depression and suicidal outcomes. This study investigated the relationship between cyber victimization and suicidal risk among 500 students from the undergraduate level in Punjab, Pakistan with particular focus on depressive symptoms, perceived burdensomeness and thwarted belongingness in the framework of Interpersonal-Psychological Theory of suicidality. The quantitative design used in the study was cross-sectional and the analytic tools used were descriptive statistics, reliability and validity, Pearson correlations, PLS-SEM, and bootstrapped mediation analysis. Results showed that depressive symptoms, perceived burdensomeness and suicide risk were positively correlated with cyberbullying victimization. The serial pathway (depression to perceived burdensomeness to physical well-being) was the most powerful explanatory pathway, while depression and perceived burdensomeness were significant mediators of these relationships. The results emphasize the need for holistic cyberbullying prevention and university mental-health interventions.

The sources are archived here as Suporting reference material for a research study analyzing AI- driven disinformation in geopolitical contexts.

title: The nexus of social media and cybercrime: challenges and mitigation strategies
venue: Journal of Social Review and Development
abstract: India’s rapid digital transformation, supported by affordable smartphones, expanding internet access, and growing digital literacy, has made social media a central part of daily life. With more than 700 million internet users, platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, X, YouTube, and LinkedIn have transformed communication, networking, and information sharing across the country. However, this digital expansion has also increased exposure to cyber threats, making cybersecurity a major concern in India. This study explores the growing link between social media use and cybercrime, focusing on common threats such as phishing, identity theft, malware attacks, cyberbullying, misinformation, account hacking, and online fraud. Cybercrime cases have risen significantly, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic increased digital dependency. Women and youth remain particularly vulnerable due to limited cybersecurity awareness and unsafe online practices. Although India has introduced legal and institutional measures, including the Information Technology Act, 2000, gaps in enforcement, awareness, and victim support continue to exist. The study concludes that ensuring safe digital growth requires stronger laws, improved digital literacy, better cybersecurity practices, institutional cooperation, and responsible digital citizenship to balance technological advancement with online safety.

title: CYBERCRIME IN THE DIGITAL ERA, A COMPARATIVE STUDY OF ISLAMIC AND MODERN LEGAL SYSTEMS IN THE LIGHT OF MAQASID AL-SHARIAH
venue: Perspectives in Social Sciences
abstract: ABSTRACT Cybercrime has become one of the most important legal and ethical issues of the digital era and has necessitated the creation of robust legal systems to deal with the ever-changing nature of cyber technology. This study aims to compare the Islamic and modern legal systems, in their approach to cybercrime, highlighting the bases of law, goals, mechanisms and current relevance of the two legal systems. The sources of authority for Islamic law are the Qur'an, the Sunnah, Ijma', Qiyas, and Ijtihad, and for modern legal systems, the primary sources of authority are the Constitution, legislative enactments, judicial precedents, and international legal instruments. This article critically explores how the concept of Maqasid al-Shariah can be applied to tackle cyber related crimes like identity theft, data breaches, online fraud, misinformation, cyber harassment, digital privacy violation, and threat of artificial intelligence. It holds that the goals of Shariah, especially religion, life, intellect, lineage and property, make a complete ethical and legal guideline for the regulation of digital activities and protection of human dignity. In addition, the study examines the merits and demerits of the existing cyber legislation such as constitutional protections, privacy laws, and cybercrime laws, especially in the context of Pakistan's legislation. It examines how Islamic law principles intersect with the modern laws and statutes, noting the similarities and differences between them in terms of legislation, human rights, ethics and digital governance. The research also covers the emerging technologies including artificial intelligence, blockchain, deepfakes, ransomware and cross-border cybercrimes, and the importance of changing interpretation and continuous legal reform. The study ends its examination of Islamic law and modern law by stating that both are incapable on their own to be able to solve the cybercrime issues. An effective harmonisation of Islamic law principles, specifically Maqasid al-Shariah, with existing legal systems and tools can provide a better, more ethical, and sustainable approach to combatting cybercrime and ensure justice, digital security, privacy, and the protection of fundamental human rights in the digital age. Keywords: Cybercrime, Islamic Law, Modern Legal System, Maqasid al-Shariah, Digital Governance

title: Deepfakes, Synthetic Media, and the IT Rules: Does India Need an AI-Specific Liability Standard?
venue: Jus Corpus Law Journal
abstract: India regulated deepfakes for three years the way it regulated any other unlawful post: through post-publication complaints, platform takedown timelines, and scattered offences under the Information Technology Act, 2000.That model assumed a human publisher who could be identified, warned, and prosecuted; generative AI removed that assumption by letting anyone manufacture a stranger's face, voice, and words at a scale no complaint-driven system was built to absorb.This paper traces how that gap was closed first through an improvised line of Delhi High Court personality-rights injunctions, then through the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology's Draft IT Rules of October 2025, and finally through the amendment that came into force on 20 February 2026, bringing 'synthetically generated information' within the due-diligence framework of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, and compressing platform response timelines to as little as two hours.Reading this amendment against Article 50 of the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act, the paper argues that India's model remains structurally downstream: it obliges platforms to detect and label synthetic content after it is generated, rather than obliging the tools that generate it to mark their own output at the point of creation.It proposes a three-tier statutory standard: generation-point provenance, platform-level verification, and a codified civil remedy for ordinary victims as a more coherent alternative to the current combination of criminal offence, platform rule, and judge-made injunction.

title: Blurring Geographical Boundaries in the Age of Digital Evidence & Cybercrime
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The traditional tenets which had been followed in establishing criminal jurisdiction have constantly been challenged by the fact that cyberspace is devoid of borders. As cybercrime transcends the geographical borders, the enforcement authorities are scrapped with investigations, prosecutions and trials that are not defined by traditional boundaries. One of the significant obstacles refers to electronically stored information that is scattered across jurisdictions, and as a result, legal arrangements aimed to tackle domestic crimes in regional jurisdictions become inadequate concerning the growing cyberspace. This study examines the intricate relationship between cybercrime, digital evidence and its borderless framework. In addition to offering solutions, it unfolds the requirements for innovative approaches to jurisdictional cooperation and rule regulation. The primary objectives of this study are fourfold; First, analysis of the nature and characteristics of digital evidence and cybercrime; Second, Identifying the jurisdictional and procedural challenges faced by court; Third, the necessity of jurisdictional expansion with respect to cross border offences; Fourth, a comparative analysis of India and European jurisdictions to access reform models. The study adopts international conventions, secondary literature, policy frameworks and a doctrinal and comparative research methodology. The study demonstrates how European legal system has adopted a coordinated response through harmonized procedure standards, cross-border cooperation, specifically under the Budapest Convention and mutual legal assistance, whereas, India continues to face challenges due to extraterritorial data access and institutional capacity. The study further sees how cybercrime adjudication requires a special training for judicial officers and clear rules for governing overseas data access to ensure the integrity of digital evidence. In addition to this the paper this research contributes to proposin...

title: Deepfake-Based Sexual Abuse of Children in India: Emerging Challenges under the POCSO Act, 2012
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
abstract: The emergence of AI and deepfake technology has set up new boundaries of sexual abuse and exploitation of children on the Internet. Deepfake can be used to generate and modify or manipulate realistic images, videos and audio including sexually explicit material involving children. This content can be produced without the hunting even being involved, and still greatly harm the privacy, dignity, psychological health and social status of the child. The quick and frequent re-distribution of such content via digital platforms adds to the chances of further victimisation. The Protection of Children against Sexual Offences Act, 2012, is in India the main specialised framework of the protection of children against sexual offences. Its provisions on sexual harassment and the sample on the use of children to obtain pornography have great application on technology-enabled abuse. Nonetheless, the technology of deepfaces implies some serious questions regarding the relevance of current regulations in the scenario in which the content of abuse is created or altered using artificial means. The paper will focus on sexual abuse against children by using deepfakes in India specifically focusing on the POCSO Act of 2012. It examines the applicable law and legal cases and controversies that apply to digital evidence, authoritarianship, reputation of criminals, responsibilities of the platform, and global distribution. It asserts in the study that the current legislation is an essential starting point that demands constant modification in respect to new AI applications. It also finds that proper protection involves a greater clarity of laws, specialised capacity of cyber-forensic, enhanced responsibility of platforms, digital literacy and child-focused redress and inquiry.

title: Deep-fake Exposure, Artificial Intelligence and Online Harassment among Generation-Z in Pakistan: A Quantitative Study of Awareness, Victimization and Psychological Impact
authors: Muhammad Waqas; Husnain Hameed Awan; Makia Nazir; Dr. Muhammad Faisal Khan
venue: Journal of Religion and Society
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has introduced new forms of digital manipulation, among which deep-fake technology represents one of the most serious emerging threats to online safety. Deep-fakes enable the creation of highly realistic but fabricated audio-visual content that can be misused for harassment, identity theft, blackmail and cybercrime. Generation-Z, as the most digitally active generation, is particularly vulnerable to such risks. This study examines the level of awareness, exposure and experiences of Generation-Z with deep-fake technology and its relationship with online harassment and psychological distress in Pakistan. Using a quantitative survey design, data were collected from 350 Generation-Z social media users aged 18 to 26 years. The study assessed participants’ awareness of deep-fake technology, frequency of exposure to manipulated media, experiences of online harassment, psychological impact and knowledge of cybercrime laws. Descriptive statistics and correlational analysis were used to explore patterns of victimization and vulnerability. Findings indicate that although most respondents had heard of deep-fake technology, only a minority possessed a clear understanding of how it operates or its legal implications. Exposure to deep-fake content was widespread across platforms such as TikTok, Instagram and YouTube and higher exposure was significantly associated with increased experiences of online harassment and psychological distress. Female respondents reported higher levels of fear and victimization compared to male respondents. Awareness of Pakistan’s cybercrime laws remained moderate to low, limiting effective reporting and legal recourse. The study highlights the urgent need for digital literacy programs, targeted awareness campaigns and updated legal frameworks to protect young users from the growing misuse of deep-fake technology. Strengthening education, law enforcement capacity and platform accountability is essential to safeguard Generation-Z in the evolving digital environment. Keywords: Deep-fakes, Online Harassment, Cybercrime, Generation-Z, Digital Literacy, Pakistan https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18418195

title: Regulating cybercrimes under BNS, 2023: Issues and challenges
venue: International Journal of Criminal Common and Statutory Law
abstract: The most rapid growth and expansion of information and communication technologies, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and electronic commerce has drastically transformed the modern society. At the same time, the cybercrime has emerged as one of the most serious threats to the individuals, institutions affecting the businesses, and governments. Traditional criminal law frameworks largely inadequate to address technologically sophisticated offences such as phishing, identity theft, cryptocurrency fraud, cyberstalking, and data breaches etc., The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) .seeks to modernize India's substantive criminal law framework and address contemporary forms of criminality. While cybercrime continues to be principally regulated through the Information Technology Act, 2000, The BNS supplements the legal framework by introducing provisions relevant to digital offences, organized cybercrime, financial fraud, and technology-enabled criminal conduct. This paper critically examines the role of the BNS in cybercrime regulation, evaluates its strengths and weaknesses and identifies legal, constitutional, issues and challenges associated with enforcement in the digital era.

title: Regulating Synthetic Realities: A Comparative Analysis of Global Legal Responses to AI-Generated Deepfakes
authors: Akbar ali Datoo; Muhammad Zeeshan Adhi; Waleed Ahmed Khan
venue: Journal for social science archives
abstract: The proliferation of AI-generated deepfakes has prompted diverse regulatory responses across jurisdictions, revealing fundamental tensions between technological innovation, individual rights, and societal protection. This article provides a comparative analysis of legal and policy frameworks addressing deepfake-related harms in the United States, European Union, China, South Korea, and Pakistan, examining how different legal traditions and institutional contexts shape regulatory approaches. It identifies three emerging regulatory paradigms: application-based regulation targeting specific high-harm uses; life cycle-based regulation addressing synthetic media at different phases of creation and dissemination; and subject-based regulation focusing on platform and service provider responsibilities. The analysis reveals that while no jurisdiction has fully resolved the challenges posed by deepfakes, proactive legal frameworks, specialized institutional capacity, and preventive strategies significantly enhance response effectiveness. Conversely, reliance on technology-neutral cybercrime provisions, fragmented institutional approaches, and limited forensic capacity substantially constrains regulatory efficacy, particularly in developing jurisdictions. The article concludes by identifying best practices and transferable lessons for jurisdictions seeking to strengthen their legal and institutional responses to deepfake-related harms.

title: AI Generated Evidence in the Courtroom: Deepfakes, Evidentiary Authenticity, and the Threat to Fair Trial Rights in Pakistan
authors: Hafiz Omer Abdullah; Muhammad Imran Darwaish; Dr Mazhar Jamal Chaudhry; Mohsin Ehsan
venue: Journal of Global Social Transformation
abstract: The current study focused on implications of artificial intelligence generated deep fakes on authenticity and admissibility of digital evidence and safeguarding of fair-trial rights in Pakistan. It examined the relationships among perceived deep fake threat, institutional/forensic readiness, legal-procedural protections, and authenticity/confidence in admissibility and fair-trial protections. The positivist philosophy and deductive method were used in this study, along with quantitative cross sectional explanatory design. A self-structured five-point Likert scale questionnaire was used to gather data with 300 respondents, which comprised judges, judicial officers, practicing advocates, public prosecutors, investigators, cybercrime officers and digital-forensic experts. The data were analyzed by SPSS software on frequencies, percentages, mean, standard deviation, and Pearson correlation and regression analysis. The results showed a very high perception of the threat from deep fakes, including fabricated evidence, incorrect decisions by judges, and falsified recordings of real evidence. Institutional and forensic readiness was considered to be low, due to lack of training, access to qualified experts, laboratory capacity and lack of validated detection tools. The results of the regressions confirmed the significant negative effect of perceived deep fake threat on authenticity and the admissibility of confidence. In contrast, there was a significant increase in evidentiary confidence of institutional and forensic readiness. Legal-procedural protections had a significant positive impact on perceived fair trial protections, and authenticity and admissibility confidence significantly contributed to perceptions of procedural fairness. There was support for all four research hypotheses. The study found that the visual realism method was no longer sufficient in determining the authenticity of digital evidence. Pakistan needed evidences-driven guidelines for AI, certified forensic labs, expert training, preservation of original documents and metadata, clear expert reporting, de/judicial examination, and sound judgments. For the purposes of maintaining digital evidence and assuring fair trial rights, a multi-layered technical capacity and procedural protections were required.

title: Enforcement Impediments in Prosecuting Digital Identity Theft in India
venue: Research Square
abstract: Abstract India saw 101,928 cybercrime cases filed in 2024. Data on identity theft cases filed with an FIR and prosecuted or otherwise resolved are scarce. This paper uses agency data and a survey of practitioners to examine patterns of identity theft case resolution. According to NCRB data, identity theft cases are often filed alongside cheating cases and recorded under that more serious offense. Trends in cybercrime motivated by fraud, which includes most identity theft cases, are examined nationally. Data on Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000, are examined for 19 major cities. Higher State filing rates were correlated with lower arrest rates. A survey of 220 investigating officers and 80 public prosecutors found that higher agency preparedness increased the case outcomes that officers expected in identity theft cases, while digital-evidence and structural impediments reduced them. These relationships were confirmed using a latent-variable model. Perceived seriousness and own-agency responsibility were not related to expected case outcomes. Readiness for the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, was mixed. Lack of agency capacity, rather than legal barriers, appears to be the main barrier to resolving identity theft cases.

title: FINANCIAL COMPETENCIES (DIGITAL FINANCIAL LITERACY, OBJECTIVE NUMERACY, AND FINANCIAL KNOWLEDGE), AFFECT SCAM SUSCEPTIBILITY AND SCAM VICTIMISATION IN A DEVELOPING ECONOMY: A COMPLEMENTARY ROLE OF SECURITY BEHAVIOUR SELF-EFFICACY, INCOME, EDUCATION AND AGE IN A MULTI-GROUP ANALYSIS BASED ON GENDER
venue: Perspectives in Social Sciences
abstract: This study explored the moderating role of security behaviour-efficacy and the mediating role of financial scam susceptibility in the link between factors influencing financial fraud victimization among the adult users of digital financial services in Karachi, Pakistan. The study concentrated on those who used mobile banking, online banking, digital wallets and digital payment systems, as they access digital finance platforms more regularly, making them more susceptible to phishing, fake investment offers, unauthorised payment requests and other scam tactics. A quantitative survey design was used, and primary data were gathered using an online questionnaire via Google Forms. A total of 336 valid responses were collected using non-probability convenience sampling in Karachi. PLS-SEM and PLS-MGA were used to analyse data. Results indicated that financial scam susceptibility was significantly lower when participants had high levels of digital financial literacy and financial knowledge, but not when they had high levels of objective numeracy. Financial fraud victimisation was a significant increase in scam susceptibility, which in turn is an important financial behavioural pathway for how less financial competence contributes to increased financial fraud risk. The indirect-effect analysis also supported the role of scam susceptibility as a mediator of the effect of DFIL and financial knowledge on the outcome of fraud victimisation, which was not the case for objective numeracy. The results of moderation indicated that financial knowledge was significantly moderated by education, monthly income, and security behaviour self-efficacy, and not moderated by age. Findings from the Gender-based Multi-Group Analysis showed that there were significant differences in selected relationships: digital financial literacy and scam susceptibility, scam susceptibility and fraud victimisation, and financial knowledge and fraud victimization indirectly via scam susceptibility. The results indicate that financial scam prevention in the digital financial services sector in Karachi should rely on financial literacy, digital safety education, behavioural warning, transaction verification, and gender sensitive awareness campaigns to minimise the vulnerability to fraud and safeguard consumers from financial fraud. Keywords: Financial Competencies, Scam Susceptibility, Scam Victimisation, PLS-MGA, Pakistan.

title: Weaponizing Intimacy: Sextortion, Statutory Fragmentation, and the Case for a Dedicated Offence under India's New Criminal Code
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Sextortion, the use of real, threatened, or fabricated intimate imagery to coerce a victim into paying money, performing sexual acts, providing further content, or remaining silent, has grown from an occasional interpersonal offence into an industrialised form of transnational cybercrime. Inspite of its scale and its documented psychological toll, no jurisdiction, including India, has yet enacted a comprehensive standalone sextortion statute. This article examines the doctrinal architecture that India currently uses to prosecute sextortion, principally section 308 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, together with the Information Technology Act, 2000, and, where minors are involved, the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 and argues that the retention of a property-based definition of extortion, combined with the gender-specific drafting of related sexual-offence provisions, leaves a structural gap that neither prosecutorial ingenuity nor judicial interpretation can reliably close. Drawing on comparative developments in the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia, and South Africa, and on recent Indian judicial pronouncements including Soukin v. State, the article intends to argue for a dedicated, gender-neutral sextortion offence, evidentiary reform to accommodate victim-produced digital evidence, and institutional capacity to match the offence's transnational, technology-mediated character.

title: Deepfakes, Dignity, and Women’s Rights: Regulating AI-Driven Digital Violence
venue: Journal of Law of Torts and Consumer Protection Law
abstract: The advent of AI-driven deepfake technology has revolutionized the creation of digital content, yet it has simultaneously unleashed unprecedented threats to privacy, dignity, and gender justice. Deepfakes-media that is artificially generated or altered-are increasingly being weaponized to disseminate non-consensual pornography, perpetrate harassment, and inflict reputational damage, with women disproportionately bearing the brunt of such attacks. This paper critically examines deepfakes within the Indian legal framework, characterizing them as a form of Technology-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence (TFGBV). It evaluates the constitutional safeguards enshrined in Articles 14, 15, and 21 of the Constitution, alongside the legal remedies available under the provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Furthermore, the paper analyses comparative approaches adopted across various jurisdictions. It argues that the existing fragmented legal framework is inadequate; consequently, there is an imperative need for a comprehensive, gender-sensitive regulatory framework that encompasses criminalization, platform accountability, consent-based data management, and effective victim relief mechanisms. The study concludes that regulating deepfakes is not merely a technical imperative, but an absolute constitutional and human rights mandate.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ONLINE FRAUD IN INDIA: LEGAL, TECHNOLOGICAL AND REGULATORY CHALLENGES AND THE NEED FOR A RISK-BASED FRAMEWORK
venue: LawFoyer International Journal of Doctrinal Legal Research.
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has transformed the nature, scale and sophistication of online fraud. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used not only to automate conventional cyber-fraud techniques but also to create new forms of deception involving voice cloning, deepfakes, synthetic identities, automated phishing, AI-generated messages, impersonation, fraudulent customer-service interactions and highly personalised social-engineering attacks. These developments challenge legal frameworks that were principally designed around human-generated communications and conventional forms of cybercrime. India possesses a substantial body of law capable of addressing AI-enabled fraud, including the Information Technology Act 2000 and the Rules framed under it, the three criminal-law codes of 2023, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and the Consumer Protection Act 2019. These instruments do not, however, constitute a unified regulatory framework. Questions of attribution, evidentiary authenticity, platform responsibility, bank liability, cross-border investigation and the allocation of liability between users, developers, intermediaries and financial institutions remain insufficiently resolved. This paper argues that the principal legal challenge is not the use of AI itself but the use of AI to create deception that causes, or is reasonably capable of causing, legally cognisable harm. It therefore proposes a risk-based and technology-neutral framework built on four principles: prevention, traceability, proportionate liability and effective victim redress. The paper examines the constitutional implications under Articles 14, 19 and 21, the evidentiary challenges associated with AI-generated material, intermediary liability and comparative regulatory approaches in the European Union, United States, United Kingdom, China and Singapore. The paper concludes that India does not require a general prohibition on AI-generated content. It requires a coordinated framework that combines criminal law, financial-fraud prevention, data protection, intermediary obligations, AI transparency, provenance technologies, rapid freezing of fraudulent transactions and specialised digital-evidence standards.

title: Gendered Online Harassment of Female Journalists in Digital Spaces in Pakistan
authors: Nida Javed; Sadia Jabeen; Aisha Muhammad Din
venue: Pakistan Journal of Gender Studies
abstract: This study examines the gendered online harassment faced by female journalists in Pakistan's digital media landscape. The objective of this study was to identify the forms of online harassment and abuse that female journalists face daily, their emotional and professional impact, and to assess the effectiveness of existing legal mechanisms and their responses. A qualitative research methodology was used; data were collected through purposive sampling by conducting ten semi-structured interviews with female journalists across the provinces of Pakistan. The data was analyzed through thematic analysis to find recurring patterns and to explore shared experiences. The findings of this study show that gendered online harassment is widespread across digital platforms and beats. Participants shared their experiences of having sexualized comments, rape threats, body shaming, doxing, and political trolling as common ones, and honor-based harassment. This harassment also had a serious effect on their mental health and professional lives, including anxiety, insomnia, fear of visibility, self-censorship, reduction of social media use, and, in some cases, complete withdrawal from journalism. Journalists from minority identities and backward regions faced more severe harassment because of cultural and honor-based norms. The conclusion states that gendered online harassment is a structural problem, which reflects patriarchal authority and male-dominated fields. Weak newsroom policies and responses, their ineffectiveness, and the operational inadequacy of the PECA Act further increase women's vulnerability. Strong legal enforcement, institutional accountability, and digital safety measures, especially digital safety training should be made compulsory to ensure a free press and the protection of female journalists.

title: Analyzing the Impact of Cyber Harassment, Cyber Stalking Victimization, and Cyber Gender Hate Speech on Social Wellbeing of Female University Students in Sialkot Pakistan
venue: Journal of Language Literature & Social Affairs
abstract: This study's main objective is to examine how cyber stalking victimization, cyber harassment, and cyber gender hate speech affect female university students' social wellbeing. The goal of this study is to determine how response to these types of online harassment has a negative effect on female students' sense of safety, social interactions, and general well-being in digital contexts. The researcher gathered the data using a survey questionnaire and the quantitative research approach. In this study, a systematic/random sampling strategy was used to calculate the sample size of (373). The study's target demographic was the female University students. Regression analysis was used to verify the impact of cyber stalking victimization, cyber harassment, and cyber gender hate speech on female university students' social wellbeing. The study's findings show that cyber harassment, cyberstalking victimization, and cybergender hate speech are all strongly correlated with social well-being. Based on the objectives and findings, this study concluded that increased exposure to gender-based hate speech and cyber harassment in online environments has a detrimental effect on the social wellbeing of female university students, potentially lowering their sense of security, confidence, and social participation. The study's practical implications demonstrate that in order to protect female students from online harassment and establish a safer digital environment that promotes their social wellbeing, educational institutions and decision-makers must develop awareness campaigns, support systems, and effective policies.

title: Prurient Cybercrime Victimisation Among Women in Delhi NCR: Exploring Digital Predictors, Psychological Outcomes, and Moderating Effects of Coping and Resilience
venue: Research Square
abstract: Abstract Younger women in Delhi-NCR have stated that they consider prurient cybercrime (online sexual harassment, cyberstalking and nonconsensual image sharing) to be a significant public health issue. The study examined the relationships between sociodemographic characteristics, digital behaviours (e.g., internet usage and digital literacy), and psychological well-being (e.g., trauma, anxiety, depression and self-esteem) in 300 female college students (ages 17–28). Quantitative and qualitative analysis of data was carried out after the completion of structured questionnaires. There is a positive association between internet use and both trauma and anxiety. Digital literacy is a protective factor against trauma and is related to self-esteem. Cyber victimisation and psychological distress were found to be related through the mediating effects of coping strategies, social support, and resilience, as shown by Structural Equation Modelling. Qualitative responses from participants revealed a high frequency of shame, anger and suicidal ideation as reactions to being cyber-victimised. To show how cyber victimisation has created serious psychological damage, the qualitative data also demonstrated. We suggest an all-encompassing method of prevention and intervention based upon the findings of research. Possible prevention/intervention efforts include incorporating digital literacy training into college curriculum offering more trauma-informed psychological assistance. Developing social support systems for young women and targeting digital safety/mental health services for policy development. Education and mental health professionals should develop gender-sensitive intervention programs. There is very little research examining the psychological effects of cyber victimisation on young women in a highly digitised region like Delhi-NCR. Our study uses a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods to give a comprehensive view of the risk/protective factors associated with cyber-victimisation. The results will inform the creation of policy, education and campaign development to increase online safety and resilience and decrease cyber victimisation-related stigma in India's changing digital environment.

title: TORTIOUS LIABILITY FOR CYBER HARASSMENT AND VIRTUAL HARM: REIMAGINING THE LAW OF TORTS IN THE DIGITAL AGE
venue: Journal of Law of Torts and Consumer Protection Law
abstract: The transformation of social interaction from the physical world to the digital environment has generated forms of injury that were largely unknown when the modern law of torts developed. Cyber harassment, cyberstalking, doxxing, cyberbullying, online defamation, impersonation, non-consensual dissemination of intimate images, deepfake abuse, identity manipulation and persistent digital surveillance can cause profound injury without any physical contact between the wrongdoer and the victim. The consequences may include loss of reputation, invasion of privacy, psychological suffering, disruption of family and professional relationships, physical-security risks and economic loss. Indian law presently addresses different dimensions of these wrongs through a fragmented combination of tort principles, constitutional rights, the Information Technology Act, 2000, intermediary regulation, criminal law, consumer protection and equitable remedies. The absence of a comprehensive statutory tort of cyber harassment, however, does not necessarily mean the absence of civil liability. Traditional principles of negligence, defamation, privacy, nuisance, intentional wrongdoing and vicarious liability possess sufficient flexibility to respond to many forms of virtual harm. This article examines whether and how the law of torts can accommodate cyber harassment and virtual harm. It develops the concept of the “digital personality” as an extension of the legally protected personality of the individual and argues that privacy, reputation, dignity, informational autonomy and digital identity should receive meaningful tortious protection. It further examines the difficult question of pure economic loss through a comparative study of Murphy v. Brentwood District Council and Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. The article also considers emerging problems associated with artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes, intermediary responsibility, platform design, anonymous perpetrators and the persistence of online material. The article proposes a technology-neutral framework based upon duty, foreseeability, proximity, control, substantial interference, causation and reasonable preventive responsibility. It argues that tort law should neither impose universal liability for online speech nor require a victim to wait until virtual harm produces physical injury. A carefully defined doctrine of digital tortious liability can protect victims while preserving freedom of speech and legitimate online expression. The article ultimately argues that the future of tort law lies in recognising that the “person” protected by tort law now possesses both a physical and a digital existence.

title: India’s Digital Banking Era: Cyber Fraud Targeting Women and Senior Citizens from Legal and Socio-Economic Perspectives
authors: Kuku Ram Kanojia; Rajesh Kumar Singh
venue: THE SCIENTIFIC TEMPER
abstract: The evolution of digital banking in India can be traced back to the early 2000s, particularly following the global concerns surrounding the Y2K crisis, which accelerated advancements in information technology and cybersecurity. Over time, experts have worked extensively to counter threats such as phishing, vishing, data breaches, and SQL-based attacks. While technological systems have become more stable and secure, cybercriminals have simultaneously developed increasingly sophisticated techniques to exploit financial systems.In recent years, digital payment platforms—especially Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and Aadhaar-enabled payment systems (AePS)—have significantly enhanced financial inclusion across India. Spearheaded by institutions such as the Government of India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), and the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), these systems have made financial services accessible to millions. However, this rapid digital expansion has also led to a surge in cyber fraud, disproportionately affecting vulnerable groups, particularly women and senior citizens.These groups are often targeted through deceptive practices such as phishing messages disguised as official communications, impersonation scams, and coercive tactics like “digital arrest” frauds. Such crimes exploit not only technological gaps but also socio-cultural vulnerabilities, including limited digital literacy and trust-based social behavior.Recent data highlights the severity of the issue. In 2025 alone, the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal recorded over 76,000 cybercrime incidents involving women. Similarly, senior citizens—especially those living in isolation—have suffered significant financial losses. Studies indicate that nearly half of individuals in these categories struggle to identify fraudulent schemes due to limited awareness and digital skills.This study adopts a doctrinal and socio-legal approach, examining statutory frameworks such as the Information Technology Act, 2000, along with recent reforms under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. It identifies critical gaps in existing legal mechanisms and highlights the need for adaptive and responsive regulatory structures.To address these challenges, the paper proposes targeted interventions, including real-time fraud alerts within banking interfaces, enhanced cybercrime investigation infrastructure, improved coordination among enforcement agencies, and the introduction of compensation mechanisms for victims. These measures aim to shift the focus from reactive enforcement to proactive prevention.Additionally, the study draws upon ethical principles from Buddhist philosophy, emphasizing values such as non-violence (ahimsa) and mindfulness (sati), to frame cyber fraud not merely as a legal violation but as a broader moral concern.

title: AI-Generated Deepfakes and Political Closures: A Comparative Study of India, UK, and USA (2014–2024)
venue: Journal of international commercial law and technology
abstract: Synthetic media, specifically AI generated deepfakes, have become a powerful tool that greatly impact the political discourse across nations. Spread using multi-layered narratives crafted around them, their impact increases to the point of shaping public perceptions. This study aims to understand how deepfakes narrow down the range of viewpoints in public discourse and marginalise dissenting voices to create “political closures.” It also seeks to identify the actors and their motivation behind the deployement of deepfakes. The researchers analyse 38 instances of deepfakes on digital platforms between 2014 to 2024, in three countries: India, the UK and the USA. India saw an increase in deepfakes before and during elections with insufficient regulations; the US saw a tussle between free speech and platforms’ self-policing; the UK showcased discussions around forward-looking laws. The majority of lenses through which the deepfakes were presented are security concerns and stricter regulations to pave the way for higher platform monitoring, speech clampdowns, and government influence on what is acceptable and what isn’t in a public discourse. While these appear as solutions, they also run the risk of threatening free speech in a democratic setup. In the end, deepfakes aren’t just synthetically generated audio-visual clips but the real framework that could enable the tech giants and states to craft agreements on what is the “ultimate truth” and what becomes of the rest

title: Cyberbullying and Student Rights in India Impact, Legal Provisions, and Prevention Strategies
authors: A Manoj; Ankith; Abdul Afran; Aliya azmath; Prof. Sumaiya Banu
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Cyberbullying has emerged as one of the most pressing challenges in India’s digitally connected educational environment. With over 85% of Indian children reportedly experiencing some form of online harassment — the highest rate globally according to a McAfee survey — the psychological, academic, and social consequences for student victims are profound and far-reaching. India reported over 50,035 cybercrime cases in 2020 alone (NCRB), with cyberstalking and cyber blackmailing among the fastest-growing categories. This paper synthesizes findings from 12 peer-reviewed studies retrieved from Google Scholar to examine the nature, prevalence, and multi-dimensional impacts of cyberbullying among Indian students. It critically evaluates constitutional safeguards under Articles 14, 19, and 21, relevant provisions of the Information Technology Act 2000, the Indian Penal Code, and the POCSO Act 2012. The paper also assesses the effectiveness of government initiatives including the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal and the I4C awareness campaigns. Employing a qualitative, descriptive methodology based entirely on secondary sources, this study identifies significant enforcement gaps and awareness deficits, concluding that dedicated cyberbullying legislation, mandatory digital literacy education, and robust institutional support mechanisms are essential to protect Indian students’ rights and well-being in digital spaces.

title: LEGAL IMPLICATIONS OF DATA BREACHES IN THE DIGITAL ECONOMY
authors: Dr. Sourabh Kumar Jain Anwesha Tripathy
venue: ACCENT JOURNAL OF  ECONOMICS ECOLOGY  & ENGINEERING
abstract: Abstract: The rapid expansion of the digital economy has resulted in an exponential growth in data generation, storage, and processing, transforming data into a critical asset for organizations worldwide. While digital transformation has significantly improved operational efficiency, innovation, and global connectivity, it has simultaneously increased exposure to cybersecurity threats, particularly data breaches. Data breaches involve unauthorized access, disclosure, or loss of sensitive personal and corporate information, leading to severe consequences such as identity theft, financial fraud, reputational damage, and loss of consumer trust. More importantly, they give rise to complex legal implications, including civil liability, criminal prosecution, regulatory penalties, and contractual disputes. This paper critically examines the legal implications of data breaches within the framework of the digital economy, with a focus on prominent global and national regulatory regimes such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act). The paper highlights the need for robust data governance frameworks, proactive cybersecurity strategies, and international cooperation to effectively address the risks associated with data breaches and ensure the protection of individual privacy rights in the digital age. Keywords: Data Breach, Digital Economy, Cybersecurity, Data Protection Law, GDPR, DPDP Act 2023, Legal Liability, Privacy Rights, Regulatory Compliance, Information Security

title: Weaponized Synthetic Media: AI-Generated Disinformation, Deepfakes, and Electoral Integrity in Pakistan's 2024 General Election
venue: Social science review archives.
abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence generated disinformation, deepfakes, and bot amplified narratives in shaping electoral discourse during Pakistan's 2024 general election. Drawing on secondary sources, news reporting, and existing scholarship, the study documents a striking pattern in which the imprisoned Pakistan Tehreek e Insaf leader Imran Khan's party used disclosed AI generated video and audio to mobilize supporters, while unidentified actors simultaneously deployed fabricated deepfake audio and video falsely attributed to Khan and his associates to suppress voter turnout through false boycott calls. The analysis situates these findings within computational propaganda theory, the concept of epistemic security, and institutionalist approaches to regulatory capacity, arguing that Pakistan's weak legal framework and its decision to suspend internet and mobile services on election day compounded the harms of synthetic disinformation. The study finds that Pakistan currently lacks any regulatory mechanism specifically addressing AI generated political content, relying instead on ill suited defamation law. It concludes with policy recommendations for the Election Commission of Pakistan, legislative reform, and civil society collaboration to safeguard electoral integrity against future AI driven manipulation.

title: CAN WOMEN’S DIGNITY ENDURE THE DEEPFAKE ERA? NON-CONSENSUAL INTIMATE IMAGERY AND THE FRAGILITY OF PERSONALITY RIGHTS IN INDIA
venue: LEX IS US LAW JOURNAL
abstract: The rise of generative AI has triggered a surge in non-consensual deepfakes—synthetic media used for revenge porn, sexualized morphing, and intimate image abuse—inflicting severe gender-based harm. Globally and in India, 96–98% of deepfake content is non-consensual pornographic material, with 99% of victims being women and girls. This technology-facilitated violence perpetuates digital misogyny, causing psychological trauma, reputational damage, social ostracism, and economic exclusion, compounded by societal stigma that silences victims. In India, the Right to Personality—protecting dignity, privacy, and autonomy over one's likeness under Article 21 of the Constitution, as affirmed in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017)—faces existential challenge from AI-enabled deepfakes. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires consent for biometric data processing and imposes fines up to ₹250 crore for breaches, yet it overlooks synthetic manipulation. Complementary provisions in the Information Technology Act, 2000 (ss 66E, 67), Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and intermediary rules offer partial remedies but lack standalone criminalization of deepfake creation. Employing doctrinal and comparative methods, this paper examines whether personality rights can endure this threat. It reviews judicial injunctions against morphed content and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026 (effective February 20, 2026), which define synthetically generated information (SGI), mandate labelling/metadata, and enforce 2–3 hour takedowns for non-consensual intimate imagery. Findings highlight gaps: reliance on general laws, enforcement hurdles (anonymity, cross-border issues), and cultural barriers to reporting. Comparative models—the EU AI Act (high-risk classification), US TAKE IT DOWN Act (criminalizing NCII), and UK Online Safety Act—suggest reforms. The paper concludes that without targeted legislation criminalizing creation/dissemination, gender-sensitive provisions, mandatory AI detection/watermarking, victim redress, and platform accountability, personality rights risk erosion. Urgent action is vital to protect women's dignity in India's digital space. Keywords: Deepfakes, non-consensual intimate imagery, personality rights, gender-based violence, revenge porn, sexualized morphing, Article 21, Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, IT Rules 2026, India.
