title: Financial Cybercrime, FinTech Adoption, and Bank Performance in an Interconnected Indian Economy: Typologies, Networks, and Systemic Implications
authors: Priyakrushna Mohanty; Rashi Modi; Aaleyah Behera
venue: IGI Global eBooks
abstract: India's rapid expansion of digital finance has transformed payment systems while heightening exposure to financial cybercrime. Real-time payments, platform-based services, and fintech integration have created risk pathways that extend beyond isolated fraud incidents. This study analyses financial cybercrime in India through a systemic lens, mapping evolving fraud typologies, payment-rail vulnerabilities, organised criminal networks, and behavioural asymmetries. It also examines the capacity of regulatory, infrastructural, and enforcement mechanisms to manage these risks under real-time operational constraints. Drawing on a structured synthesis of academic and policy sources, the paper develops the Systemic Cybercrime Mitigation Framework for Digital Finance (SCMF-DF), which integrates prevention, detection, containment, recovery, and adaptive learning to address cybercrime as a financial stability concern.

title: Investigation of Cybercrime under BNSS and Proof of Digital Evidence under BSA: A Critical Analysis
authors: Balasaheb G. Pawar; Rajesh N. Makasare
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract The unprecedented growth of information and communication technology has fundamentally transformed both the nature of crime and the methods employed for its investigation. Cybercrime is no longer confined to conventional computer-related offences but extends to online financial fraud, identity theft, unauthorized access, cyberstalking, data theft, ransomware, social-media offences, digital forgery and technology-facilitated organized criminal activity. Investigation of such offences presents distinctive legal and technical challenges because the crime scene may exist in virtual space, the offender and victim may be situated in different jurisdictions, and crucial evidence may be stored on mobile devices, remote servers, cloud platforms or other digital systems. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), which came into force on 1st July 2024, seek to respond to these developments by integrating technology into investigation and by expressly recognizing electronic and digital records within the law of evidence. The BNSS facilitates electronic reporting of cognizable offences, mandates audio-video recording of specified investigative processes, strengthens forensic investigation and recognizes electronic modes throughout criminal proceedings. Of particular significance to cybercrime investigation is the statutory emphasis on preservation, seizure, forensic examination and documentation of electronic devices. The BSA, on the other hand, substantially reorganizes the evidentiary framework relating to electronic records. Sections 57 to 63 deal with primary and secondary evidence and the proof and admissibility of electronic records, while section 39 recognizes expert opinion concerning information transmitted or stored in computer resources and other electronic or digital forms. The new framework must, however, be understood against the historical development of electronic evidence under the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 following the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the judicial evolution from State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu to Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal. This article critically examines the investigation of cybercrime under the BNSS and the proof of digital evidence under the BSA with particular emphasis on collection, preservation, authenticity, chain of custody and admissibility of electronic evidence. It analyses the historical evolution of Indian electronic-evidence law and examines significant decisions of the Supreme Court and High Courts.

title: Cyberbullying and Child Safety Online in India: Evaluating the IT Rules and the Juvenile Justice Act
venue: Indian Journal of Jurisprudence and Reviews (IJJR)
abstract: The proliferation of digital technologies has exposed children to unprecedented risks of cyberbullying, necessitating robust legal frameworks for their protection. This paper critically examines the effectiveness of India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, and the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, in addressing cyberbullying and ensuring child safety online. Through doctrinal analysis and evaluation of enforcement mechanisms, this study reveals significant gaps in implementation, coordination among stakeholders, and victim support systems. While the IT Rules impose due diligence obligations on intermediaries and the JJ Act provides rehabilitative frameworks, challenges persist in terms of definitional clarity, digital literacy, and swift redressal mechanisms. The paper argues for a comprehensive, child-centric approach integrating legal reforms, technological solutions, and educational interventions to create a safer digital environment for Indian children.

title: The Affective Politics of Cybercrime: Mapping the Discourse of Victimhood in Aik Aur Pakeezah
venue: Liberal Journal of Language & Literature Review
abstract: The research paper examined the affective politics of cybercrime in the Pakistani drama Aik Aur Pakeezah (2026). Aik Aur Pakeezah is written by Bee Gul and directed by Kashif Nisar. The paper used the theoretical framework of Sara Ahmed’s affect theory. The researcher addressed the emotions of shame and fear that stick to victims’ bodies and set the preparator free. It moves beyond the technical and legal grounds of cybercrime towards the aftermath that is culturally, socially and morally grounded faced by victims. The research has two objectives; At first, it examined shame and fear as tools to silence victims in Aik Aur Pakeezah. Secondly, it investigated the circulation of shame and displacement of blame from preparator towards the victims. It employed the qualitative textual analysis of selected episodes and scenes to examine the mentioned objectives. The concepts of stickiness, affective economy, sticky signs, shame and fear are applied to Aik Aur Pakeezah in analysis. The findings illustrate that the two objectives operate as a single continuous affective process. It discussed the use of Honour based vocabulary such as Izzat, Ghairat. The emotions of shame and fear are reproduced and displaced due to the use of vocabulary. The analysis is extended to the discussion of male victimhood. Through the character of “Faraz’’ in context of cybercrime in Pakistani television drama Aik Aur Pakeezah. Keywords: Affect theory, Cybercrime, Victimhood, Shame, Fear, Pakistani Television drama, Honor culture. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21821180

title: Digital Media Use, Awareness of Cybercrime Laws and the Mediating Role of Digital Literacy: The Psychological Underpinnings
authors: Muhammad Sajjad Shahid; Sara Komal; Jahangir Ashraf
venue: Journal of Professional & Applied Psychology
abstract: Digital media use is increasing rapidly in Pakistan, particularly among university students. However, when it comes to awareness among university students regarding cybercrime laws, it is highly limited due to lack of digital literacy. Therefore, this study aimed to examine role of digital literacy as a mediator between digital media use, and awareness of cybercrime laws. The study utilized a cross-sectional correlational research design and used purposive sampling to collect data from the participants. Initially, 300 participants were approached in Islamabad, Lahore, and Karachi, out of which 46 withdrew from the study, yielding a response rate of 84.66%. The study included three standardized questionnaires: the Social Media Use Integration Scale, the Cybercrime Awareness Scale, and the Digital Literacy Scale. The results demonstrated significant associations among variables. Furthermore, mediation analysis depicted that digital literacy partially mediated the relationship between digital media use and awareness of cybercrime laws. Additionally, no statistically significant mean differences were found between gender with respect to study variables. These findings emphasize the importance of promoting digital literacy programs in universities to help students’ understanding of cyber risks and relevant legal protections.

title: Why Cybercrime Keeps Winning: A Plain Look at the Root Causes and What the Law Can Do About It
venue: Iconic Research and Engineering Journals
abstract: Every day, millions of people lose money, data, and peace of mind to cybercrime. The standard response — more laws, tougher penalties, better software — has not stopped the problem from growing. This paper argues that the real causes run deeper: most people simply do not know enough about online risks to protect themselves; weak password habits leave accounts wide open; individuals and businesses alike lack the practical skills to respond when something goes wrong; and criminals are quick to twist every new piece of technology into a weapon. None of these are purely technical problems. They are human and institutional ones, and they call for human and institutional answers. The paper examines each cause in plain terms, draws on legal frameworks from India and other jurisdictions, and offers practical steps for lawmakers, law enforcement, schools, and the private sector.

title: Digital Vulnerabilities and Legal Awareness: A Study of Cybercrime Exposure and Prevention Among Women in the Twin Cities of Odisha
venue: Indian Journal of Public Administration
abstract: Digitalisation has emerged as a double-edged reality, offering opportunities while simultaneously generating new forms of risk, as reflected in rising trends of cybercrime against women in Odisha, India. This article examines the vulnerability of women to cybercrime and their awareness of cyber law in the tier-II cities — Bhubaneswar and Cuttack. A mixed-methods design is used, based on 100 surveys and twenty in-depth interviews with respondents to capture patterns and lived experiences. Based on network governance theory and symbolic interactionism, this article examines how socio-cultural norms and institutional structures influence women’s experiences in digital spaces. The research uncovers poor institutional coordination, enforcement and digital unawareness that results in underreporting. The article recommends more robust digital governance, swift institutional reaction and growing awareness, so that women can safely engage in digital spaces.

title: Cybercrime Legislation and Enforcement in the Twenty First Century: A Critical Analysis of Legal Frameworks, Operational Challenges, and the Balancing of Security with Civil Liberties
authors: Humail Zainab; Sidra Ilyas; Saira Ali
venue: The Journal of Research Review
abstract: With the explosion of connectivity via the internet, cybercrime has emerged as one of the most widespread and expensive security threats in today's society and will cost societies $10.5 trillion a year by 2025. This article examines cybercrime legislation and enforcement in the twenty first century in a comprehensive manner with the help of international law, criminology and public policy perspectives. This analysis starts from a detailed classification of cyber offenses based on three categories: crimes against cyber systems, crimes using cyber systems and crimes in cyber systems; and identifies the characteristics of cyberspace that challenge conventional territorial jurisdiction. The article examines critically the international legal landscape and compares the Budapest Convention of the Council of Europe with other regional instruments which have come into existence as well as with the proposed United Nations convention. In the context, a detailed case study of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016 in Pakistan highlights the tensions between comprehensive criminalization and civil liberties protection, including documented overblocking of online content. Four dimensions of enforcement challenges are considered systematically: jurisdictional ambiguity, difficulty of attribution, lack of forensic capacity and low reporting rates. Finally, the article emphasizes the importance of not only having coherent legal frameworks in place, but also of continuous investment in institutional capacity, in PPs, and in the need for a balanced security approach and respect for fundamental rights.

title: HASHED AND CHAINED, YET DOUBTED: RELIABILITY OF DIGITAL EVIDENCE IN THE ERA OF CYBERCRIMES
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Digital evidence has assumed the position of the backbone of the modern criminal justice system on account of the contemporary proliferation of cybercrime, yet several unaccounted factors pertaining to its alteration, duplication and even deletion has not been able to save it from being perpetually questioned on grounds of reliability. This paper examines the exact question by the synthesis of three recent scholarly studies, taking into consideration the narrative review of the legal and forensic dimensions of electronic evidence, the doctrinal study of the Indian criminal legal background, especially post-enactment of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (Hereinafter referred to as 'BSA') and the qualitative study of the legal standards and the practices of chain-of-custody across several jurisdictions. This paper attempts to make a distinguishing premise between 'admissibility', which serves as a threshold question and 'reliability', which serves as the weight deserved by an admission. It makes an analysis of the authentication, chain-of-custody, expert testimony, cognitive bias and cross-border collection and procedural fairness as the core factors for determining reliability. It also traces the evolution of Indian criminal justice's certification requirement ranging from section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act (herein after referred to as 'IEA'), 1872 to section 63 of the BSA, 2023. Another additional consideration discussed here is the re-moulding of forensic practice by Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, Internet of Things and Deepfake Detection. The paper also advances an argument that reliability cannot only be secured by mere legal codification, rather ought to be matched by standardised forensic protocols, adequate laboratory capacity and judicial training. title: A CORPUS-ASSISTED COMPARATIVE STUDY OF CYBERCRIME REPRESENTATION IN DAWN AND THE GUARDIAN
authors: Tuba Munir; Muhammad Abdur Rehmaan; Maliha Shahid
venue: Applied Linguistics Research Review
abstract: Cybercrime has become one of the fastest-growing issues in the contemporary digital world. This study examines the representation of “cybercrime” in Pakistani newspaper Dawn and British newspaper The Guardian through a corpus-assisted comparative analysis. The research aims to explore how cybercrime is linguistically constructed in both newspapers by identifying the frequency of key lexical items, their collocational patterns, and their contextual usage through concordance analysis. The study is grounded in corpus linguistics. It employs a mixed-methods approach as it combines quantitative and qualitative analysis to provide a deeper understanding of “cybercrime” representation in selected newspapers. The data for this study consists of 200 articles from the online archives of both newspapers. They have been specifically searched by using the keyword “cybercrime”. Furthermore, the analysis was conducted in three steps using Sketch Engine. The frequency analysis reveals that Dawn is stronger in crime framing, whereas The Guardian focuses more on security concerns. Then, collocation analysis examines the words commonly associated with the keyword “cybercrime”. It reveals the dominant themes and concerns highlighted by each newspaper. The concordance (KWIC) analysis provides contextual insights into how cybercrime was framed and discussed. The findings reveal noticeable differences in the representation of “cybercrime” between the newspapers. Dawn mainly constructs cybercrime as a legal, institutional, and governance issue. However, The Guardian presents cybercrime as a global technological problem. Moreover, the research contributes to the field of corpus linguistics by providing a comparative analysis of cybercrime representation in national and international newspapers.

title: Deepfakes and Due Process: Rethinking Authenticity of Social Media Evidence in India’s New Digital Evidence Regime
venue: International Academic Journal of Social Sciences
abstract: The use of social media has become the central point of criminal investigation and trial, providing real time data of behavior, communication, and the location of suspects on WhatsApp, Instagram, and X platforms. However, such material is only accepted by courts when it meets great requirements of relevance, authenticity, integrity and legal collection as per international rules of digital evidence (23711). This theoretical and comparative research examines the transformation of the Indian regime since the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and IT Act, 2000 (Sections 65A-65B) to Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 which balances electronic records with traditional documents whilst maintaining an intensive and metadata intensive certifications procedure under Section 63 (51018). Using the international literature on social media forensics, metadata-based authentication of digital evidence, and deepfakes, the research identifies core admissibility requirements and compares the practice in India with the international practice (23471416). It recognizes the main issues, such as manipulation and AI generated deepfakes, lapses in the procedure, cross border access to data, insufficient forensic capabilities and judicial skills (135131619). The article explains that the new framework in India is mostly convergent with the best practice in the international world but will be weak without standardization of forensic procedures, platform-specific applications, international partnership, and systematic training of investigators and courts (235716). It ends by suggesting improvements to enhance authenticity checks, chain of custody documentations, and privacy controls to enable the utilization of social media evidence without derailing the rights to fair trials.

title: Reconciling Deepfake Regulations vis-à-vis Human Rights: A Comparative Legal Analysis Across Jurisdictions
venue: Review of Futures Markets
abstract: Synthetic media produced by generative artificial intelligence, commonly called deepfakes, have become an industrialised instrument of financial fraud, electoral manipulation, and image based sexual abuse, and they now threaten the evidentiary foundations of courts and human rights investigations. This Article assesses how four jurisdictions, the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and India, had addressed the problem by mid 2026, and it measures each regime against the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), in particular the guarantees of a fair trial in Article 14, privacy in Article 17, expression in Article 19, and political participation in Article 25. The comparison reveals four distinct regulatory philosophies: rights constrained, state-led regulation in the United States; upstream criminalisation of the technology supply chain in the United Kingdom; transparency-based, risk-tiered governance in the European Union; and accelerated intermediary liability in India. Each protects some rights at the expense of others, and all depend on provenance technology whose metadata is easily stripped and whose cryptographic assurances are weaker than they appear. The Article also examines the “authentication deficit” confronting the International Criminal Court. It concludes that domestic statutes alone cannot adequately address a borderless technical problem and proposes an additional protocol under the United Nations Global Digital Compact establishing “Provenance by Design,” combining mandatory preservation of provenance metadata by distribution platforms with the formal adoption of the Berkeley Protocol by international tribunals, and disciplined throughout by the necessity and proportionality requirements of Article 19(3) of the ICCPR.

title: Impact of Cybercrime on the E-Commerce Industry in India: A Systematic Review of Consumer Vulnerability, Regulatory Challenges, and Cybersecurity Preparedness
authors: Sanjna Agarwal; Professor Dr. Adeel Maqbool
venue: Well Testing Journal
abstract: The accelerated digital transformation of India’s economy has positioned e-commerce as a dominant engine of national growth and innovation. However, this expansion has simultaneously intensified vulnerabilities to cybercrime, leading to substantial economic disruptions, erosion of consumer trust, and legal complexities. This systematic review critically synthesizes scholarly literature, government reports, and industry data published between 2015 and 2025 to evaluate the multifaceted impact of cybercrime on the Indian e-commerce ecosystem. The review examines five interconnected dimensions: (a) the evolution and structural dynamics of Indian e-commerce in the context of increasing cyber threats, (b) the nature, scale, and typologies of cybercrimes targeting consumers and digital marketplaces, (c) policy, regulatory, and jurisdictional challenges under India’s cyber law regime, (d) consumer awareness and behavioral responses to cyber risks, and (e) the adequacy of cybersecurity frameworks, enforcement institutions, and corporate governance mechanisms. The findings reveal critical gaps in cyber incident reporting, digital literacy, and compliance infrastructure, exacerbated by rapid technological adoption and a mobile-first consumer base. Although the government has introduced new data protection and cybersecurity mandates, practical enforcement and inter-agency coordination remain limited. The review underscores the need for resilient cyber safety strategies, consumer-centric protections, stronger accountability standards for e-commerce platforms, and national capability building in incident response. This review also identifies critical theoretical and empirical gaps and proposes an integrated conceptual model linking cybercrime exposure, structural vulnerabilities, consumer trust, and e-commerce participation. The study contributes an integrated framework for future research and policy formulation to support secure and sustainable growth of India’s digital economy.

title: Cyber Harassment in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Emerging Challenges, Opportunities, Legal Responses and Policy Recommendation
venue: Journal of Political Stability Archive
abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed communication, education, employment, social interaction and access to information. At the same time, AI has created new possibilities for cyber harassment and technology-facilitated abuse. Traditional forms of online harassment, including threatening messages, cybers talking, impersonation, doxing and non-consensual dissemination of private material, can now be produced and distributed with greater speed and sophistication through AI-enabled tools. Generative AI has further complicated the problem by making it possible to create realistic but fabricated photographs, videos, audio recordings and written communications. Deepfakes, AI-generated sexual imagery, automated impersonation, targeted harassment and sophisticated phishing or social-engineering campaigns represent emerging risks for individuals, particularly women, children, journalists, public figures and other vulnerable groups. The relationship between AI and cyber harassment is not entirely negative. AI can also assist in detecting abusive content, identifying coordinated harassment, authenticating digital evidence, improving reporting mechanisms and supporting law-enforcement investigations. The central challenge is therefore not AI itself but the manner in which AI systems are designed, accessed, deployed and regulated. This article examines the changing nature of cyber harassment in the AI era, identifies its principal forms, analyses potential advantages and disadvantages of AI, considers legal and institutional responses, and proposes recommendations for governments, courts, law-enforcement agencies, educational institutions, technology companies and civil society. Particular attention is given to Pakistan, where the expansion of digital participation has increased the importance of effective responses to technology-facilitated gender-based violence. Pakistan adopted the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016 (PECA), subsequently amended in 2025, while the country also developed its first National Strategy to Counter Technology-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence in 2026. The article argues that effective protection requires a combination of law reform, digital literacy, technological safeguards, survivor-centred justice, institutional capacity and responsible AI governance.

title: CONSTRUCTING TRUST THROUGH DECEPTION: A FORENSIC LINGUISTIC INVESTIGATION OF SCAM COMMUNICATION
venue: Journal of Applied Linguistics and TESOL (JALT)
abstract: This study uses forensic lens to examine linguistic, psychological, and interactional strategies used by Pakistani scammers to deceive the victims, across boundaries, through phone calls. The data for the scam call was collected from publicly available YouTube channels specializing in scam-baiting content, such as Scam Sandwich and Scam Baiter. The data was manually transcribed to highlight salient language and paralinguistic features. The transcripts were analyzed by examining them through Olsson’s (2004) Forensic Text Analysis framework and Interpersonal Deception Theory (Buller and Burgoon, 1996). The results indicate that deceptive language, institutional jargon and inconsistencies in language and grammar are used to establish credibility and control. It further reveals that the fraudulent narratives follow a somewhat predictable, yet slightly variable structure; problem introduction, invoking authority, demanding urgency, and financial or technical demand to deceive the victims. At the interactional level, scammers use politeness and reassurance and they use adaptive communication to maintain conversational dominance. The study also reveals that deceptive performances are unstable in the face of confrontation, because when confronted by exposers, inconsistencies in the narration, shifts in tone, and behavioral adaptations appear. In brief, the study demonstrates that scam calls are a negotiation and manipulation of language and psychological tricks and that they are co-constructed on an interactive basis during the call. The findings can be applied to the field of forensic linguistics, offering context-sensitive examination of spoken scam discourse, and suggestions for implications for scam detection, public awareness and digital security.

title: Intellireport Cyber: a Unified Framework for Multimodal Cybercrime Categorization and Severity Assessment
authors: Kalpana Bodke; Adithya Arumugasamy; Amish Mishra; Muthuraj Mudaliar
venue: International Conference on Computing Communication Control and automation
abstract: India's fast pace of digitalization has triggered an explosive surge in cybercrime cases, while current reporting systems remain mostly manual, text-based, and are not designed to triage and preserve evidence in real time. In this paper, a prototype multimodal AI framework, named IntelliReport Cyber, is introduced that allows for structured cybercrime reporting, automated categorization, and severity based prioritization for the Indian scenario. Complaints are fed into the system in both text and voice, with both the complaints and the model languages being code-mixed, and the system uses the Hinglish-aware transformer models, namely HingRoBERTa and HingBERT. Multi-Task Learning (MTL) architecture classifies cybercrime type while predicting the severity (Low/Medium/High/Critical), which lets you triage high risk cases in the early stages. A grid-search is performed over the values of$\lambda \mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0. 3}, \mathbf{0. 5}, \mathbf{0. 7}$and$\lambda \mathbf{s}=\mathbf{1}- \lambda \mathbf{c}$, and the configuration with the best performance is chosen on the validation set. The framework is enhanced with a rule-based legal mapping, based on Indian cyber law, and a guided forensic evidence collection module. Evaluation is carried out on an Indian cybercrime complaint dataset where class imbalance issues are taken into account using synthetic augmentation techniques such as back-translating, paraphrasing, etc. for minority classes like ransomware and impersonation. The performance of the speechto-text component is measured with Word Error Rate (WER) with a 12.4% WER on Hinglish voice input. Results show a consistent performance on all types of crimes, and are sharper results in the case of handling Hinglish complaint compared with baseline multilingual models. The topics of privacy, ethical concerns, and feasibility of deployment are also addressed. The proposed framework emphasizes the role of AI in multimodal reporting as a valuable tool to further the benefits of cyber governance by reducing reporting delays, increasing the quality of complaints and enhancing the responsiveness of the law enforcement.

title: Cyberstalking and Harassment of Women: Legal Framework and Enforcement Challenges
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The growth of internet access, smartphones, social networking sites and messaging applications has created valuable opportunities for women’s education, employment, expression and participation in public life. At the same time, digital tools can be misused to monitor, threaten, sexually harass, impersonate, blackmail and intimidate women. Cyberstalking and online harassment may involve repeated unwanted messages, monitoring of electronic communications, publication of private information, non-consensual sharing of intimate images, fake profiles, doxxing and coordinated abuse. These acts can affect safety, mental health, reputation, livelihood and freedom of expression, and may spill into offline life. This paper examines the legal framework in India and the challenges involved in enforcing it. It discusses constitutional protections, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), the Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act), the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, and workplace protections under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013. It also considers reporting mechanisms, digital evidence, jurisdiction, platform cooperation, victim privacy and institutional capacity. The paper adopts a doctrinal and descriptive methodology based on legislation, official government resources and legal principles. It argues that India has several applicable legal provisions, but effective protection depends on timely investigation, consistent interpretation, trained personnel, accessible reporting, preservation of evidence, platform accountability and a victim-centred approach. Recommendations include specialised training, standard operating procedures, stronger digital-evidence practices, rapid response to intimate-image abuse, legal aid, public awareness and better coordination across jurisdictions.

title: Digital Forensic Accounting in the Era of Cybercrime : A Global Bibliometric Review
venue: Pattimura Proceeding Conference of Science and Technology
abstract: This study uses bibliometric analysis to examine developments and research trends in the field of forensic accounting from 2005 to 2025. Publication data extracted from the Scopus database is analyzed using VOSviewer software to map statistical patterns, visualize academic networks, and identify key research topics in this field. The results reveal dynamic shifts in publication volume caused by factors such as the increasing complexity of financial crime, advances in the integration of digital technologies, heightened expectations for transparency, evolving regulatory frameworks, increased interdisciplinary collaboration, and improved internal control mechanisms. The high volume of journal articles indicates strong global academic interest. In addition, the analysis highlighted significant contributions from both developed and emerging economies, including the United States, India, United Kingdom, Indonesia, South Korea and Australia. Key research topics include risk management, fraud detection, digital forensics, fraud analysis, digital compliance, and financial governance. This study underscores the ongoing need for research to improve fraud detection and prevention strategies, promote global academic collaboration, and strengthen efforts to maintain financial integrity and transparency

title: Modular RAG-Based LegalTech Architecture for Cybercrime Analysis and Mitigation
authors: Namrata Shetty; Sanjay Bang; Kalyani Abhyankar
venue: International Conference on Trends in Quantum Computing and Emerging Business Technologies (TQCEBT)
abstract: Cybercrime cases are regularly producing hybrid queries that need both the technical evidence and regulatory requirements to be interpreted along with the legal rules that are specific to jurisdiction. Even general-purpose large language models are not reliable in such environment as unsupported legal claims, missing reporting obligations, and lack of traceability of the source can still be present. An architectural design of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based legaltech is introduced, to analyse and mitigate cybercrime. The architecture breaks down the workflow into query decomposition, dual-domain legal and cybersecurity retrieval, evidence fusion and reranking, grounded answer generation, verification and escalation, which are overseen by a control-tower orchestration layer. An implementation based on prototyping and a controlled evaluation protocol are defined with definite Indian legal and cybersecurity corpora, queries of a practitioner-style cyber-law and comparative generator settings. In this configuration, the best overall profile corresponds to GPT-5.4, then Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-V3.2 and Perplexity Sonar is considered an external grounded-product baseline. The pattern of results suggests that the main benefits are generated by the workflow control, evidence grounding, and verification as opposed to the unconstrained generation alone. The article presents a modular cyber-legal RAG architecture, an experimenter-congruent experimental design, and a blueprint of deployment towards grounded legal AI in cybercrime-related processes.

title: THE DARK SIDE OF AI: CRYPTOCURRENCY AND CYBERCRIME: REGULATORY GAPS IN DIGITAL ASSET TRACING

abstract: THE DARK SIDE OF AI: CRYPTOCURRENCY AND CYBERCRIME: REGULATORY GAPS IN DIGITAL ASSET TRACING Vishwajeet Singh, LLB 3rd year (6th semester) Student at Amity Law School, Lucknow Campus (India) Dr. Mudra Singh, Assistant Professor at Amity Law School, Lucknow Campus (India). It maps the modern crime stack, from AI-assisted phishing and social engineering to ransomware, pig butchering, mixer use, and cross-chain laundering.

title: Technology Facilitated Gender Based Violence in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan: Logging Women out of the Economy
authors: Hafsa Alvi; Niyati Shah; Jonna Lundwall
venue: World Bank, Washington, DC eBooks
abstract: This Knowledge Brief examines how technology-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV) is emerging as a critical barrier to inclusive digital transformation in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. It shows that while digital tools can expand women’s access to economic opportunities, online harms such as surveillance, coercion, image-based abuse, deepfakes, harassment, and gendered disinformation can push women out of digital spaces and reinforce existing constraints on their participation. The brief argues that TFGBV is not only a safety issue but also an economic and development challenge, with consequences for women’s labor market entry, digital entrepreneurship, civic engagement, access to services, and psychological well-being—especially in contexts shaped by restrictive gender norms, conflict, fragility, and weak legal protection. It calls for stronger legal and institutional frameworks, platform accountability, survivor-centered reporting and support systems, privacy- and safety-by-design approaches, and prevention measures that embed women’s digital safety into digital economy, service delivery, education, and social protection strategies.

title: Technology-Facilitated Sexual Violence in India: Women’s Experiences of Violence and Oppression
venue: Routledge eBooks
abstract: Delving into the experiences of victimisation, responses to, and impacts of Technology-Facilitated Sexual Violence (TFSV) perpetrated by unknown individuals in India, this book unpacks five forms of victimisation that women identified and explained through their accounts: cyberstalking, gender-based sexualised vitriol, image-based sexual abuse (IBSA), doxxing, and unsolicited contact. New technologies can reinforce gender inequalities and enable harmful, exclusionary behaviour. This book demonstrates how technology-facilitated victimisation incidents are interconnected along a continuum of harm, often co-occurring with offline violence and experienced by women as cumulative assaults on their well-being. Informed by interviews with 20 women survivors, it sheds light on how women are marginalised, and how intersecting layers of identity, like religion, caste, and sex and gender, shape the socio-cultural contexts in which they experience victim-blaming, honour killings, and control over their sexuality. Consequently, the book highlights how TFSV is intertwined with intersecting structural inequalities in local and global contexts, arguing that failing to recognise this interconnectedness would inevitably limit our understanding of the wide range of harms that survivors face. Filling an empirical gap in the literature on women’s encounters with TFSV by unknown perpetrators in India, this book will be of value to students and scholars of criminology, cybercrime, socio-legal studies, feminist studies, victimisation, gender studies, and TFSV.

title: Trapped Online: Cyberbullying Victimization, Emotional Regulation, and Psychological Entrapment Among Young Adults in Pakistan
authors: Abeera Arshad; Shafia Manzoor; Maria Afzal; Ayesha Saeed; Muhammad Aslam Adeeb
venue: Pakistan Journal of Positive Psychology
abstract: The modern youth are more likely to be spending a greater portion of their lives online, and they are particularly at risk from a unique kind of harassment cyberbullying. Drawing on the defeat entrapment model and Gross's process model of emotion regulation, the present study examined the relationships among cyberbullying victimization, two emotion-regulation strategies (cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression), and psychological entrapment among Pakistani university students, and tested whether entrapment mediates the association between victimization and emotion regulation. The Cyberbullying Inventory for University Students, Emotion Regulation Questionnaire, and Entrapment Scale were administered on students aged 18-25 (N = 241) at public and private educational institutions. The results found that there was a positive correlation between cyberbullying victimization and entrapment and a negative correlation between cyberbullying victimization and expressive suppression. The results of partial least squares structural equation modeling revealed that entrapment had a significant and partial mediation effect on the relationship between victimization and both cognitive reappraisal (negatively) and expressive suppression (positively). The findings extend the defeat entrapment model to the digital sphere and highlight the possibility of psychological entrapment as an intervening mechanism that can be targeted in interventions with cyberbullied young adults, especially other non-Western cultures like Pakistan where there is limited research.

title: Social and psychological impact of deepfakes: a comprehensive bibliometric review
authors: Saddam Hossain; Desul Sudarsan; Hanan Zaffar; Naved Ahmad
venue: Global Knowledge, Memory and Communication
abstract: Purpose Deepfakes, which first appeared in 2017, use artificial intelligence (AI) to generate modified but incredibly realistic digital content, including political satire, posing serious moral, legal, and societal concerns. The purpose of the study is to identify the evolving landscape of deepfake technology, with a focus on its psychological and societal impacts. Design/methodology/approach The researchers carried out a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of research from 2019 to 2024, using data obtained from the Web of Science and Scopus bibliographic databases. After combining 688 bibliographic entries from both databases using Bibliometrix R. After eliminating non-English publications and studies irrelevant to the bibliometric scope of deepfake research, a total of 463 articles were included for further study. Findings Based on our results, the researchers found that academic scholarships on detection techniques, misinformation, and social impact has grown rapidly, particularly in China, the United States, and India. Six main study areas have emerged, such as deepfake detection methods, information integrity, machine learning, social media influences, forensic analysis, and facial manipulation. The findings reveal that the increasing complexity of deepfake generation and its consequences for ethical concerns significantly affects digital trust, privacy infringement, and the spread of misinformation. Originality/value More interdisciplinary techniques combining AI, social sciences and ethics are required despite notable gains in detection. To reduce the risks associated with deepfakes, the study highlights the significance of strong detection technologies, regulatory frameworks and public awareness. The psychological effects of deepfake exposure and the creation of moral standards for appropriate AI use should be the focus of future studies.

title: Cybercrime in the News 2019–2026: article-level dataset and coverage tables
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A dataset of cybercrime and online-fraud news from a global news index, January 2019 – July 2026, built with the Prism News API (historical and real-time news, https://radar-api.fliarbi.com/news). Every row is one news article about cybercrime, with its date, location, tone, editorial priority, themes and the organisations it names, plus a link that returns the full article through the API. Rows in this release 24,600 articles (25.1% of 97,889 matched articles to 31 July 2026) Full coverage counted 97,895 cybercrime articles, January 2019 – July 2026 Countries 144 primary locations in the sample Research paper cybercrime-research-paper.pdf (findings, figures, methods) Findings for citation FINDINGS.md (13 findings, each with its Wikipedia target) Maps World, India (official outline) and US state maps of over- and under-coverage Licence CC BY-NC 4.0 (attribution and a link required) Key findings Cybercrime's share of the news rose 2.15-fold, from 3.95 articles per 10,000 in 2019 to 8.5 in 2025, and rose in every year. December 2024 was the peak month: 12.14 cybercrime articles per 10,000 news articles. India's share of located cybercrime news (47.99%) is 3.64 times its share of all news; the United States' (16.5%) is 0.34 times. Cambodia (39.95), North Korea (19.54), Myanmar (14.85) and Thailand (6.1) are the most over-represented countries. Between 2023 and 2025, cybercrime's share of India's news rose from 19.81 to 33.3 per 10,000, and Pakistan's rose 4.3 times. 81.4% of cybercrime articles are negative in tone (all news: 33.6%); 86.2% are rated critical priority (all news: 42.6%). Place tags derived from ordinary words ("Congress", "Earth", "Winter") were treated as unlocated in every location field (15.3% of city-tagged articles). Paper and patent counts match titles. Full method: the research paper, §2. Limitations Part of the news index was offline when this release was built (92.88% of rows readable), so counts are lower bounds. Shares and lifts are less affected if the gap is spread evenly across topics. The index thins after May 2026. 2026 values (January–July) are partial. Indian outlets are numerous in the index, and Indian reports often name the "cyber crime" police unit in the opening, so India's share may be high partly by vocabulary. Place tags derived from ordinary words were treated as unlocated, which removed 15.3% of city-tagged articles; location shares are computed on what remains. The city field is still noisy, and some US state tags rest on surnames or brand names read as towns. Use country for geography. Tone, priority and themes are machine labels from the article opening. title: “A Study on Cybercrimes in Banking Sector: Views of Customers in Bengaluru City”
authors: Prof.Jalaja K R Prof.Jalaja K R; Chinmayi Shekar V; Indumathi B Indumathi B
venue: Journal of Research in Humanities and Social Science
abstract: Banking is the heart of India’s financial service sector. Banks today operate in a highly globalized, liberalized and a competitive environment. In order to survive in this environment banks have to use IT. Indian banking industry has witnessed a tremendous development due to sweeping changes that are taking place in the information technology. With the effect of Liberalization, Privatization and Globalization (LPG) and increased competition, innovations have been made in the banking sector to improve banking service quality. All these resulted in reforms of banking sector from paper transactions to e-transactions. Now customers are using plastic money, e-money rather than paper currency and banking system has also improved to a great extent, now it is customer centric era where customer is the king and services are to be delivered as per customer needs. 68% of Indian consumers are now using online or mobile banking to conduct financial transactions. So banks are facing the dual challenges of increasing penetration and high growth trajectory. Though IT brings lot of changes in banking sector which includes both Positive and Negative impacts in Banking one of the major threat present world is facing is Cybercrimes. In 2021, there were over 4.8 thousand cases of online banking frauds reported across India. This was a big increase in the number of banking fraud cases than the previous year.

title: Cyberbullying in Pakistan: Exploring Effects, Impacts and Strategies for Prevention
venue: Journal of Pakistan Administration
abstract: The study addresses the growing issue of cyberbullying in Pakistan, particularly with the rise in internet and social media use. It explores the psychological and emotional consequences of cyberbullying on victims, including anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts. The study also evaluates the effectiveness of Pakistan's legal frameworks, especially the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016, in combating online harassment. Despite PECA's existence, the study finds that its implementation faces challenges such as low conviction rates, difficulties in gathering digital evidence, and a lack of enforcement resources. Furthermore, cultural and societal factors, such as the stigma surrounding mental health, contribute to the underreporting of incidents. By comparing Pakistan’s situation with that of India and the United States, the research highlights the specific legal and societal challenges in Pakistan, offering recommendations for improving awareness, legal responses, and victim support systems. The study concludes that a more robust, adaptive legal framework, enhanced digital literacy programs, and greater cooperation among stakeholders are crucial to effectively tackle cyberbullying in Pakistan.

title: The Vigilant Public: Awareness, Skepticism, and Perceived Democratic Impact of AI-Generated Deepfakes Among Indian Voters
venue: International Journal of Communication Media and Linguistics
abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has made synthetic political media deepfakes and cheapfakes an increasingly salient concern for democratic communication. This study examines public awareness, perception, skepticism, and self-reported behavioral response to AI-generated political content among a diverse sample of 404 respondents. Using a structured survey instrument covering demographic profile, awareness, individual perception, decision-making impact, media skepticism, and democratic participation, the study finds near-universal awareness of AI (99.5%) but comparatively lower recognition of specific terminology such as ‘deepfake’ and ‘cheapfake’ (85.6%). One-sample chi-square goodness-of-fit tests confirm that response distributions on every attitude item depart significantly from chance (p < .001 in all but two cases), indicating that respondents hold clear, non-random positions rather than indifferent ones. Two-proportion z-tests show that respondents overwhelmingly agree that AI-generated media undermines the trustworthiness of political information (58.4% vs 31.2%, z = −5.27, p < .001), and that exposure has made them more cautious in decision-making (70.8% agreement, z = 14.40, p < .001). A recurring third-person pattern emerges: respondents report personal resilience to influence (61.9% say their own opinions are unaffected) while simultaneously reporting that AI-generated media erodes trust and discourages public dialogue at a societal level (69.8–73.0% agreement). The findings suggest a public that is highly aware but deeply skeptical, one that is adapting through heightened vigilance rather than blind acceptance, with clear implications for platform labeling policy, media literacy interventions, and electoral regulation. Keywords: artificial intelligence; Deepfakes; cheap fakes; political misinformation; voter perception; democratic participation

title: An Overview of Cyberbullying: Concepts, Indian Laws, and Intervention Programs for Children and Adolescents
authors: Prabhu James Ranjith; Mysore Narasimha Vranda; M. Thomas Kishore
venue: Indian Journal of Social Psychiatry
abstract: Concerns regarding children's mental health in India are increasing as the country's population grows. Bullying and cyberbullying among students is a prevalent issue that educational institutions are struggling to mitigate. Children and adolescents are especially affected by the negative impacts of cyberbullying. Numerous and continually evolving new technologies are used to harass people online. This study aims to explore the characteristics of cyberbullying, different laws of cyberbullying in India and abroad, and various interventions for cyberbullying. Therefore, this study creates awareness of cyberbullying among school counselors, teachers, school administrators, and researchers.

title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Detecting and Preventing Financial Scams in the Banking Sector
venue: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital banking and online payment platforms has transformed the banking sector by making financial transactions faster and more accessible. India has witnessed a sharp rise in technology-enabled financial scams alongside the growth of UPI, mobile wallets, and app-based banking. Reports indicate a significant increase in digital payment frauds, phishing attacks, and UPI-related scams in recent years, raising serious concerns over consumer safety and trust (The Economic Times, 2023)1. This growing incidence of cyber-enabled fraud has compelled banks to rely increasingly on Artificial Intelligence (AI) for fraud detection and prevention. However, despite technological advancement, customer confidence in digital banking systems remains fragile (Mint,2024)2. This study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence in detecting and preventing financial scams in the banking sector, with a focus on customer perception and usage behaviour. The article covers major scams such as phishing and spoofing attacks, OTP and UPI frauds, fake banking applications, identity theft, and social engineering–based financial frauds that are frequently reported in Indian media (The Times of India, 2023)3. Primary data were collected from 50 online application users who regularly conduct financial transactions through scheduled interview and analysed through descriptive statistical methods. The study concludes that AI-driven solutions must be complemented by robust regulatory frameworks, enhanced cybersecurity measures, and targeted financial literacy initiatives. Preventive measures such as advanced AI monitoring systems, multi-factor authentication, and continuous user awareness programs are suggested to strengthen customer confidence in digital banking systems.

title: AHIMSA IN THE ALGORITHM AGE: REVIVING NON-VIOLENCE AND KARMA FROM ANCIENT INDIAN TEXT TO PREVENT AND REMEDY DIGITAL HARMS IN CYBERCRIMES
venue: Transformative Education A Multidisciplinary Journal
abstract: In the algorithm age, where cybercrimes proliferate through AI-driven harms like deepfakes, algorithmic bias, and data breaches, ancient Indian principles of ahimsa (nonviolence) and karma (causal ethics) offer a profound framework for prevention and remediation. Revived from texts such as the Bhagavad Gita, Upanishads, and Arthashastra, these doctrines reframe digital violence as "severance of vitalities" encompassing not just physical injury but virtual erosions of agency, autonomy, and dignity. This paper explores ahimsa's legal transposition into cyberspace, advocating algorithms imbued with non-harm imperatives to mitigate discriminatory outcomes under India's Article 14 (equality) and Article 21 (dignity, as per Puttaswamy judgment). Karma's retributive logic underpins remedial mechanisms, aligning perpetrator traceability with IT Act 2000 provisions and emerging cyberlaw reforms, while rejecting Big Tech immunities akin to U.S. Section 230. By integrating Jain definitions of himsa with Maslow's needs hierarchy, we propose sovereign ethical audits for AI systems in smart cities and e-governance, fostering dharma-compliant designs that prioritize self-preservation and collective harmony. Such a synthesis empowers Dharmic communities to shape global standards, transcending Western utilitarianism for culturally resonant jurisprudence that curbs remote harms in autonomous vehicles and national IDs. Ultimately, embedding ahimsa-karma in code ensures karmic accountability, transforming punitive cyberlaws into proactive shields against digital adharma.

title: Comparative Analysis of National Frameworks Addressing AI-Driven Cybercrime
venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
abstract: This chapter provides a comparative analysis of national frameworks addressing AI-driven cybercrime across the European Union, United States, United Kingdom, Middle East, and Asia. It contrasts the EU's layered, risk-based regulatory model—integrating data protection, AI classification, and cybersecurity directives—with the United States' sector-specific and largely reactive enforcement approach. The UK's Online Safety regime illustrates a duty-of-care model emphasizing safety-by-design and ethical oversight, while Middle Eastern strategies, particularly in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, intertwine AI deployment with centralized state security priorities. In Asia, India and South Korea demonstrate hybrid models blending legacy cybercrime statutes with emerging AI governance mechanisms. The chapter highlights divergences in legal definitions, enforcement philosophies, and ethical safeguards, showing how regulatory variation affects compliance costs, innovation incentives, geopolitical alignment, and cross-border cooperation.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Cyber Fraud Prevention in Digital Banking: A Comparative Legal Analysis of India, the United Kingdom and the United States
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital banking has transformed the detection and prevention of financial fraud. Machine-learning algorithms, behavioural analytics, biometric authentication and automated transaction-monitoring systems enable financial institutions to identify suspicious activities at a scale that conventional rule-based systems may not achieve. However, the same technological developments have created new legal challenges, including algorithmic opacity, discriminatory outcomes, privacy risks, false-positive transaction blocking, and uncertainty concerning responsibility for AI-assisted decisions. Simultaneously, cybercriminals increasingly exploit AI to facilitate impersonation, phishing, synthetic identities and fraudulent payment instructions. This paper examines the legal and regulatory implications of AI-based cyber-fraud prevention in digital banking, with particular reference to India, the United Kingdom and the United States. It adopts a doctrinal and comparative legal methodology to analyse relevant cybercrime legislation, data-protection requirements, financial-sector regulation and institutional accountability. The paper argues that effective AI-based fraud prevention requires more than technological accuracy: financial institutions must also demonstrate lawful data processing, proportionate monitoring, appropriate human oversight, explainable decisions and accessible consumer remedies. It proposes a governance-oriented approach in which the deployment of AI is accompanied by documented risk assessments, independent validation, continuous monitoring and clear responsibility for adverse outcomes.

title: Awareness of Cyber Frauds Among Youth in India: A Review Based Study
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
abstract: In the modern digital era, the use of the internet, smartphones, online banking, social media, and digital payment systems has increased significantly among youth. While digital technology provides many benefits and convenience, it has also increased the risk of cyber fraud. Cyber fraud includes illegal online activities such as phishing, online scams, identity theft, hacking, and digital payment fraud. These activities can lead to financial loss, misuse of personal information, and security threats. The present study focuses on cyber fraud awareness among youth. The main objectives of the study are to understand awareness regarding cyber fraud, identify common types of cyber fraud, study the factors affecting cyber fraud awareness, and examine precautionary measures to reduce cyber fraud threats. The study is based on secondary data collected from research papers, journals, books, reports, and online sources related to cybercrime and cyber fraud. The findings of the study indicate that cyber fraud is increasing rapidly in the digital environment and youth are among the most affected users due to their frequent use of online platforms. The study also highlights that factors such as digital literacy, internet usage, and knowledge of cyber safety practices influence cyber fraud awareness. Safe online behavior, strong passwords, awareness of suspicious links, and proper cyber security practices can help reduce cyber fraud risks. The study concludes that improving cyber fraud awareness and promoting digital safety education are important steps for protecting youth from cyber threats and creating a safer digital environment

title: STOLEN FACES, SILENT VIOLATIONS: DEEPFAKE TECHNOLOGY AND THE CONSTITUTIONAL CRISIS OF CONSENT
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The face is not only a significant aspect of someone's identity now in the digital era, it is data. Artificial intelligence is now able to manipulate a facial image or a voice via the power of Artificial Intelligence to produce hyper-realistic fake content, such as a smile captured on a photo, a voice captured on a video or a facial expression uploaded on social media. A technological "experiment" that seemed to be part of the future rapidly has become a legal and constitutional issue. The perpetration of any image or video that is manipulated or fabricated is another problem that is far more dire: the loss of the consent, dignity, and personal autonomy of the individual. The deepfake technology employs artificial intelligence and machine learning to produce fake (but very realistic) sound and visual images of people. At first, it was created as a novelty and a means of inspiring innovation; now it is increasingly being used with the intent to harass, misinform, use for political manipulation, and for digital exploitation. The advent of the deepfake in India has brought in lacunas in the legal system especially regarding the constitutional safeguarding of privacy and dignity as enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution.

title: Cyberbullying in Pakistan: Legal Gaps, Gendered Harms, and Social Consequences in a Deepening Digital Environment
venue: Journal of Law & Social Studies
abstract: Cyberbullying has emerged as a significant socio-legal challenge in Pakistan, intensified by rapid digitalisation, increased internet accessibility, and widespread engagement with social media platforms. This study critically examines the multidimensional nature of cyberbullying, focusing on its psychological, social, and legal implications within the Pakistani context. Particular attention is given to the disproportionate impact on women and marginalised groups, driven by entrenched sociocultural norms, stigma, and systemic underreporting. The research evaluates Pakistan’s principal legislative framework, namely the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016, highlighting structural deficiencies in enforcement, evidentiary challenges, and persistently low conviction rates. Through a comparative lens, the study situates Pakistan’s experience within broader global patterns, identifying common regulatory and technological challenges in addressing cyberbullying across jurisdictions. Furthermore, the study explores the potential of emerging technological interventions, including artificial intelligence-based detection systems, alongside the role of educational initiatives, parental engagement, and media awareness in mitigating online abuse. The findings underscore the necessity for an integrated approach combining legal reform, institutional capacity-building, and socio-cultural transformation. The paper concludes by advocating for strengthened national frameworks aligned with international standards, enhanced digital literacy, and coordinated global cooperation to effectively combat cyberbullying and safeguard digital rights in Pakistan.

title: Regulation of Deepfakes, Identity Fraud and AI-Created Harms under New Penal Provisions
venue: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
abstract: Deepfakes, AI voice cloning and synthetic identities now sit at centre of digital risk landscape in India. These tools allow hyper realistic alteration of faces, bodies and voices, so they enable intimate image abuse, financial fraud and targeted political manipulation on huge scale. Recent Indian and comparative scholarship shows that such AI created harms strike directly at privacy, autonomy, reputation and even public trust in democratic processes. At same time, legal responses stay fragmented across Information Technology Act 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 and Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, none of which yet define deepfakes or synthetic media in express terms. This paper studies how new penal architecture should address deepfakes, identity fraud and wider AI created harms. It maps provisions on cheating, impersonation, obscenity, defamation, cyber offences and digital evidence under BNS and BSA and then tests their capacity against deepfake related misuse such as non-consensual pornography, fraud and political disinformation. The analysis is placed against proposals for dedicated Deepfake Prevention and Regulation framework in India and recent Deepfake Prevention and Criminalisation Bill introduced in Parliament. Doctrinal and comparative method is used to conceptualise “AI created harms” and “identity fraud,” to link them with victim consent, expectation of privacy and reputational interests. The paper finally argues that Indian penal policy must become victim centred and technologically informed while still respecting data protection guarantees and due process in investigations and trials. This paper argues that the current fragmented approach is inadequate. It proposes a unified, victim oriented regulatory framework. That integrates criminal law, data protection and intermediary responsibility. Such an approach is necessary to ensure both effective enforcement and protection of fundamental rights.

title: Artificial Lies, Constitutional Truths: Deepfakes and the Future of Free Expression
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: In India, the constitutional discourse surrounding freedom of speech and expression has been significantly disrupted by the rapid advancement of digital technology and artificial intelligence. The right to freedom of speech and expression, guaranteed under Article 19(1) (a) of the Constitution of India, is premised upon the availability of truthful information, informed public participation, and the preservation of democratic dialogue. However, the exponential spread of false, misleading, and manipulated content through online platforms has posed serious challenges to these foundational values. Among the most concerning manifestations of this technological shift is the rise of deepfakes, artificial intelligence-generated audio, video, or visual content that is deceptively altered to appear genuine. By mimicking voices, faces, and actions with increasing realism, deep fakes possess the capacity to mislead the public, distort public perception, damage reputations, manipulate electoral discourse, and undermine trust in authentic media sources. In this sense, deepfakes do not merely constitute false information; they threaten the broader concept of informational integrity upon which meaningful freedom of expression depends. This article examines the emerging legal and constitutional dilemma in India, where the protection of free speech as a fundamental right must be balanced against the pressing need to preserve information integrity, public order, and democratic accountability. While free expression remains central to constitutional governance, its misuse through technologically fabricated content raises legitimate concerns regarding deception, privacy violations, defamation, and societal harm. The paper further analyses how the accelerated growth of artificial intelligence and digital communication technologies has complicated traditional understandings of speech regulation. It argues that deepfakes represent a new frontier of legal concern requiring a nuanced regulatory response that safeguards legitimate expression while preventing malicious manipulation. Ultimately, the study highlights the urgent need for legal reforms, platform accountability, and technological safeguards to ensure that innovation does not erode the constitutional values of truth, dignity, and democratic discourse.

title: The Mediating Role of Digital Literacy Between Financial Literacy and Investment Scam Awareness
authors: G. Mithila; Lingesiya Kengatharan; V. Sinthujakanna
venue: International Journal of Accounting and Business Finance
abstract: This study analyses whether digital literacy mediates the relationship between financial literacy and investment scam awareness. Despite the rapid expansion of digital financial services, there remains limited knowledge of whether financial and digital literacy interact to shape resistance to online investment scams. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among undergraduates who were selected through stratified random sampling in Sri Lanka. Financial literacy is measured through budgeting skills, financial attitude, financial product literacy and risk awareness. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was applied to estimate the direct effects and mediating effects. Budgeting skills, product literacy and risk awareness enhance digital literacy, while financial attitude shows no meaningful effect. Digital literacy exhibits the strongest direct influence on investment scam awareness. Mediation analysis confirms that digital literacy transmits the effects of budgeting skills, product literacy and risk awareness to scam awareness, whereas financial attitude remains non-significant. The study conceptualizes digital literacy as a coping appraisal mechanism that enables individuals to operationalize financial knowledge in digital financial environments. Guided by Protection Motivation Theory, the study interprets financial literacy as supporting threat appraisal and digital literacy as supporting coping appraisal. The single institution, cross-sectional and self-reported design may restrict generalizability and causal inference. Future studies should use multi-site samples, longitudinal designs, fraud simulation experiments.

title: Regulation of Artificial Intelligence, Deepfakes and Liability under the Information Technology Act, 2000
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
abstract: Deepfakes reveal a gap between harm that is obvious to the senses and blame that can be attributed. Stating the law as on 13 October 2026, this article analyses India’s Information Technology Act, 2000 and the amended intermediary rules, along with the relevant constitutional and personality-rights case law. By way of doctrinal analysis, it distinguishes the elements of offences from regulatory obligations to prevent harm, from the conditions of intermediary exemption and from civil remedies. The amendments of February 2026 establish synthetic-content labelling, provenance requirements and differentiated takedown deadlines, yet do not turn every failure to comply into criminal liability. While existing laws cover a number of the fraudulent impersonation and sexual exploitation elements inherent in these cases, wholly synthetic intimate imagery, the evidentiary attribution of content to a particular person and parallel access to remedies remain difficult. The analysis therefore proceeds on a differentiated account of responsibility, in which the conduct, knowledge, control and available immunity of each participant are addressed separately once an underlying wrong has been identified. It advocates clear, tailored guidance, proportionate verification and victim-centred processes, as opposed to blanket developer liability. Regulation is effective only with responsible attribution, not merely with the rapid removal of content or the disclosure of synthetic origin.
