title: Examining the Escalation of Cybercrimes Against Women and Children in India: A Critical Analysis of the COVID-19 Period (2019-2021)
venue: Leadership Education Personality An Interdisciplinary Journal
abstract: In the face of an ever-evolving digital landscape, cybercrimes have emerged as a pervasive threat, encompassing offenses committed using computers, the internet, and electronic technologies. Despite the enactment of the Information Technology Act in 2000, designed to define and safeguard citizens against virtual criminals, the incidence of cybercrimes in India has not abated. This research paper delves into the alarming escalation of cybercrimes against women and children, a demography particularly vulnerable in the digital sphere, during the critical period of the COVID-19 pandemic (2019-2021). This study examines state-wise data on cybercrimes against women and children, categorizing their types, prevalence, and rates of chargesheet filings and convictions. It also explores the complex factors behind the rising cybercrime rates and the stark contrast with India's low conviction rates.

title: Navigating the Emergence of Deepfake Technologies and its Legal Regulations: A Critical Analysis of This Legal Complexity for Synthetic Media with Special Reference to Human Rights Violation
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract: In the era of Artificial Intelligence ‘deepfake technology’ is one of the most vulnerable software; by using this Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) software, the wrongdoer can convert or replace the original images and audio into a fake one. This technology gaining popularity from 20th century, sometime provides some benefits in various sectors in education, customer service, public awareness etc. Due to deepfake technology, a wrong message circulates in the air, and also various kinds of threats come forth, e.g., cyber defamation, harassment, blackmailing, fulfilling political agendas, threats to national securities, etc. The Ministry of Electronics & IT (MeitY) has been taking various regulatory initiatives to address these issues. The IT Act, 2000, DPDPA, 2023, BNS, 2023 covers some portion related about cybercrimes. The Indian Cyber Security Threat Report, 2025, the rapid development of social engineering technology is making it easier to make manipulating content, fake audio and videos. The DFDC dataset is also recognised as a standard dataset for deepfake detection. But till now no fixed laws and sufficient laws regarding this. This worse invention not only violate the constitutional mandates such as right to privacy (Art 21), also hampers human rights of the individuals. In this paper the researcher will address the national framework also do a comprehensive study of some developing nations such as USA, UK and China. This study limited to doctrinal method and aims to contribute some recommendation about the ongoing discourse of misuse especial focus on human rights violation and right to privacy.

title: Deepfake Technology, Misinformation and Media Regulation: Emerging Trends and Challenges
venue: Naveen International Journal of Multidisciplinary Sciences (NIJMS)
abstract: Deepfake technology has moved from a niche computer vision experiment to a mainstream concern for journalism, electoral processes, and public discourse. Synthetic audio, video, and images now circulate alongside genuine reporting, and the boundary between the two grows thinner each year. This article studies the rise of deepfakes, their entanglement with misinformation, and the regulatory responses unfolding across India, the European Union, and the United States. It draws on a dataset of 2,223 peer-reviewed and preprint publications in Communication and Media Studies retrieved from Dimensions for the period 2017 to 2026, supported by VOSviewer co-authorship maps and citation analysis. The piece blends qualitative discussion with a light bibliometric reading of the field. The analysis shows publication output rising sharply after 2019, climbing from 46 records in 2019 to 768 in 2025, with India contributing 111 papers and ranking second globally after the United States. Scholarly attention concentrates on misinformation, social media platforms, journalism, and democracy, while regulation, governance, and law receive less coverage. The article argues for four planks of a workable response: platform accountability, mandatory labelling, source verification, and media literacy. The findings point to a research gap on enforcement, cross-border coordination, and the position of small language communities in detection systems. The piece closes with directions for further work. Keywords: Deepfake, Synthetic media, Misinformation, Fake news, Platform accountability.

title: Cyber Fraud in Online Trading: A Critical Analysis of Regulatory Frameworks and Investigative Challenges in India
authors: Deep Dubey and Dr. Ram Kumar Sahu
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
abstract: The rapid digitalization of the Indian financial sector has led to an exponential increase in online trading, which has simultaneously exposed investors to sophisticated cyber-fraud mechanisms In 2020 alone, India reported approximately 1.16 million cyberattack cases, reflecting a growing vulnerability in the digital economy This research provides a critical analysis of the current regulatory frameworks, primarily governed by the Information Technology Act of 2000 and the Securities and Exchange Board of India guidelines, to assess their effectiveness in protecting retail investors .The study identifies significant investigative hurdles, including jurisdictional complexities, an overlap between the Indian Penal Code and the IT Act, and a shortage of technical expertise within law enforcement agencies . By evaluating recent stockbroking frauds and enforcement lapses, the paper concludes with policy recommendations aimed at strengthening judicial procedures and enhancing technological capabilities for fraud detection.

title: Cyberbullying Victimization and Psychological Distress: Mediating Role of Loneliness
venue: IGI Global eBooks
abstract: Cyberbullying is a major psychosocial risk for young adults, linked to adverse mental health outcomes. The study examined loneliness as a mediator between cyberbullying victimization and psychological distress among undergraduates in Northern India. A cross-sectional survey was conducted, and 427 students who reported cyberbullying victimization were included. Cyberbullying was measured using the Cyber-Bullying and Victimization Experiences Questionnaire, loneliness by the UCLA Loneliness Scale and psychological distress by the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale. Mediation analysis showed cyberbullying victimization was significantly associated with both loneliness and psychological distress. Loneliness also significantly predicted psychological distress. Additionally, loneliness partially mediated the relationship between cyberbullying and psychological distress, indicating both direct and indirect effects. These findings underscore loneliness as a key psychosocial mechanism and highlight the need for interventions targeting cyberbullying and social isolation among undergraduates.

title: Cyberbullying Victimization and Interpersonal Communication Satisfaction among Pakistani University students: Examining the Mediating Role of Self-Esteem
authors: Naveed Abbas; Denaz Satti; Dr. Ulfat Nisa
venue: Social science review archives.
abstract: Background: Digital communication is now central to university life in the world, especially in Pakistan, and it emerged cyberbullying as an increasing psychosocial concern among students. Aim: This study explored how being targeted online relates to students' satisfaction with their interpersonal communication, and also examining the mediating role of self-esteem. Method: A quantitative correlational research design was employed and collected data from 200 university students, who completed standardized self-report measures of cyberbullying victimization, self-esteem, and communication satisfaction. Pearson correlations, multiple regression, and a mediation analysis were conducted to examine the proposed hypotheses. Results: The findings reflected that cyberbullying victimization was negatively correlated with interpersonal communication satisfaction (r = -.15, p <.05), showing that students with higher cyberbullying victimization expressed lower interpersonal communication satisfaction. Cyberbullying victimization was negatively linked with self-esteem (r = -.14), but this association was not statistically significant. Self-esteem showed a positive but non-significant relationship with interpersonal communication satisfaction (r = .05). Multiple regression analysis demonstrated that cyberbullying victimization significantly predicted interpersonal communication satisfaction (β = - .15, p = .039), while self-esteem was non-significant in predictor (β = .03, p = .690). Overall regression model was not statistically significant and described 2.4% of the variance in interpersonal communication satisfaction (R2 = .024, F(2,197) = 2.40, p = .093). Additionally, Mediation analysis revealed that self-esteem did not mediate the association between cyberbullying victimization and interpersonal communication satisfaction because the indirect effect was not significant (β = -.014, 95% CI (-.126, .049). Conclusion: The results explain that cyberbullying victimization has a negative but significant relationship with interpersonal communication satisfaction. Although, self-esteem does not work as mediator in this association. The present study adds empirical evidence within the context of Pakistani culture and suggest to explore further psychological and social factors that may describe the outcome of cyberbullying on students’ interpersonal communication.

title: CYBERBULLYING IN THE DIGITAL AGE: LEGAL CHALLENGES AND SOLUTIONS
venue: International journal of engineering science & humanities.
abstract: The digital age has seen a rise in cyberbullying, a form of online harassment that has serious negative effects on the mental health of victims. Its characteristics, such as anonymity and wide scope, make it difficult to combat. The same faces enforcement challenges due to a lack of specific definitions, and jurisdictional conflicts persist. Comprehensive legislation, harmonised international standards, increased law enforcement cooperation, and legal assistance to victims play an imperative role in addressing it. This paper highlights the crucial role of digital literacy in curbing this global issue and further outlines the laws adopted by different jurisdictions to guide efforts to eliminate it. Furthermore, it discusses the active steps taken by the Indian judiciary and the legislature's concern about eliminating this issue.

title: From conventional cyberstalking to AI-driven automated sextortion: A socio-legal analysis of AI-enabled sexual exploitation against women and children in India and the emerging challenges of digital modesty, consent, online safeguarding, and regulatory governance
venue: International Journal of Law Justice and Jurisprudence
abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has fundamentally transformed the digital ecosystem, creating unprecedented opportunities for innovation while simultaneously facilitating sophisticated forms of cybercrime. Among the emerging technology-enabled offences, AI-driven automated sextortion has become one of the most alarming threats to women and children due to its capacity to generate synthetic intimate content, automate online grooming, manipulate digital identities, and facilitate large-scale cyber-enabled sexual exploitation. Unlike conventional cyberstalking, which relied primarily on repeated online harassment, surveillance, and intimidation through digital communication, AI-powered technologies such as deepfakes, voice cloning, facial recognition, generative artificial intelligence, and automated chatbots have expanded the scope, speed, and impact of cyber-enabled offences. These developments have challenged traditional legal concepts relating to privacy, modesty, consent, dignity, and criminal liability, exposing significant gaps within existing legal and regulatory frameworks. The present study adopts a doctrinal and socio-legal approach to examine the transformation of conventional cyberstalking into AI-driven automated sextortion with particular reference to women and children in India. The paper critically analyses the adequacy of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and other relevant legal instruments in addressing AI-enabled sexual exploitation. It further examines international regulatory developments relating to artificial intelligence governance and platform accountability to identify comparative best practices.

title: Cyber Harassment in Journalism: Effects on Self-Censorship on Mental Health of Female Journalists in the Pakistani Media Landscape
venue: Lahore Institute for Research and Analysis Journal
abstract: The issue of cyber harassment towards numerous female journalists in Pakistan is gaining prevalence leading to self-censorship and mental health concerns among them. The current study investigates the pervasive issue of online harassment targeting female journalists in Pakistan using the spiral of silence theory as its lens. It aims to analyze the impact of online harassment on female journalists' tendencies toward self-censorship and its implications for their well-being. Adopting a quantitative methodology, the study employs a close-ended survey administered to female journalists from diverse urban centers. A purposive sampling technique has been used and correlation analysis has been conducted to examine the relationship between online harassment, self-censorship and mental well-being. Findings from this research have shown that a high percentage of women journalists are harassed through online harassment daily, though these women journalists contribute significantly to the flourishing media sector in Pakistan. However, many respondents showed reluctance in reporting the harassment incidents. Online harassment also depicts an alarming trend, since a majority of the women journalists who experienced harassment wish to leave journalism altogether due to the negative effects brought by online harassment. These findings underscore the urgency of interventions to address and mitigate the impact of online harassment on female journalists.

title: Strengthening Human Rights and Social Justice through Digital Governance: A National Framework for Addressing Technology-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence (TFGBV) in Pakistan
venue: Qlantic journal of social sciences.
abstract: The digitalization of Pakistan has outgrown the significance of institutional framework required to safeguard citizens, especially women and gender minorities, against technology-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV). With greater connectivity, there's been cyber harassment, image-based abuse without consent, and AI-driven deepfake abuse, highlighting a growing divide between digital opportunity and security. Regardless of this, Pakistan has not established a coordinated institutional framework to support the realization of the law for survivors, particularly the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016 and the addition of its amendment in 2025. This article attempts to explore the extent and nature of TFGBV, assess the responses of the Pakistani government and the country's legal and institutional framework, compare it with the other countries including South Korea, Australia, the United Kingdom and the European Union, and recommend TFGBV National Coordination Framework. The study, based on the qualitative documents analysis, comparative case studies and policy analysis, reveals that there is a major shortcoming in the criminal law in Pakistan, which is lack of institutional responsibility. There are seven or more agencies with overlapping and poorly coordinated mandates and a conviction rate of about 3.5 percent, and this compromises survivors' trust. The article advocates a single empowered coordination cell tailored to the institutional and financial environment in Pakistan. Notably, the Ministry of Human Rights and the UNDP’s National Strategy to Address TFGBV (2026-2030) independently align on a similar model of coordination cell.

title: Digital Evidence In Cybercrime Investigation: Challenges Under The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023
abstract: This study explores the admissibility of digital evidence under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, with particular emphasis on the legal and practical challenges involved in its implementation within the Indian judicial system. Employing a doctrinal research methodology, the study examines relevant statutory provisions, judicial precedents, and academic literature to evaluate the evolving framework governing electronic evidence. It analyses critical aspects such as the authentication of digital records, certification requirements, maintenance of the chain of custody, and the significance of digital forensic techniques in establishing evidentiary credibility. The research also assesses the implications of emerging technologies, including cloud computing and encryption, on the collection, preservation, and admissibility of electronic evidence. The findings suggest that although the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 represents a significant step towards modernising the law of evidence by formally recognising electronic records, several practical concerns, including inadequate technical expertise, infrastructural limitations, and procedural complexities, continue to impede its effective implementation. The study concludes that a balanced framework combining robust legal safeguards with technological innovation is essential for ensuring the reliability and effectiveness of digital evidence in judicial proceedings.

title: Transnational Cybercrime Jurisdiction under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023: Mapping the Gap Between Substantive Reach and Procedural Enforcement
venue: Jus Corpus Law Journal
abstract: Cybercrime is often considered naturally transnational: ransomware servers may be located in one country, the victim in another, and the data flows through a third.In recent years, we have seen that India as a nation has adopted the Bhartiya Nagrik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), but still, the territorial assumption regarding the jurisdiction and trial of the case depends upon the Code of Criminal Procedure Act 1973.Various laws, such as the extraterritorial provisions of the IT Act 2000, in the Indian legal system still struggle to have effective provisions that deal with cybercrime that has taken place outside Indian Jurisdiction.In this article, we will map out the jurisdictional void across investigation, trial, and enforcement outcomes against offenders who are abroad.We will also evaluate the procedures of BNSS and address these gaps effectively using these procedures.Our main objective will be to conduct a critical analysis of the matter to formulate a framework combining statutory amendments, treaty accession, and institutional capacity building.

title: CROSS-BORDER JURISDICTION AND ILLEGAL ONLINE GAMBLING PLATFORMS: EXAMINING REGULATORY CHALLENGES IN INDIA
authors: D Asir Antony Gnana Singh; Mohan, Harshit
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Within the Indian context, the Information Technology Act, 2000, along with allied cyber regulatory frameworks, provides an important legal basis for examining digital platform activities and cyber-enabled transactions. However, the application of these frameworks to cross-border online gambling platforms continues to involve evolving jurisdictional and enforcement-related considerations (CKS, 2024). This paper adopts a doctrinal research methodology to examine the jurisdictional and regulatory challenges associated with illegal online gambling platforms operating across borders. The study analyses the interaction between cyber law, intermediary platforms, and cross-border jurisdictional principles while maintaining a neutral and analytical legal perspective.

title: Digital Identity Theft and Online Trademark Fraud in India: Rethinking Cyber Governance at the Intersection of Technology and Intellectual Property
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The proliferation of electronic trade in India has changed the notion of commercial identification. Domain names, social networking profiles, electronic store fronts, and electronic identities have become essential factors in verifying legitimacy and origin. Any abuse of such electronic identifications constitutes not only cyber-fraud but also trademark violations. Nevertheless, Indian laws cover these crimes in isolation, namely, under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Trade Marks Act, 1999. This paper explores the relationship between digital identity fraud and electronic trademark violation, reviewing the statutes, jurisprudence, and policy considerations, and making recommendations for a unified regulation of digital markets.

title: The Evidentiary Crisis of the Digital Age: AI-Generated Deepfakes and the Fragility of Judicial Truth-Finding
authors: Akbar ali Datoo; Muhammad Owais Rabbani; Syed Razi Hasnain; Waleed Ahmed Khan
venue: The Critical Review of Social Sciences Studies
abstract: The emergence of AI-generated deepfakes represents a fundamental disruption to the evidentiary foundations of modern criminal justice systems. This article examines how synthetic media technologies capable of producing hyper-realistic audio and video content indistinguishable from authentic recordings undermine long-standing assumptions about the reliability of audiovisual evidence. Drawing on criminological theory, comparative legal analysis, and empirical case studies, the article argues that deepfakes precipitate an evidentiary crisis that transcends traditional concerns about evidence tampering. Unlike conventional forms of manipulation that leave detectable traces, deepfakes can be generated as entirely synthetic artifacts with no corresponding real-world event, collapsing the evidentiary framework built on the premise that falsification occurs subsequent to an authentic original. The article analyzes the "liar's dividend" phenomenon, whereby the mere existence of deepfake technology enables plausible denial of authentic evidence, and examines how this dynamic complicates investigations, prosecutions, and judicial decision-making. It further considers the disproportionate impact on developing jurisdictions with limited forensic capacity, using Pakistan as a case study to illustrate the institutional and doctrinal vulnerabilities that exacerbate the evidentiary challenges posed by synthetic media. The article concludes by advocating for heightened authentication standards, specialized judicial training, and the development of forensic protocols capable of restoring confidence in digital evidence without compromising due process protections.

title: CYBERBULLYING AMONG TEENAGERS: LEGAL REMEDIES AND SOCIAL CONSEQUENCES
venue: LawFoyer International Journal of Doctrinal Legal Research.
abstract: CYBERBULLYING AMONG TEENAGERS: LEGAL REMEDIES AND SOCIAL CONSEQUENCES Vaishnavi Saxena, B. Com LL.
